Title: Raw piece of paradise
Text:
Just wrapped up eight days in Sri LankaÂs Arugam Bay - a rather rare part of the world in that itÂs still relatively raw and untouched by commercialization and development. It truly is a surferÂs paradise, with a main point in Arugam Bay itself and various others within 15-20 minutes by Tuk Tuk. We spent most of our time at Whiskey Point as that was where the swell was best Â we visited in early June. The beach is also spacious at that point and offers a lot of room to throw a towel down and swim/surf. Not much else though so would not recommend to stay near there. Arugam Bay is definitely where itÂs at as there are restaurants/cafes and a few bars. 

Some points to make:

This destination is about surfing, yoga and chilling. ThereÂs waves for all kinds of riders and many day trips on offer - safari, jungle, etc. ItÂs crucial to go during the right season though. I imagine most restaurants and places are closed otherwise, which would be a shame as youÂd not get to explore this lovely place for what it is - a dream for many travelers! 

ThereÂs not much of a beachfront; itÂs filled with boats and so you probably wonÂt spend much time laying on the beach in A Bay. This didnÂt bother us as we were busy surfing and then catching a break in the room mid day. But I can see some people putting up a fuss over this so figured itÂs worth a mention. If you want to sunbathe a lot, stay somewhere with a pool. 

The mornings and evenings are lovey but it does get pretty hot & sweaty in the afternoon. Do yourself a favor and make sure you get a room with A/C. Nothing like being able to chill out in a cool room after a busy morning out on the beach or riding around. 

The area is predominantly Muslim so there are a lot of limitations on alcohol availability. You canÂt get beer or hard alcohol at that many places - maybe 3 to 4 spots along the main strip. Only one bottle shop with actual hard liquor (down a road at the end of Arugam Bay where there is a holiday inn sign) and one with beer (MeenaÂs) to buy your own. IÂd suggest packing a bottle if you wanna enjoy drinks in your room or whatever where youÂre staying. Def places to grab cocktails though so no sweat if you just want a rum and coke here and there. This is something I wish I knew in advance - def wouldÂve liked to have my own supply for my room and by the pool in the afternoon or evening! That being said, Arugam Bay is cheap and the cocktails will only cost you like $3-$5 at the bars that have them so you can drink to your heartÂs desire even on a budget. Hideaway ResortÂs Bar has great cocktails. Spice Trail bar has wine and bubbles (by the bottle) - both are next to each other. 

Last thing: we split our stay between two places .. Bay Vista, with a beach view and balcony .. and Spice Trail, which had a pool. This was such a good combo. We loved sitting on our balcony and enjoying the beach views for a few days. But it was equally enjoyable to go for a refreshing dip in the pool when we moved resorts. Both in the best location as well. All in all, we had an awesome trip with loads of surfing & lots of down time to chill and read. ItÂs a very mellow and chilled out place so definitely go expecting that kinda vibe. Happy surfing ??

Also, photo attached for transport service we used. Very comfortable and efficient for journey to Arugam from Colombo. Sanju is a great guy!

Text:
Arugam Bay is an amazingly overrated surf spot. Surfwise expect a slightly above average wave with 100-300 drunk idiots in the lineup on main point with 0 etiquette from dusk till dawn. Title: Off season in Arugam bay
Text:
Just back from Sri Lanka, where I spent 2 nights in Arugam bay. Even though I knew it was not the peak season in the east of the country,I never expected it to be so quiet. I think it was a combination of being off season and Covid, that had the place looking like a ghost town.  There were very few restaurants and bars open while we were there and the streets were deserted after 8pm. It didnt help that there were power cuts also happening and lots of places had no electricity, which made it eerie walking home in the darkness.
In saying all that, we stayed in the Spice trail which was a great choice and the people were very friendly. They also arranged a safari trip to Kumana park, which is only a 45 min journey away and we saw lots of animals, with very little other people around. The beach is a real working beach with lots of fishing boats along the shore constantly going in and out with their catches. So dont expect a beach with lovely stretches of sand with plenty of sun loungers. Its not that type of beach.
I would certainly like to visit again when its peak season, to really see this place at its best and then make a better judgement.

Title: Surf is epic, place is too busy...
Text:
The wave at main point on its day is truly world class and so easy to surf! If you can get one ...the wave is incredibly busy due to its ease of paddling out and take off. The town itself was pretty busy and akin to other westernised Asian countries, bars blaring out loud music till all hours of the morning on the weekends. We had a car so stayed a few miles out of town for most of the trip in Papermoon which was very nice and also staying on the point at Upalis was an awesome experience! Also there are some great restaurants in Arugam Hideaway and thaththas roti shop were by far the highlights! 

The local wildlife is incredible drive a km out of town at sunrise and sunset and you will see dozens of elephants crocodiles and amazing bird life! Lagoon Safari is a must!

Overall we had a great time as the waves were consistently amazing every morning! But Arugam itself left a lot to be desired and is definitely one for the backpackers and party goers.

Title: WORLD BEST SURFING BREAK
Text:
Arugam Bay is a bay situated on the Indian Ocean in the dry zone of Sri Lanka's southeast coast. The bay is located 320 kilo meters due east of Colombo, and approximately 4 kilo meters south of the market town of Pottuvil.

The Arugam Bay area is home to a number of quality surf breaks, the most popular of which being 'Main Point' located towards the south of the bay. This is a right hand point break, with a rock/reef bottom, and has a number of sections with occasional barrels. Other breaks in the area include Whiskey Point and Pottuvil Point to the north, and Elephant Rock, Peanut Farm and Okanda to the south. These breaks have attracted a steady stream of international tourists for several decades. Arugam Bay has a good local surf scene and is home to some of Sri Lanka's most talented surfers. In recent years surfers from Arugam Bay have dominated national competitions.

Title: Caching the moonlit surf
Text:
The first time I visited Arugam Bay was back in 1994, when the Sri Lankan civil war  was at full tilt, and visits to the East coast were by the foolhardy or do or die surfers from Australia.

 it was just before christmas that year, when about 7 of us, in two vehicles, left Colombo early one cool December morning, and took the road to first Ratnapura, and then turned Eastwards on the Embilipitiya road to Arugam Bay. It took much of the day to reach there, as the roads were B roads, badly maintained, full of snaking twists and turns.The saving grace was the breathtaking scenery: we passed waterfalls, rice paddies, and sleepy vilages and towns until we reached Moneragala, the nearest large town to Pottuvil and the Bay. We had a late lunch at the Rest House there.
From here on, it was the war zone, The road was deserted, except for the odd bus and trucks carrying produce. Checkpoints, manned by army mostly , dotted the road.We had to stop and show our IDs inumerable times. From Siyabalanduwa onwards the checkpoints were manned by the Special Task Force, STF, the paramilitary special ops force that policed the East Coast.Tension was in the air. The checkpoint personnel were monosyllabic, surly at times, with red-rimmed eyes, pointing to sleepless nights and a lot of stress.Although the LTTE had not mounted a big operation in the East coast that year, there were small incursions al the time. I drunk it all in-the tension went hand in hand with the dark green foliage of the dense forests on either side of this road. If we got blown up on this road, it was all worth it-died on the road to Arugam Bay, chasing a wave, what an epitah, I thought.
When we passed Siyambaladuwa, the vegetation began to change.It was no longer wet zone tropical but dry zone, with its spiky foliage, a more yellowish colour, smaller leaves, and sparser.And the heat began to ratchet up.There were landscapes of green rice paddy fields stretching to the horizon on both sides of the road now. Occasionally there were small tractors trundling on the road. More checkpoints.
Then we reached Lahugala Forest Reserve, which was by the road, from which one was supposed to see Elephant herds snacking on the lush grass of the tank bed there. We stopped, and there were a couple of Grey Ghosts there. Their trunks swayed as they tore up the grass.It was our first sight of the magic of the jungles here, and well worth the 8-hour drive. It was getting towards dusk, and we had get off this road before the light went.
The road now was really bad, pot holed and very small, untouched since the 1950s , it seemed. On both sides were dry paddies and salterns, streching to the horizons. The road didnt allow for a speed in excess of 10 mph:it seemed quicker to walk, but we would probably get shot by the STF, who were probably patrolling out somewhere out there.
The final checkpoint was reached, when we got to Pottuvil, the dusty, one road, one horse - million tractor little town which would be immortalised in our minds as Potters. We stopped for a while in Potters, drinking in the sights while slaking our tea habit in a tea boutique. A town of bycycles and tractors, and rusty, beaten up up vans and STF soldiers carrying T-56 automatics. We had stocked up with fresh veggies and food in Moneragala, as wher we were headed to had a cook.There was only one hotel/guest house  in the Bay, the Stardust hich was owned by a Danish couple who had been here ages.But they charged major bucks for rooms.I and two friends, a couple, were going to stay in the run down guest house owned by a family friend. The others, another couple an their teenage son would stay in the Stardust.
There was a glorious sunset dying as we crossed the bridge into the Bay.The winds blowing from the sea promised something, maybe crab curries and grilled prawns.
The Stardust was immediately identifiable, set back on the left in its neat sandy grounds, a sold white building, with some small cabanas out facing the sea. We were in the Hideaway, a ramshackle old building, hidden away in a mass of Bourganvillea and some scattered coconut trees. It was run by a very dodgy caretaker, who met us smoking a cheroot, dressed in a sarong, and very suspicious of these dusty, sweaty oiks from Colombo, with a white girl in tow. After some preliminary sparring, he agreed to let us stay in the rooms upstairs.There were cabanas, but they were falling down, rat and mosquito infested, he said.
The owner of the Hideaway was involved in a court case trying to get rid of the caretaker, who had a reputation of using the place for prostitution and drugs. Arugam bay always had great rep for the best grass in Sri Lanka: I wanted to do some inhaling while I was there, i was all part of the package.
Problem-there was no cook:we would have to do our own dinner. Of all of us, I had the most experience of cooking, my friends were in the fry-ups, toast and cereal brigade.I got them slicing and dicing, and we had brought some chicken, which I managed to get into a semblance of a curry. The other layabouts did a salad, and we tucked in after a shower in our rickety rooms, which had  fans and mossie nets. No crabs and prawns tonight, but we were too tired to care, and after dinner we headed of to the Stardust down the road, the night starlit and still.
After several ice cold beers,and lots of chat , making plans for the days ahead we called it and staggered back, nearly dissappearing into some of the potholes on the road.

I collapsed on my bed, arranging the mossie net as well as I could and left for noddieland. 

I was woken up suddenly by what seemed to be the apocalypse breaking over the bay.It was World War Three:the bulding was shaking, there were flares lighting up the outside, and I could see tracer fire acing into the night,The noise was horrendous.Convinced I was going to die imminently, I ran next door to where my friends were, and leaped into their room. They were under the bed. I joined them.
"What the hell is going on?", my pal's English girlfriend yelled, as another mortar seemed to alight in the garden, shaking the paper thin walls.
"I think the Tigers are coming, J-, and I want you to surrender to them, seeing you are a tourist you'll;;be okay and as we are together they wont kill us" said my pal ,her boyfriend.Always thinking ahead my buddy R-.
I really wished I had eaten a crab curry and got hold of some Bay weed tonight:atl east I would have gone out with great memories. I thought of my mum back in Colombo, an all the things I hadnt done yet, the women I hadnt dated yet, the music I hadnt heard, the cars, I hadnt driven, the countries I hadnt been to,a long long Bucket list.
Then, as suddenly as it had begun, the fireworks stopped. 
We crawled out, shaken and well stirred, and looked out at he darkness.The Hideaway had no power anyway, so  it was dark everywhere.No sign of life, no signs of Tigers walking up the path, nothing. The stillness of the night returned, and even the cicadas began to chirp cautiously.It was around 3 am.
We opened some scotch to celebrate being alive, and went back to bed.
The next morning, we asked the first SF guy we saw what had happened. He laughed, albeit rather hysterically, I thought.
"Oh, that?Nothing to worry about, we were just getting rid of our old ammo stocks before the New year" he said walking away quickly.
Dumbfounded, we looked at each other and chalked it up to more of inimitable Sri Lankan humour.
The next few days were idyllic:we pickniked in a green dale beyond which we saw a hoard of copulating turtles, their shells glistening in the sun, saw ancient temples on beaches,saw Elephants and Buffalos together on th roadside, and visited Kudumbigala rock monastery, where the silence of millennia ruled the heights and meditation caves, the haunt of Bear and Leopard. We body surfed in some forgotten cove where the fish nibbled at our toes , and visited deserted, empty beaches running for miles., visited the hushed grandeur of Radella tank, where forest giants stalked the bund.
 I got my crab curry but no hash, which I got on another trip. Over it all lay the feeling of a frontier, a place forgotten by time and the hordes  of the  20th century. 
I have been to Arugam bay many times since then,  caught the surf one full moon night,but the world has changed:Gone are the checkpoints, the palpable taste of danger and tension in the air,Gone too are most of the Elephants. But Kudumbigala monastery remains the same, human history nothing but a blip in its millennial count, its caves a silent reminder of eternity.

The Hideaway is now a thriving resort, famous for its food, and the Stardust is still there,, although the Danish Manager was swept away in the  grea Tsunami of 2003. There are a host of small hotels and guesthouses, and the surfing is now on global to-do lists by all surfers.The jungles are still there, now dwindling sadly.The 21st century has come to the Bay.

But the feeling of a frontier is still there,although our experience was quite special.Perhaps you have to be Sri Lankan to realise we saw a frontier just before it began to change. When what we got couldnt be charged to a credit card or to a wad of dollars.

To paraphrase  the Roman Pliny we "watched the cold star Saturn, and saw honey come out of the air at the rising of the Dog-star just before the dawn." 

 Tread softly the dust of Arugam Bay, it carries memories.

Title: a highlight - very relaxed place
Text:
Arugam bay was a real highlight for us on a 6 week trip around sri lanka. 

SL seems to be a bit rip-off these days, compared with our last trip here in 2004, with silly prices for food and accommodation, especially in the south, south-east and near the "safari" zones.  But Arugam bay restored our faith. It's one of the last refuges of backpackers in the country (along with crazy hikkaduwa) and we had a real relaxing time here mixed with some exciting cycling journeys along the coast towards Panama village.

We stayed at Beach Hut, always busy even out of season, we learned. Cheap rooms and genuinely great food.

The main beach area is not the tropical beauty of, say, Thailand or malaysia, but that's more or less the case for all of sri lanka where the waves are generally enormous (ok if you're a surfer) and the beaches steep, not to mention strewn with plastic rubbish. Arugam beach was also a fishing beach which, apart from the inevitable scattered rubbish, made it all the more interesting.

Nearby trips can be made to Pottuvil town and, further north, Pottuvil point, a popular surfer hangout in season but almost completely empty when we visited. Be careful swimming here due to currents from the lagoon (even if it looks very picturesque). Also Panama village, south of arugam, is possible by bicycle or tuktuk where the journey itself is great, rather than the village which is ok for some food and drinks. An English guy has bought up the land encompassing the point so the current peace may or may not change in future. at the moment there is only a restaurant and a few basic huts at the point itself but I guess this is a busy place in surfing season. The caretaker, sidike, is a wealth of local info and good company for a chat. it's a lonely job he has!

Food is available from the guest houses or restaurants along the main road running behind the beach. We ate in the Beach Hut most nights as it was reasonably priced and very good Indian food.

If you ask Mr. Ameen who is the owner of SHIM to buy fresh fish for cooking, he will gladly oblige. By the way Mr. Ameen prepares a wicked fish barbecue. Try it if you stay there.

You will witness the most beautiful sunrises ever in Arugam Bay. Hope you will enjoy your visit as much as I did.

Title: THE place to stay in Arugam Bay!!!
Text:
Hideaway is an absolutely gorgeous place and I believe the best accommodation and restaurant there is in Arugam Bay. Of my four-week round travel in Sri Lanka with my two young children, this place - it's beautiful aesthetics, loving attention to detail, superior food and incredibly kind and helpful owner Sharon and her staff; all culminating in creating the most enjoyable and relaxed, tranquil and peaceful atmosphere - stayed with us and would most certainly be the one to come back to. 

The bed and breakfast centers around the owner's old family holiday home, set back from the beach across the main road. The property consists of the main house and 6 or 7 bungalow-style units amidst a luscious, palm-tree adorned and color-kissed garden. 
The downstairs veranda style set-up of the main house functions as the reception, restaurant and open-air living-room - complete with old cupboards full of books, big rattan chairs and stone benches atopped with bright-colored cushions inviting you time and again to sink in and relax - all in one. Upstairs, enjoying a wide and beautiful balcony are a few rooms for rent. The bungalows come in various sizes. We stayed in one of the newer ones, which was a spacious (humongous bed and bathroom), minimalistic, clean - simply gorgeous unit.

Arugam Bay is a small village on Sri Lanka's south-eastern coast, which has become a (family)-surfer's heaven. The main street is lined with one bed&breakfast  - some bigger hotels starting to sprout about, which hopefully will not do too much harm to the very chilled and relaxed, not yet too overcrowded feel of Arugam Bay - cafe, imbiss, restaurant, bar, surfer-boutique and corner-shop next to the other, which makes for perfect beach-holiday strolling and hanging-out: picking up your breakfast before descending on to the gorgeous main beach, which has a few great (mid-)day hang-out spots; sorting yourself with any snacks or beach-wear utensils anytime; enjoying one brilliant dinner after the other during your stay - unless of course Hideaway just keeps tempting you back in - probably the most stressful decision-making aspect during our stay!!! 

I can only whole-heartedly recommend a stay in Arugam Bay and here at Hideaway!!!

Title: Excellent for real swimming
Text:
Great beach (the best we've seen in Sri Lanka, out of 4 or 5) IF: 1) you don't want bars and annoying vendors on the beach, 2) you don't like crowds, 3) you like fine-grained sand and a clean beach, 4) especially, if you like swimming Â not wading, but really swimming. There is a rock between the bay and the sea, it's about 900 meters from the beach, so it's a great swim.  When the sea is calm, you can swim very near the rock and see all kinds of fish (not much of coral reef, though, and whatever there is is dead).  When the sea is not so calm, be very careful Â I stayed at least 10Â20 meters away from the nearest visible rock, and I could still see some rocks beneath me.  

The downsides: 1) The sea is very opaque (cloudy) Â you can't see further than 1 meter, perhaps a little more.  This is because of the very fine sand floating in the sea (near the beach) and, above all, because of microscopic algae making the water green.  2) On the way from the beach to the rock, there is an area where somewhat dirty-looking foam gathers Â you might want to swim around it.  3) Of course, as transpires from the above, if you like beach partying, this is not a beach for you.  4) The waves can be strong, so I am not sure it's a good beach for small kids.

Title: Seedy beach town, horrified by turtle welfare
Text:
Having walked down beautiful AdamÂs Peak, been mesmerized by the scenery in Ella, soaked in the ambience of Tangalle and Mirissa, Hikkaduwa was not only a huge disappointment, but also felt dreadfully unsafe.

Whilst Tangalle and Mirissa were lined with the flora and fauna of Sri Lanka, there were a few coconut trees in Hikkaduwa, but mostly the view is of delapidated, eery, empty hotels. Unlike elsewhere where you could easily get delicious Sri Lankan food for a good price, this place was full of naff restaurants serving expensive Western food, and poor quality at that. 

Perhaps the most difficult thing is the large groups of local men just wandering around gawking at tourists and in particular hassling women. Having travelled lots of the South for two weeks we expected some people to peddle their wares, but this was constant and at times quite aggressive. At one point whilst I was trying to read my book I had to tell somebody to back away because he was pestering so much. Hardly relaxing.

In terms of the tourist population, whilst in other places it was full of backpackers travelling around, here it was mostly what seemed to be people on package deals just here for the beach. Unfortunately, it did give it quite a chavvy vibe and felt somewhat cheap but not cheerful, and not actually even cheap!

*Perhaps most distressing was the Âturtle watchingÂ* Basically, a group of Sri Lankan guys encourage large sea turtles onto the shore (possibly captured and brought in) and feed them seaweed to keep them close. If tourists were to feed them seaweed they have to pay a fee. I gather if they dont pay they get quite intimidating. These tourists then go up to these beautiful creatures and distress them by petting them and taking pictures with them. It really is heartwrenching to see, and astounding how oblivious so many tourists are to how awful this practice is.

Sri Lanka has so much beauty and excitement to offer - thank goodness I only spent one day here as it doesnÂt show you how great Sri Lanka is. I would discourage anyone from visiting this place.

Title: Busy, commercial but a lot to do
Text:
IÂm not typically a beach person, I find the more popular beaches to be much the same around the world (packed full of overpriced bars/restaurants etc) but there are some amazing things that set this beach apart from the rest. 

We headed down to the beach around 8am with the hope of seeing a wild giant sea turtle feeding and we were lucky enough to find one! This was one of our main hopes for this trip as we love animals. There were a couple of people there already and shortly after there were more and more people but they all seemed to be respectful and gave the turtle space to do as it pleased. There are some officials who ÂpoliceÂ the area so they would stop anyone from touching the turtle etc. 

Having been amazed by the turtle we then used our own snorkel in the shallows and it was full of various fish and other marine life , there were plenty of people offering snorkel tours to a close by rock (by boat) which we may do tomorrow. 

We walked up the beach and stopped at a place for some breakfast, it was average but we just needed to eat something. ThereÂs plenty of choice for food but IÂve found that the better places are a short walk inland from the seafront. 

We went back to our room to top up our sun cream and headed back to the beach where we had a drink in the shade before renting some body boards and having some fun in the waves! The waves are very strong so I would not let children play in the sea without an accompanying adult!

Although IÂm not a fan of beaches in general I found it was rich in marine life which was incredible to see and the body boards were 300 rupees each for an hour which seemed like good value.

Text:

Not knowing the topography of the sea I expected the school to inform me having never surfed the area before. 
 
In short if you have been to Mirissa before here or are planning to go to Mirissa before Hikkaduwa then stay away.

Title: Clean Beach During Off Season
Text:
I definitely loved Hikkaduwa beach, I don't know how it is during peak season but I was here in July. There wasn't a lot of people and I loved it. It felt like a clean beach to just stroll in and relax in. It was also a good beach to swim in.

 They also have wild turtles swimming here where the locals help you  get seaweed to feed the turtles so it will come to shore. 

I initially saw a crowd of people and asked what was happening. I was curious. I was saddened though that a local approached me and asked for money for me to see the turtle--- they said if i didn't give them money then it wouldn't come to shore. 

I dive anyway, so I just walked away and let it be. However, they do exist in the area. You can see them naturally in knee length deep, of course, the locals are just trying to get money out of you. 

I generally loved my whole trip in Sri Lanka --- it felt safe even when I was alone.  What I got really tired of though is tuktuk drivers over charging tourists. 

In Hikkaduwa, the locals would approach me every so often because most were in groups and I was alone.   Don't get me wrong, I love mingling---I am a people person. I love meeting new people and I like interacting wiht locals but in Hikkaduwa it was a bit much! 

I would laze in the beach andthey would sort of wake me to just strike a lot of conversations, usually sales related.  Often, a group of french people rescued me because they kept asking about my hotel and if I wanted to come over which of course I didn't.  I do love mingling with locals but it just gets a tadbit too muich if  they constantly come when you are lazing and resting. I guess, I was a target since most were in groups or couples and I was alone. 

All else, I still did enjoy Hikkaduwa.

Title: A Lovely Beach ( a bit marred by humans)
Text:
Our Hotel had entrances directly onto the beach so we took regular strolls along it as well as swam / snorkelled from it.

It is a public beach (why not), and there are plenty of people around but it is not unpleasantly crowded.and the food / beverage shacks etc add to the ambience.

Yes there are boat vendors etc along the shore, but they generally accept a polite no, and don't hassle you further.

We especially liked the area to the North, where most of the locals went (en masse), to enjoy themselves, and seeing them happy, made us happy too.

Going into the sea from this beach is very easy and no rubber footwear required,

Warning, be vigilant of the many small tourist boats that operate in a most cavalier way in the same area.
I snorkelled out lots of times, wearing bright flourescent gear.
However, I had to stop many times, and shout loudly at the boat crew, to make them aware of my presence.( they were too busy amusing their customers by doing fast 'doughnuts' in the water and throwing bread over for the fish)
This was very unsafe practice and dangerous to swimmers..
The authorities, should segregate the boats from swimmers by roped off areas with marker buoys, as they are in many other parts of the world.

It is also  a great shame to see ignorant people feeding the fish bread etc and feeding / stroking the turtles.too.
Titillating as it may be for you, please stop and think, as you are changing the diet and behaviour of the marine life. Thereby, you are quite literally killing them.
Maybe some informative notices need to go up along the beach ( and make sure they are in written in the Russian language too ).

We still love the place, and would not hesitate to return here at any time.

Title: Fancy a short trek that leads you to the beach? Recommend the Jungle Beach Trek
Text:
Jungle Beach is really a short walk from Unawatuna (about 40-60 min) through the jungle then climb down to the beach that is secluded and overlooks Galle.

So better get here quick before it loses its charm.
The positives is that because the area still belongs to the Dept of Wildlife, they have stopped or done away with the previous make-shift restaurants that were right by the beach at Jungle Beach.
It seems to be more of a place where a lot of locals come in for a day/weekend trip. Since we went there on a Sunday, it was very busy. Also a tad noisy but everyone seemed to be having a good time. 
You can swim here too but the sea is now seems to be littered.
Strangely though the walk from Unawatuna and though the jungle seemed clean and came across only a few discarded PET bottles.
The climb is only slightly difficult but recommend shoes unless you are a flip-flop pro in which case you can still easily do the climb up and down unless you are unlucky to do the trek on a rainy day.
Make sure to take lots of water though, as it is humid.
There are a few restaurants around in the vicinity before you climb down to the beach that offers local food for good prices. We didn't have lunch there, so no idea how the food was.
If you don't fancy eating after the walk, you can always a grab a bite to eat once you get to Dalewala road which has all the touristy shops/restaurants.

Title: Glorious mirissa
Text:

A beautiful walk along the front will take you past the many restaurants and diners, and sun beds are readily available and free! 
The service at restaurants can vary from incredibly poor to very good, depending on which one you choose, the busier ones are often poor service and waiters can just ignore you completely, so if you do stop for a drink, don't wait for them to come to you! 
Prices are more expensive on the beach and can be unreasonable if you've got poor service. Beware of the surf during the day, it gets very high and very strong, small children would need supervising and even string swimmers need to be cautious! 
A must visit when in mirrissa!

Title: Very beautiful and clean beach, service & area around it could be much better
Text:
The beach is very nice and clean, the water was very warm (around 28 degrees) and also clean and there were some nice big waves sometimes (that's if you are into big waves). 
But be aware that it can get very crowded sometimes. We were in February 2019 and until 10 am you had to occupy a sun bed, otherwise they was nothing free anymore until around 4 pm (or you had to be lucky). 

One thing which i didn't like: all the restaurants (to whom the sunbeds belonged) were telling you at around 4:30 pm-5 pm to get off the sunbeds, because they were replacing them with tables for dinners. I found that they did this much too early ! It was exactly the time when the sun wasn't that strong anymore and it was really nice to lie in the sun and you had to go. I know that it gets dark really fast there, but still , I wish they had begun with this at 6 pm or later. 
The area around the beach is not nice though. There is a LOT of garbage lying around  everywhere and stinking (especially in the small river, yuck), there is a lot of dust and a lot of noise from the traffic on the main street and also no sidewalk, so you had to pay a lot of attention to the cars coming from both sides. So not really a place to walk relaxed in the evening.
The service on the beach is terrible (with a few exceptions). Very slow waiters, you had to wait a lot for everything (menu, drinks, food, even the bill), they forget a lot from the orders and for some of them there is 10% percent service charge already included ( a service which is as I said terrible). But the service and the food is generally much better on the main street than on the beach (we found some places with really amazing food and very good service). 
So 4 stars for the beach itself, which is very beautiful, but not for the area surrounding the beach or the service on the beach.

Title: Little tired but good for a stop over
Text:
We stayed here for one night, breaking up our stay in Sri Lanka before taking a flight from Columbo to Male. 

Unfortunately when we arrived they had messed up our booking so thought we were due to stay the next evening. Once they had realised this was incorrect it was sorted pretty quickly and consequently I think we actually got a room upgrade, after all it was our honeymoon. 

The hotel has a nice pool which also has some amazing sea views. It has its own beach and a number of other facilities. I got the impression however, that despite the very impressive entrance and grand nature of the hotel it was quite tired and dated. If IÂm honest it needs quite a significant amount of investment to bring it back to its former glory. The staff also failed to make the best impression - there seemed a lack of coordination and knowledge, for example when we received a call to say our driver had arrived we returned to reception only to find no one seemed to know who our driver was or had any recollection of the fact theyÂd called us. 

We ate in the seafood restaurant on the beach which was lovely and very good value for money. You weigh out your fish and itÂs cooked to how you like it, id defiantly recommend this. 

Breakfast in the Grovenors restaurant was a bit of a shambles. Whilst the food was okay  we were put out by the very poor service - we were not seated so tried to find our own seat to find all of them had reserved signs. When we had no option but to sit in one of these we were confronted with a very cross waiter who told us to move but could not suggest a seat. Not ideal! 

Overall for a quick pit stop in Columbo I would recommend this hotel, however not for more than a couple of nights.

Title: Health Hazard
Text:
A beautiful stretch of beach several miles long completely ruined by the amount of rubbish strewn across the whole length of it.

Plastic of all descriptions from tooth brushes to old toys, and of course many many plastic bottles.  Also glass bottles whole and smashed,  as well as other detritus.  Yet worse than this from the wild life perspective is the bits of old fish nets and lines scattered all over the place. A real danger to all forms of marine life.

Feral dogs run loose and defecate everywhere,  worse still my wife witnessed a local also defecating on the edge of the water.

A half-hearted attempt is made to clean the beach by use of a tractor and sand scoop but does not cover even half the beach leaving most of the beach untouched. Saw one so called recycling bin that was used as a general rubbish bin, apart from that there appears no attempt to recycle any of this mess.  

At one point a stream runs across the beach then out to sea that smells strongly of sweage . There is also a small pond that also smells the same.

All the beach bars  and hotels that front onto this stretch of sand serve all their drinks with plastic straws and there are thousands of them every where you look on what should be a lovely natural space.

So if you do walk on this beach keep your saddles on

Title: Buddha's Lake of compassion
Text:
I was in Kandy for 4 days. Stayed in a hostel near the train station and Kandy Lake is about half an hour walk from the train station. The Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic is located at the southern end of the lake. The grand Victorian architectural style colonial Queens Hotel stands robustly opposite the lake.   

Kandy Lake reminded me of Hoan Kiem Lake in Hanoi. It was winter when I visited Hanoi few years back and I enjoyed my stroll around the lake in the comfortably cold weather. When exhaustion set in, I would just relax on the bench at the lakeside admiring the tranquility of the atmosphere. 

But the experience at Kandy Lake was different. The weather was terribly hot and humid in the month of March and the air was still. There were not many benches available and most were fully occupied by the locals. The incessant traffic flow at the northern end of the lake flooded my lungs with much toxic pollutants. It was not a place where you can really appreciate the lake scenery. 

The stretch of the lake near to the temple was much more peaceful as only few vehicles ply this road. While strolling along this stretch of the lake, I was surprised to find a gigantic monitor lizard crawling at one side of the lake. This is my first time seeing such a gigantic lizard emerging out of the water. 

At another corner, oblivious to the curious eyes of the onlookers, few beautiful geese with brightly colored feathers were seen mating and having fun in the water. The long slim legged white cranes hunt for her prey beneath the water surface. It was a fun filled nature world for the birds and animals as they wandered freely in their natural instinct at the lake side. 

As I passed the Temple of the Tooth Relics, I could see flock of devotees carrying bouquet of flowers in their hands climbing up the stairs into the temple halls. As dusk slowly crept in, the lake view became dim while the neon lights in the temple shone brilliantly out and brighten one end of the lake. 

This was Buddha's Lake of compassion. The fishes, the monitor lizards, the cranes, the geese and whatever form of lives on top or beneath the lake are well protected in this land of the Buddha. That makes Kandy Lake different from West Lake, Sun Moon Lake, Hoan Kiem Lake, Houhai, Xihai and the rest of the lakes.  

As I walked my way to my hostel, the quotes of Buddha resonates in my mind:

'Besides the respect of the lives of human beings, all the animals and plants should be on the list too. That is the real humanitarianism.'

Title: Wildlife haven and spectacle
Text:
We visited Tissa reservoir, which is one of five in the area, a number of times during our three night stay in the area. It has an abundance of wildlife including the globally threatened Spot-billed Pelican and Watercock. We also saw three species of Bittern (Yellow, Black and Cinnamon). We also found a pair of Greater Painted Snipe on the north west corner, a difficult bird to find anywhere in its African and Asian distribution. 

Also along the western edge of Tissa Reservoir are heronries comprising a number of species. Some trees at dusk can resemble British Magnolia trees (whilst actually being the roost of mainly Cattle Egrets). 

The most spectacular sight for us was seeing the many thousands of Giant Fruit Bats leaving their roost at dusk and flying past an illuminated temple through our telescope.

Title: Marvelous Ancient Bathing Ponds
Text:
Kuttam Pakuna (Twin Ponds) 

Kuttam Pakuna (Twin Ponds) are two bathing tanks built in the middle of a garden in 6th century AD by King Aggabodhi for the monks and students, as part of Abhayagiri Monastery Complex in sacred city of Anuradhapura. It reflects wonderful skills possessed by the Sri Lankans 2000 years ago in architectural engineering and hydrological technology. Both ponds are 51 feet wide and laid down in a row. The larger one is 132 feet long and 17 feet deep while the smaller one is 91 feet long and 14 feet deep. Underground tunnels were built to fill and empty the ponds.

Title: Interesting, but nothing spectacular
Text:
Let me first preface by saying Anuradhapura, of the "cultural triangle" sites, is the most out of the way, and least worth your while as a result.  I would only recommend it if you were staying in Sri Lanka over 10 days or if you are a big historical/cultural buff.  The ruins at Polonuwara and Sigiriya are more impressive.

The baths themselves are worth about 5-10 minutes of your time, hardly worth the amount of time taken just to get there, especially if you are using a bicycle or public transport.  They are, after all, the ruins of two baths (enter drumroll...).  The surrounding area is decidedly not tourist friendly, unless you prefer that look.  There are filthy (and closed at the time of my visit) bathroom facilities, a small shack selling a drink across the road, and lots of cows wandering about.  The area around was muddy (since it had rained recently), and the pools are not closed off.  Good as it preserves a better "look", but bad if you have small children.

I would recommend only at the tail end of a visit to Anuradhapura, which itself I would only recommend as a bottom tier attraction within Sri Lanka.  The exorbitant entrance fees alone make you almost obligated to enter.

Text:

You can catch a bus from Nuwara Eliya to Ambewela.
But we preferred this route:
1. Bus N.E. to Nanuoya 15min-22LKR
2. Train Nanuoya to Ambewela 20min-15LKR (Ella train)
(You can enjoy stunning views over farms, tea plantations, Horton Plain and waterfalls)
3. Walk from Ambewela train station to Ambewela Farm 30min-free :)
(You won't miss the farm sign. The road is really well maintained, views are gorgeous, generally a pleasant walk)
4. Farm admission fee is 200LKR for adults, kids -1/2price
Inside there are cows, baby cows, goats, rabbits and a small cheese factory. To be honest, nothing expressive. Sheds are very smelly, animals are a bit dirty, no information about the farm history or how the cheese factory operates. Restaurant didn't have any proper meals (it was a big disappointment for us as we planned to have our lunch there). Should mention that the actual farm area is well looked after. 
Well, at this point you have to turn back and take the same road to the train station.  
5. You can come back by the same train+bus or take a direct bus to N.E.
** before you start your trip check the train and bus schedule :)

Title: Interesting and enjoyable, but feel sorry for the workers
Text:
You can't visit Sri Lanka without going to see a Tea Plantation, right ?!

So we were really pleased that our trip included a stop over here. Obviously there are lots of tea factories all over Sri Lanka, and we only visited this one, so cannot compare to any others, but I assume they are all very similar.

The tour takes you round the tea processing factory, as they explain the various stages of processing and different types of tea, and includes a cup of tea afterwards in the nice looking restaurant.

There is also the obligatory shop to purchase the vast number of teas from, much of which seemed a little high in price considering they made it on the premises (?). The teas in the fancy packaging seemed quite expensive and we felt it was a bit of a tourist rip-off, so we bought some of the cheaper variety to take home as a souvenir !

The whole thing took approximately one hour, which is just about right.

I was a bit disappointed that this  didn't  include a tour of the actual tea fields which surround and rise up into the hills around the tea factory.

However....  If you ask nicely then the tour guide will let you take a sneaky detour round the back into the plantation fields, where you can take photos of the tea and also some of the tea pickers - who will gladly pose for the photos if you give them some Sri Lanken Rupees (LRK) tips !

Whilst we enjoyed the experience, we felt saddened and astonished when we saw and found out about the quality of life and working conditions the workers were still enduring in the 21st Century.

None of them seemed to have any protective equipment, ear defenders, goggles, hard hats... despite working around noisy, fast moving and potentially dangerous looking machinery. Many of them were not even wearing shoes !!!!

Apparently the tea pickers earn something like just 500 rupees, which is just over Â£2, per day. And in return for this, they get very hard and rough skin on their hands from picking the leaves all day. Not the best life to live, is it ?!

So if you visit here and they do pose for photos, please be generous and give them a tip !  If just 2 tourists give them just  Â£1  tip for some photos, then that doubles their daily wage !

Location_Name: Damro Labookellie Tea Centre and Tea Garden
Title: Shrouded in Mystery
Text:
Damro was the first tea factory we visited in Sri Lanka. It was recommended by several tuktuk drivers and our homestay host. 

The tour was complimentary and lasted about 20 minutes, as we walked through the factory. We visited on New Year so there were no leaves being blow-dried. Our guide looked tired and recited off a script. She did nonetheless entertain our pesky questions well. After the tour we got to taste a cup each of FF1 tea in the lounge, but sadly we werenÂt particularly impressed. Strangely, there wasnÂt the option to try other types of tea - we would have wanted to try the loose leaf types like OP and BOP which we later discovered were more to our liking. We were, funnily enough, allowed to buy cakes, which admittedly were cheap and decent. Ultimately, as we had liked our hostÂs tea, which was from damro, we proceeded to make the mistake of buying too much tea on our first stop.

It was only after visiting the Mackwoods museum in Nuwara EliyaÂs city centre that we found out more about the history of Damro - it was a furniture company that had just (as of 2016) ventured into the plantation business, acquiring great swathes of land, including the Labookellie tea lounge, and a significant stake in the Mackwoods brand (the second oldest tea company after the parent company of Lipton). 

Make what you will of our experience - we still canÂt figure out if we are happy with our purchases 4 days later. But the experience as a whole was somewhat uncanny. The price of tea in the gift shop we found to be average - higher than the Zesta / Lipton types in supermarkets but lower than most single-estate tea companies we visited elsewhere in Sri Lanka. Our advice would be to stay off the teabags (which we tasted and found to be quite ordinary) and stick to the loose leaf teas.

Title: A Working Museum....
Text:
OK, having read the previous reviews, lets try and give some balance.... The tea factory is a wonderful relic to the belief, that if it isn't broken, don't mend it and in common with other factories, the process has not changed throughout the centuries. Similarly, some of the machinery is well over a hundred years old and in fact the tea factory is in effect a working museum. Yes the tea in the shop is overpriced, we we found this to be true at other similar establishments and as for the taste...don't forget that the tea drunk in England is blended tea, a concoction very often of teas from a number of countries. Pure tea is often drunk without milk and can be an acquired taste.
You cannot visit Sri Lanka without visiting a tea factory and Glenloch set in the uplands in Nuwara Eliya is a typical set up. People wanting tips is typical of the culture and tourists should not be surprised; wages are very low, so If you feel a service has been carried out, then a small reward could be given, but if not, keep your hands in your pockets. The same applies to overpriced tea !

The view from there is truly amazing over all the tea growing hills. Once you've arrived, follow the signs all the way up the wooden stairs until you arrive on the top floor. The insightful tour by a professional guide lets you discover the various areas of the factory associated to different states of the tea production, explains the different qualities of tea and the influence of market demand. After the tour, you may taste the locally produced tea on a balcony with an amazing view on the plantations. You may also buy the locally produced tea (a big plus for the staff NOT being pushy at all!) which really comes at a bargain, especially for pure Orange Pekoe and its vanilla or jasmine flavoured version. In fact, we've loved their tea so much that we've ordered their tea online for home delivery since!?

The tea factory tour was 300 rupees each, a really good price. Only guided tours available, but we only had to wait 10 minutes for one to start. Text:

a visit to this estate is highly recommended!

Title: Decadence, Myth, Eros, Art, Still Hang in Colonial House and Grounds - beware of steps
Text:
We recommend taking a tuk-tuk there as the directions to the house are minimal. Also, there are many steps (some of them high) and uneven terrain in the grounds and garden, which could be challenging for the elderly or differently-abled. 

This is were Bevis Bawa retired after his brief career in the army and where he surrounded himself with a bevy of boys, young men, gentlemen and similar masculine companions. While the grounds are nice, we liked the house the most. Beautifully designed, decorated and furnished, it truly reflects Bawa's taste and upbringing. The Picassos, Gauguins and Cocteaus - despite being copies - reminisce of the atmosphere and the erotic fauna that the house enjoyed in the 50s and 60s. Walking in the open-air Roman-style baths in one of the room's private courtyard, we wondered what the darkened and foggy mirror would say if it were ever allowed to tell what it saw!

The current resident, the former head gardener to whom Bawa donated the house (!), is doing a good job preserving the house as it was when Bawa died: simple, elegant, decadent, and yet ready for a pool party and music and boys, should the former ghosts decide to visit one night. A magical place indeed.

Title: Sad to see the Bawa name tarnished
Text:
As a fan of Bawa's work, it was disappointing that our entrance to the property began with a bad start, firstly because the caretaker was not happy with our arrival at 2:30pm. Then sadly a member of our party was falsely accused of potential wrong-doing (I.e walking into an entry and bending to look at a painting whilst we used an outside restroom) -this was made by a female who lived on the property, not the caretaker. The caretaker' excuse for the yelling was thinly veiled by an explanation of previous trouble they had experienced with past visitors. The visit had now kicked off to a bad start and the caretaker did not offer to take us around the gardens and describe the beauty and landscape architecture. We were left to wander aimlessly through the overgrown gardens before having a tour of the house. 
It is clear that the caretaker is very knowledgeable, and he provided curt and limited explanations of the beautiful works inside the home itself.
This was not what we expected especially with our comparison visit to Lunuganga, and some previous internet reviews prior to our visit to Brief Gardens. So you may need to piece together your own reading and research prior to visiting this tranquil acreage. It is clearly a magnificent property with alarmingly priceless artworks out in open display and unprotected from the elements. 
The property is in a hidden location along an unkept road that all but disappears at the gate. This journey itself is an adventure! The road is only just big enough for a 10 seater van. 

So sadly, our 1000 rupee entry fee pp was seen as very expensive for our party of 5, and it is a quandary because the property needs the funds from entry fees to maintain the property. Perhaps some better management and direction is required to preserve such a beautiful history.

Title: BRIEF rather too brief
Text:
As an antidote to the hedonistic beaches of southern Sri Lanka, we decided to go inland and explore the attractions that lay within. A visit to the Brief Garden associated with Bevis Bawa (1909-1992) older brother of the more famous Geoffrey Bawa, the renowned architecht,seemed to be just what the doctor ordered. The road trip to the location once one left the main Galle Road at Bentota and traversing narrow rural roads and ups and downs was itself a challenge as there was virtually no signposting. When we finally reached it, the imposing entrance to Brief ( named after the association with lawyers holding briefs)with its ivy covered walls and cement sculptures standing guard over the iron gate was startling.Another shock was the steep entrance fees - Rs 1000SLK per head - which was collected at the door after which we were sheperded into the gardens to find our way about while an earlier Sunday meeting of a local association concluded its tea party.
The gardens are the real star of the show, and despite the size having been reduced to just five acres, one could visualise the arboreal grandeur that must have existed in its full majesty.
A botanist-guide who knew the trees and the manner in which they came to be would have been appreciated. We finally were admitted to the main house - just about a hour to closing time - and got a rather canned conducted tour where the guide repeated himself several times. 
The architecture and the imprint of Barbara Sansoni and Donald Friend,the Australian artist during his five-year stay there in the 1950s are absorbing to explore,The sculptures , paintings, courtyards, open air showers and fountains all made their own quiet statements.
One could have lingered more but closing hour beckoned  and a cuppatea - which sadly never came - would have befitted the admission ticket and the host.

Text:
We had already visited Lunuganga, the nearby gardens and home of Geoffrey Bawa, before we came to Brief, the home and gardens of his older brother, Bevis.
Whilst not as famous, nor as vast as Lunuganga, Brief is an interesting place to visit if you wish to get an insight of the lifestyle of the well-heeled Sri Lankan demi-monde.
The home itself is a beautiful old plantation house that Bevis Bawa improved and still contains beautiful antiques, fascinating old photographs and some important artworks - most particularly a wonderful (albeit somewhat time ravaged) mural by the Australian artist Donald Friend, who came to visit Brief for a week and stayed for 5 years. When you see the gardens you can understand why. Brief may not be as grand as Lunuganga, but it is equally as likeable and the staff member who showed us around the house was extremely knowledgable and generous with his time.

Title: Overt suggestiveness?
Text:
We visited Brief Garden while staying at Lunuganga. If you can swing it, I would say it is worth seeing both (Lunuganga should be reserved well in advance, phone ahead for Brief). Either one is a welcome reprieve if you've been spending too much time on Bentota's beaches. (I know, not possible for some.)

If you do manage to see both gardens, the comparisons will be inevitable. As you may hear, both Bawa brothers were talented but with differences in their approach. It should be noted that (the older) Bevis' Brief Garden was first and was the precursor to inspire Geoffrey's Lunuganga, if not eventually spurring Geoffrey's entire architectural career. And the two properties are very different to begin with. Brief is inbound within the jungle, while Lunuganga is larger with a lake bordering its opposite ends. 

The experience of Brief is intimate in size, the garden is organized by designated paths with lushly dense tropical foliage. Following these paths, you happen upon sudden openings and clearances that are humanly scaled - almost like garden "rooms". Some of these open spaces might have a water feature, formal stairs, or spaces sized for activities. The feeling of the garden as "rooms" is more clearly evident in the garden spaces behind the house (such as the outdoor shower area) that the tour guide will take you through. 

Lunuganga is more pastoral in comparison. Indeed, Geoffrey kept cows on it (still there) that maintained its legal status as agricultural land. There is a spatial flow to the rolling hills and stepped plateaus that contrast to the jungle walkways of Brief. Lunuganga is often cited as one of the factors that ultimately led Geoffrey to get formal architectural training. This may add to the sense that Lunuganga is the work of someone more concerned with space. As far as I can tell, Bevis designed his garden primarily as an enthusiast.

I am surprised that few if any comments on TA thus far make mention of what appeared to be Bevis' undeniably overt orientation. In one sense, it should not matter. Yet, I think it provides a fascinating angle from which one can reflect on the brothers and their relationships to their gardens and the world. There are records which suggest Geoffrey may have also veered this way, although they are only inferences, as he did not openly project this image as his brother did.

Entering Brief Garden, you feel like you are allowed into Bevis' private world. Homo-eroticism abounds - some blatantly obvious, some quite suggestive, some with a touch of cheeky humour. It reads as a place where he was free to let loose and enjoy life on his own terms without abandon. Viewed in this light, outdoor spaces which are "intimately scaled" take on a further dimension. (Something happening behind those moving bushes?)

Likewise, Lunuganga is an interesting documentation of Geoffrey's world. You could almost chart his career as an architect in parallel to its evolution. While Brief seemed somewhat of an inner sanctum, Lunuganga had an expansiveness to it where one did not necessarily "hide" so-to-speak. (There are plenty of physical hiding "spots" but I'm referring more to the mentality.) For example, the male sculptures on display at Lunuganga are significantly more demure in posture - classical rather than wildly expressive. Was this the influence of English propriety alongside English landscape design? Was he acting in accordance with the etiquette expected of someone of his growing renown? Or was Bevis so forwardly extravagant it makes us pale in our moralities?

Title: Beautiful botanic garden
Text:
The Hakgala Botanic Garden, just outside of Nuwara Eliya, is definitely worth a visit. As some have noted, the entry fee for foreigners (LKR1500) may seem a little expensive, but as a visitor, you can see where the entrance fee is going. An army of gardeners keeps this place very well tended. 

The garden is at an altitude of around 1700 metres, and features a lot of temperate plants and trees. Monterrey Cypresses features prominently here, but there are also Bunya Bunya Pines and Norfolk Island Pine Trees from Australia. There's a rose garden, several greenhouses, a rock garden, and also a Japanese garden. I thought the Japanese garden was lovely, but struggled to see much relation to traditional Japanese gardens. There is also a section of the garden that was part of a tea plantation, where camellia sinensis trees have been allowed to grow out. I was fascinated to see them, as they grow to 10 - 13 metres once they're no longer pruned tightly. 

I'd recommend getting to the gardens early, as they are pretty popular. There's a small canteen inside, but there are a lots of small shops immediately outside the gates. 

I'll let the photos of this place speak for themselves...

The management had implemented a strict no plastics policy, so they check and remove and plastic bottles and bags at the entrance. Personally I think it's a very good policy. Inside the park, there is a small cafe, where you can get snacks and drinks. There is also a small outlet where you can buy plants. 

One major drawback is the lack of parking. You have to park on the side of the main road, which in itself is narrow and bendy. There is a parking charge and attendants who look after the vehicles. Title: Nice but not spectacular garden.
Text:
We decided to give this garden a visit on our first Sri Lanka trip. It is located about 30minutes from Nuwara Eliya town. This botanical garden is spread across hectres of hilly terrains and beautifully maintained. The entering price is quite steep for tourist (1100Lakhs per person) as compared to locals (50Lakhs). It is not as magnificent as those botanical garden in some part of the world that I have been but it has numerous type of plants, ranging from medicinal plants, cold climate colorful flowers and very old aged mature trees. Due to its large area, the stroll can be quite tiring especially when we walked along the small rocky paths. If you need to get a buggy however, it is available at 1000Lakhs per hour but the number of buggy is very limited. My mom and her friend waited almost 1 hour for any available buggy but failed.

There are upper gardens and lower gardens. We lost track of our whereabouts but we first encountered Rose Garden. Since it is May and it is spring, there are many blossom colourful roses. Red (definitely), pink, white, blue, yellow etc.

The Japanese garden is nothing to shout about with its water features and some unimpressive bonsai. Probably can skip it if you are not up for a long uphill stroll.

This place is a good diversion of the busy Nuwara Eliya town but it comes with high price and the garden is not really spectacular. It is still a good place for relaxing stroll with family, but definitely not for those with weak knees or legs. Unless you are lucky and there is available buggy for you to rent.

Title: Nice garden; good way to spend an afternoon for nature lovers
Text:
If you love nature, this garden is definitely worth the trip.

ENTRANCE: The line for the tickets can be a bit unruly - crowds just hanging in front of the window to collect tickets.  Tickets can be a little pricey, especially if you are not a local.  Having said that, it may be worth what you pay for.

TRANSPORTATION: Since the garden is quite extensive, you can hire a buggy to take you around the park.  This may be a good option if you are a family with elders or toddlers who may tend to get tired with long walks.  They are priced reasonable and can be hired from near the entrance.

PARK: You are provided with a map of the garden.  Definitely recommended as some of the areas you might miss out on if you are not referring to the map.  Some areas of the park give you a good view of the city from up above - definite photo opportunity.  When we visited, the flowers and plants were still blooming, so colors were a little limited.  Nevertheless, it was still a fulfilling experience.

You may also see family of monkeys - just be careful if you are holding any edible items - they may come and grab it.  But for the most part, they keep to themselves.

FOOD: There was a small canteen that served drinks, crisps and other food items.  Nice spot to catch your breath a little, view the surroundings.

OVERALL: A good visit if you have an hour or two to spare.

Title: Nice place for relaxing.
Text: Hakgala Botanical Garden is one of the five botanical gardens in Sri Lanka. It is the second largest garden in Sri Lanka. The garden is contiguous to Hakgala Strict Nature Reserve. Hakgala Botanical Garden is situated on the Nuwara Eliya-Badulla main road, 16 km from Nuwara Eliya. Hakgala Botanic Gardens, about 28 hectares in extent, lie under the shadow of the Hakgala Rock. The garden was established in 1861, under George Henry Kendrick  as an experimental cultivation of Cinchona, a comercial crop thriving at the time. Once after the Tea replaced the Cinchona, it was turned into an experimental Tea cultivation. In 1884 it transformed to a garden. Since then many sub tropical and some temperate plants were planted in the gardens. The Botanic Gardens are locally reputed for their collection, the rose garden, Magnificent trees, indoor plants, flowers. The climate of the Gardens is subtropical, cool and freshThere are over 10,000 species of flora planted here. However USD 12.5 for SARC coumtries and USD 25.00 per person for a foreigner is bit expensive.

Title: A decent stop without too much sales pressure.
Text:
Our driver suggested this place en-route from Habarana to Kandy and, though we were dubious (anticipating some kind of hard sell), we were getting bored and sleepy with the long drive so we figured we would just treat it as a rest break.

Once out of the car, we were offered the use of the restrooms and then a guide was assigned to us and he then spent the next hour taking us around the garden showing us some of the spices and other plants growing in the grounds.  There was plenty of te usual stuff you;d expect - cinnamon, nutmeg, aloe vera etc and it was actually kind of interesting.  At two points in the tour, we were offered tea which had various spices in it (e.g. cinnamon tea) which was nice and the guide obviously knew his plants.

At the end of the tour, they tried selling us a head and shoulders massage using some of their home-made ointments to which we declined (was thinking about lunch and heading onwards to Kandy) so we were then directed to the shop which was obviously always going to happen.  However, to my surprise, once in the store, there was no hard sell  - the guide did point  a few things out and hovered around but there didn;t feel like any real pressure to buy (although we bought a spice box as a gift for family).

After exiting the shop, we had lunch with our driver who recommended the fish curry (not a huge surprise as that seems to be the staple in Sri Lanka) but I was up for it so agreed and out came a multitude of dishes including curries, rice and other accompaniments.  The food was a really good and we all enjoyed it although I wasn;t massive happy about all the damned flies crawling over everything - at one stage the bowl of rice looked like a dessert with currants..  but anyway, there's probably not an awful lot they can do about it in the open.  we are also surprised to see the total food bill which worked out at around Â£12.. which, for so much food that three of us couldn't eat it all, plus drinks, was a steal.

So in the end, it was actually a decent stop.  There's approximately two million and forty spice gardens in Sri Lanka (made-up number obviously) so I daresay there's some good ones and some bad ones but this one seemed pretty good.

Title: One of the nicest green spaces i've ever experienced
Text:
One of the nicest green spaces i've ever experienced

Just a quick glance at all the trip advisor reviews on here and its obvious the botanical gardens are popular and highly rated.

I can only add weight to that and say that we thoroughly enjoyed spending an afternoon here, though you could spend a full day if you had the time. We were contemplating just having a rest day round the pool at the hotel but decided to make the journey here and we were SO glad we did.

Other places should look to this place as an example of a well thought out, maintained and looked after urban green space.

It contains a bewildering variety of plants and trees, giant fruit bats hanging from and flying between the trees, monkeys you can get right up close to, lakes, and an orchid house with some of the most amazing flowers.

There is a cafe / buffet restaurant in the park, but this would make a lovely place to bring a picnic.

If you appreciate and enjoy nature and green spaces then this is a must visit if staying in or near Kandy. It is approx. 15 mins from Kandy city to here by tuk tuk and the fare should cost about 5 GBP. If you have already been on a tuk tuk with a mad driver then you will understand what an 'experience' this is, and if you haven't then do try to experience this at least once in your travels !

Victoria Park, Nuwara Eliya

All in all, a great place to hang out.

Title: The City of ÂGaleÂ
Text:
The horrendous rain simply would not stop all morning. The moment it became a drizzle, we grabbed our guide and off we went for our planned Fort tour. 

The drizzle then became a small storm. We were not dressed properly to take in the relentless wind and poodle of water, with our umbrellas threatening to fly away during our walk around the walls for defensive purposes.

It was the most speculator sea ever. Gazing out, I could imagine how the four metres high waves swept over the train station and bus station located right next to the Fort, and those inhabitants in houses on that Boxing Day. 

Our Tuk Tuk driver told us his then fiancÃ© had an urgent need to pray at the temple really early that morning.  Everything and everyone in her family was gone upon her return. He then took her in and gave her a home. IÂd told him to treasure her - what immense luck to be the sole survivor.

We entered the Fort from the old main gate. The walls were erected by the Portuguese in the 1500s and later added on by the Dutch and the English. During the walk, the guide pointed out the Fort Lighthouse and the many Bastions. The UNESCO Fort was truly a fusion of fantastic European architecture with Asian influence. 

The 300 year-old Dutch Reform Church was a humble establishment. No one was in there during our visit. The stained glass panels were worth looking at. We ended our tour at our hotel. 

I so named the City of Galle as the City of Gale right after our eventful walk that day.

Title: Fort Jaffna - well preserved and presented
Text:
Seeing the Jaffna Fort 'as it is' gives real insight into a fort's hostile purpose and the sombre consequences for anyone inside who lost ground. Whilst the walls are beautifully solid, the internal buildings have been reduced to rubble.
There is a lot to take in. 
When we visited an archaeologist on duty at the site told us about a joint Jaffna Uni Archeological Department/UK Durham University initiative. This has only recently revealed "...if Jaffna's history was condensed in a day, the colonial era would only start at just 3 minutes before midnight..'' Using ground penetrating radar (GPR) surveying they know that below the current site sits another preceding the colonial period, and finds show activity well prior to the Portugese, Dutch and British: finds include Roman coins and Chinese porcelain. What a blast?! Some of these finds are on display in cases in a separate chamber in the fort wall, just to the right, if you are facing the entrance from inside the fort. Allow about 1-2 hours to walk around and take in the views, contemplate the past hostilities, the sea birds and the remoteness of it all, and come in the morning if you can. 
There are WC (traditional). BYO tissues. BYO hat and drinking water. It's about the 30 minute walk from the Jaffna RS or Jetwing Northgate, you can get a tuk tuk there. It was still free when we went (6 August).

Title: Dambatenne Tea Plantation: Walk From The Factory to Lipton Seat and Back
Text:
This is one of my favorite places in SE Asia. We only spent one morning there, but I would be happy to return for multiple consecutive days just to walk around and enjoy the views.

Many people only speak of Lipton Seat as a place to go in this area, but I was unimpressed by the actual Lipton Seat. It essentially is just a view-point of the land looking off the mountain at the land below, not a view of the rolling hills patterned with tea trees. The true beauty of this area is the entire tea estate you go through en route to Lipton Seat. The best time to go is the morningÂthe earlier the better. It started to get clouded over by 10 AM, so if you are walking, arrive early. I would recommend arriving to the Dambetenne Tea Factory between 7:00 - 8:00 AM (or earlier). Then, just start walking up to road, which is about 7km to the top. There are tuk-tuks which can take you up or down, either for a round trip quick ride to the top or by walking one way and riding the other. However, you would likely miss a lot of the wonderful views in a tuk-tuk. We leisurely walked up and walked down in about 4 hours, and stopped for tea and appetizers at the top (which were delicious). Along the way down, we decided to get off the road and walk down the same paths as many of the workers picking the leaves and it was absolutely wonderful to interact with them. They were so friendly and welcoming and wanted to chat with us, encouraging us to come with them as they continued to walk and work. 

ItÂs one of the most beautiful place in SL, in my opinionÂand the women working in the fields are equally beautiful and filled with generosity and love. ItÂs the true embodiment of Sri Lanka.

There are many ways you can reach the Lipton Seat panorama, from Haputale : bus to dambatenne tea factory (about 10km) + another small bus or tuktuk to the lipton seat gate (or hike but mind the heat) (about 5km) + uphill hike or tuktuk to the top (1 km). At the Haputale tuktuk stand, drivers will be happy to negociate a cheap fee up to the very top, as there are few tourists.

Title: Stunning Views
Text: As there were 4 of us we took a pair of tuk tuks from our guest house to the top of Lipton's Seat which is about 5,000 feet in elevation. The road wound its way up and up through the tea plantations round countless hairpin bends (not dangerous) before reaching the entrance gate where there is a small entrance fee to be paid. The views from the top are almost 360 degrees and are stunning. We were possibly lucky with the weather as it was a cloudless deep blue sky and we could see for miles in all directions.The vivid green of the tea plantations set against the sky was very photogenic......lots of photos to be taken here!! At the top there is a fine statue of Mr Lipton himself and a small cafe where we sat and enjoyed the views. The air was cooler here and although it was hot when we were there I can imagine on a cloudier day it could be pretty chilly! Instead of taking the tuk tuk back down we decided to walk back down through the tea plantations. This was superb, we took it at a leisurely pace and just enjoyed the scenery, the friendliness of the locals particularly the smiling schoolchildren who make their way up and down this steep hill every day! We walked as far as the Dambatenne Tea Factory and then took a tuk tuk back to town from there. This was yet another highlight of our trip and one i highly recommend.....away from the crowds too!

We much enjoyed the views on the way and seeing the tea pickers at work.  I received many looks of amusement and perhaps disapproval on account of my walking sticks and hiking boots, which surely seemed way over the top, but I also exchanged a good number of smiles.

When we reached the top at least half of the view was covered in mist, but we really didn't mind.  It was the journey for us that mattered more than the "prize".  And, the restaurant at the top had surprisingly good food and perhaps the best tea I tasted on our entire trip.

We walked back down to the tea factory and were lucky enough to catch a local bus back to Haputale which was a super fun experience -- devotional tchotchkes on the dashboard and popular Hindi music playing all the way for a cheap price.  

Definitely worth the visit.

Title: The early bird catches the worm ... in this case the view weather permitting!
Text:
We visited Lipton's Seat while staying at Haputale. The advice was to get a taxi to drop us off at the top, walk the 7 kilometres downhill through the tea plantations and catch a bus back to Haputale from Dambatenne which we duly did; we were not disappointed. 

We got to the top by 06.00 which was plenty of time to settle down and wait for the sun to rise. At that time of the morning, and at that height, it gets pretty cold so I definitely recommend a fleece and windproof. The views are stunning but of course are totally dependant on the weather. We were lucky and had great 360 degree panoramic views; absolutely stunning and an experience that will stay with us forever.

At the top you can get hot tea and roti freshly cooked over a wood fire which was very welcome after our early morning start.

The walk downhill (I note some reviewers walked up as well as down - I consider myself to be a strong walker and I wouldn't have liked to have done that so hats off to them!) is equally enjoyable. The incredible views of the summit are gradually replaced by rolling tea plantations and tea planters villages until finally the tea factory at Dambatenna comes into view.

All in all a wonderful experience although, of course, totally dependant on the weather. Here's wishing you good luck on the weather front when you get the chance to visit Lipton's Seat.

Title: Great Views But Nothing Unique If You've Seen Other Tea Plantations
Text:
Main Tip: If you've been to tea plantations in Nuwara Eliya you can skip Lipton's Seat. If not, I would make the trek out to visit. 

It was about a 1.5 hour tuk tuk ride from Ella on some scary roads once you get closer to Lipton's Seat. If you have a fear of heights - this is not the drive for you. I'd highly recommend taking a tuk tuk over a car if you can, the roads are extremely narrow  and I saw multiple cars have a difficult time getting through. If you are self-driving (as we were) I would absolutely discourage self-driving here because there is very little room for error. You can also take a bus to Liptons Seat (get off at Haputale) and take a tuk tuk from there.

The view from the top by Lipton's statue is pretty and shows off tea plantations in every direction. You can either walk back down to the entrance (about 8km) to catch the bus or meet your ride or simply ride back in your tuk tuk once you are done looking around. There are places along the way (walking or riding) where you can look around and wander a bit through the rows of tea plants.

Go early - the fog/mist rolled in around 9:30 am and I was told it can get bad enough later in the day that driving is difficult. Given those roads that is not a risk I'd ever want to take! Also people often take pictures of the tea ladies working but remember - they are paid the equivalent of less than $3 usd a day and they are not animals in a zoo who are performing for your entertainment.
