Title: Unique views
Text:
We were staying at White Monkey - Dias rest, around 12km from lipton's seat (4km out from Haputale town). Some of the other guests advised we take a tuktuk or a car up to Lipton's seat, as the walk would be too long and strenuous. However, we had our hearts set on the walk - the pivotal reason we were visiting Haputale - and so decided to hike up the next morning anyway.

We left the guesthouse around 6am and had a beautiful two and a half hour hike to Lipton's seat. We passed a small lake, walked through cloud forest and past lush tea plantations. There are signs along the way with words of wisdom about environmental issues and protecting the planet as well as a count down towards lipton's seat. The views going up were different to any that we have ever encountered and it has been our favourite hike in Sri Lanka so far.

The walk can be strenuous at times, but it is mainly a gradual incline on a good path with plenty of places to rest or get snacks or water.

At the top we were greeted with tea, toffee, rotti and corn cakes: so delicious and just what we fancied after the hike. The views are stunning, however the mist and clouds surround the view point from around 8:30am onwards, so try aim to be there before. At the top you can get a tuktuk back down, or walk to the tea factory where there are plenty more tuktuks willing to take you back into town.

Polonnaruwa is the second largest city in North Central Province, but it is known as one of the cleanest and more beautiful cities in the country.

Title: Awe-inspiring. Must visit.
Text:
This is one of the ancient capitals of Sri Lanka, centuries old and with a number of sites contained therein. Entry is USD 25 for foreigners and USD 12.5 for children (half rate for nationals of SAARC countries). Payment can be made in USD or LKR, but change is returned in LKR only. Paying in USD is every so slightly cheaper when you do the reverse forex rate calculations. 
Upon paying the entry fee, you can enter the area and see all the various attractions. There is not a lot of information available on-site, so hiring a guide can be worthwhile. There is a museum in the building where you buy tickets, entry to which is complimentary with the Polonnaruwa tickets. However if running short of time, can skip this (which is what we did).
Since there are around 26 sites within the premises (all spread apart), it can easily take upwards of 1 whole day to see the place in its entirety and enjoy its beauty. If running short of time, you need to plan in advance and shortlist the places you want to see and first finish those (and then, time permitting see as much of the rest as possible). The Golden Quadrangle, Palace Complex and Gul Vihara are some of the places that i would recommend as must-see.
Suggest carrying a lot of water, wearing hats and covering knees.
As with most historic ruins, children and people without a sense of history will find this dull, so i would suggest they opt out (instead of paying 25 USD and then realising that they didnt appreciate the beauty of the ruins).

Title: Worth a visit
Text: The world heritage ruins at Polonnaruwa appear to be on the list of every tour that passes through Sri Lanka's cultural triangle.  We were staying locally so could get a head start on most of the tours before they poured in.  Most people seem to cycle around the ruins and I could see why this would be attractive - it's cheap, easy and safe, and you can move between the different sites fairly quickly.  However, we were advised by a local to head to the top of the site by tuktuk then walk back to town, and I'd highly recommend this approach too - you'll get to see a lot more wildlife when you're walking, and trust me there's a lot to see if you keep your eyes open!  Saying that, you'll probably be fairly tired by the end, and make sure you take plenty of water.  The ruins comprise of a number of main sites interspersed by smaller, less-visited sites.  Be prepared for crowds at the main sites, with far fewer tourists at the smaller ones.  All are worth a visit though. Title: Excellent historical site of ancient kingdom in Sri Lanka
Text:
We stayed at Sigiri and travelled out each day to Polonnurawa and Anuradhaphura. 
Polonnurawa is certainly worth a visit. There is really a lot of history here. We came with a tour guide so we got the low down on the history.  
Again expect to pay for the admission which is around 3500 LKR ( pls check before going ) each.  This is about the same price as for Anuradhaphura . The majority of the  entrance fees go towards maintaining the site and further excavations, so you are funding a good cause.  After paying for the admission do go round the museum which is where you get the admission tickets.   The visit to the museum is worthwhile especially if you donÂt have a guide. It explains each monument and the history behind it.  And also the history as to why the Kings moved from   Anuradhaphura to Polonnurawa to start a second kingdom.
All the places are concentrated in one small area so walking from one to another is quite straightforward.
Polonnurawa  started in the 10th Century as the capital city  and ended around the 12th Century . 
Apparently it had lain undiscovered until British archeologists began probing in the late 19th century when the whole area was covered in forests.  When you look at the buildings do look at the surrounding trees. Their bases are about 1.5 m to 2 m above the ground of the excavations. It will have taken some serious excavations to get to the monuments.
Some places are just spectacular.  The Royal palace for one, the second is the lake or a ÂtankÂ as they call it.  This huge lake of 25 sq km was manually excavated in the 12th century by people and elephants.  It really is quite an awesome task. 
There are some temples which are in ruins and previously held the Scared Relic of the Tooth ( now housed in Kandy).  Just do note that the dress code applies to temple ruins as to living temples. No shorts, or crop tops and no slippers on the temple grounds ( even abandoned ones).  A few visitors were caught out and not allowed in. 
Having visited both Polonnurawa and Anuradhaphura I think if you donÂt have enough time then Polonnurawa is the better choice.  But if you have the time and inclination then do visit both places .

Title: History and Heritage at its Best!
Text:
We visited this site in early February on a fairly warm day i.e. temperature about 23 degrees. We had guide with us. The advantage of a guide is that they can help you make the most of your visit by selecting out what to see and more importantly they have the knowledge of what is inter-connected and in close proximity too. 
This is massive heritage site and you cannot explore all of it in one day so selecting out points of interest and finding them is a challenge. Best to read up about it before you arrive as that may help you select out what you think suits you best. Alternatively just meander and explore. 
There is an option to hire cycles and that could be a good way to explore the site. Whether walking or cycling or with a driver guide you will almost certainly come across structures which will amaze you. The architecture is a delight if you have not previously seen buddhist or hindu heritage sites before. One of the joys was seeing carved granite carvings in the structures which convey stories. Hindu architecture is very different from Buddhist architecture. One revers the Buddha without much reference to the animal kingdom and the other is prolific in carving animals, 'grotesque' masks and moonstones with story telling symbolisms threaded throughout the buildings and statues. One is also relatively simplistic in design while the  other is over complicated, yet they are in harmony too.
So this a site where you can marvel at the size and shapes of early structures, whether they be structures like a giant wedding cake or stupa's which are round and dome like. Another joy of visiting this place is the sense of freedom you have to explore it. However there is an obligation that visitors show extra respect for those sites with a special religious significance. This presents no problems if your address is appropriate i.e. no knees (men and women) showing and the female head is covered. However this applies only to certain special places here not all of them. This is also a site that has grass and avenues of trees to contrast with the massive  brick structures. 
Until I visited this place I never realised that bricks were being made in the 12 century and were being used to build multi storey buildings and places of worship. 
If you are not keen on heritage ruins and history you will probable not rate these sites very much. For me it was interesting, enjoyable, varied and wonderful because of it heritage. I have not previously seen a nothing quite like it on this scale despite travelling to over 20 countries.

From the museumÂs exit, walk northwest through a small garden to the group of ruins on the shore of the lake known as Parakramabahu Samudera. Then walk east and cross the main road, to the entrance to the other section of the ruins. Your ticket will be checked again.

The ruins are in three main clusters: the lakeshore cluster (also known as the ÂislandÂ group), the royal palace cluster and the quadrangle cluster, each about 500m from each other. I am rating his site as merely "average". Even allowing for the fact that ruins that are 800 - 1100 years old can't possibly be in good condition, when I compare it with other archaeological sites of similar vintage around the world, Polonnaruwa is not outstanding. Title: Interesting ancient city
Text:
We spent an enjoyable few hours exploring this ancient site.  We were on a bit of a tight time deadline and were torn between Polonnaruwa or Anuradhapuda, am glad we chose the former as it's a fairly compact, self contained site, with good access to all the ruins.  Yes it's not as glamorous as other countries' ancient sites, but it is of great historical and cultural significance in Sri Lanka and several of the buildings are well preserved to say they were buried beneath jungle for centuries!

There is ample parking and good visitor facilities (toilets, wash facilities, food and drink)
We travelled around by car, which was straightforward enough.  There are several services hiring out push bikes, which seemed a pleasant way of getting around.

We had a very informative guide book, which we used to navigate and inform our route round.  There are some information boards dotted around, but they don't give particularly detailed descriptions.  As with any historic site visit, there are several 'guides' hanging around offering their services, if you are without a guidebook and find a good guide I would recommend it as you will miss out on a lot of information and even miss some of the well hidden sites altogether!

You do need to remove headwear and footwear to enter a large number of the sites, so come prepared and maybe bring something to dust the gravel off your feet after.

I would highly recommend a visit here during a tour of Sri Lanka's 'cultural triangle'.

We heard this site is like your own personal Indiana Jones adventure and we could see why as we had the forest all to ourselves away from the tourists. A fantastic experience, we hope to one day revisit.

Title: Pleasant walk in the forest, that's about it.
Text:
On reading some of the reviews of Ritigala on TripAdvisor, I was expecting some kind of Indiana Jones-esque ancient ruin in the jungle.  It's not.  

As we had already used half a day in a Sigiriya visit, my partner and I decided to take a trip to nearby Ritigala during our final day in the Habarana area.  Our driver took us as far as he dared and we then clambered aboard the the tuk tuk that had followed us from Habarana (on reflection, we should have just got the tuk tuk from there).   After a short ride along a bumpy dirt track, we arrived at a few scruffy buildings and were ushered inside one to sign the visitor book and also pay the 'donation' fee of 500Rs each.   can't complain about the 500Rs as that is pretty much pocket change to most westerners.  From there we were offered a tour guide to which we declined as we preferred just to explore ourselves.  

The ruins are not impressive at all - they don't seem particularly ancient.  If you've been anywhere there are some impressive ruins  - e.g. Pompeii, Athens or Latin America, you might even walk past the Ritigala ruins assuming that the real ruins are further on.  Well, they aren't.   When you reach a point where there's a square with some old building foundations, the rest of the path is blocked off - apparently it's because of the risk from dangerous wildlife (snakes, scorpions etc)..   I'd actually have been quite interested in seeing some of those but safety first, I suppose.

On the positive side, it's a reasonably pleasant walk in the forest with all the Sri Lanka forest noises that you'd expect - we didn't see much in the way of wildlife -  a few interesting bright red bugs and a couple of monkeys in the trees but it's more of a walk in the park than a walk on the wild side.

Truthfully, I'd skip Ritigala unless you have a lot of time to kill and have run out of other things to do.

Title: Ritigala
Text:
We decided to go to Ritigala only 14 km from Habarabana to try to get a bit of the beaten track. It was very much a success. 

The park is an old monastery with surprisingly well conserved ruins. Tourists have obviously not truly spotted this place (yet!) and the artefacts are not covered in glas etc. but appears to be as they were left by the monks a few thousand years ago. 

At the entrance about 2 km from the actual park there is a visitor centre which is quickly overseen. We did not see any official staff but were met by 3-4 men with a jeep who adviced us that an ordinary car could not make it the last 2km to the park as the road was damaged. Instead they proposed to take us by jeep and give us a tour for 4000 rupees. We took it for a scam (of which there are many in Sri Lanka) but when we decided to walk the last bit one of them insisted on following us at least to park. To make a long story short the truth was that the road WAS impassable by ordinary car and the elephant danger was in fact very real. The elephant stories were later validated by pictures and other locals. As elephants are present all year nobody should try to walk, but in dry seasons (we visited in January) any car can do the trip.

We ended up asking the "guide" to follow with us the entire trip which was a good decision as - his poor English aside - was very knowlegable about the site and show us stuff we would never have found by ourselves. 

The trip includes a approx 4km hike up a mountain side (medium intensity) and lasts about 2-3hours. Title: The Ultimate Challenge: Conquering Sigiriya Rock
Text:
Sigiriya Rock, also known as Lion Rock, is an impressive landmark located just 30 minutes away from Dambulla village in Sri Lanka. The rock can be reached by tuk-tuk or bus and is a must-see destination for any traveler to the country.

It's recommended to arrive early to avoid the crowds and make the most of your visit. The entrance fee is $30, but it's worth it for the breathtaking views from the top. The climb is of moderate difficulty, so make sure to wear comfortable sneakers and bring a bottle of water to stay hydrated along the way.

As you make your way to the top, you'll pass by ancient ruins and intricate frescoes, all while taking in the stunning scenery around you. Title: Stunning and a little scary but well worth it
Text:
My vertigo has got worse with age. It was put to the test getting up the stairs to the top of the rock, but thankfully one of the local guides put his hands on my waist and guided me up. It gave me a little bit of security that I needed to finish the trek.
The fact there was one of Sri Lanka's many cute stray dogs at the top of the rock just rubbed salt into the wound and made me realise I should have been a little more robust.

Sigiriya is one of Sri Lanka's best-known sites to see and it easy to understand. It is an incredible archaeological site, and the mind boggles when you reach the top passing the ancient steps people clambered up, and you realise a whole civilisation lived here. The views from the top are truly breathtaking and well worth the wobbly legs on the way up. Monkeys and butterflies and fortunately no hornets were enough distraction from the rocky drop below. 

The walk-up is a workout, and I was dripping with sweat when I reached the top but having said that it was over 30 degrees, so dripping with sweat was just the norm. 

If you go to Sigiriya and don't think you will make it to the top, then I would recommend not going. Getting to the top is what this excursion is about, and once there, the sense of achievement is tremendous but more significant is the experience of what you see all around. 

There are plenty off guides around if you want one. I would have got one personally, but my partner is a little more frugal and not as free-tipping as I. But when a man is willing to hold the waist of another grown man with wobbly legs to get him to the top - he deserves a tip.

Sigiriya is the kind of place that now lives in my dreams, and for that, I am grateful.

Title: Worth the steep climb
Text:
An amazing place that you must visit, if you're in Sri Lanka. Most package or guided tours will take you here (or get a taxi/tuk-tuk), and if they have any sense, you'll arrive early in the morning, That way you not only miss the queues at the entrance, but you can be up, down, and gone before the hot sun makes it even more difficult! There are a lot of steps (1200), and some of them are steep/high, and some of them are a little bit scary - especially if you have a poor head for heights. There are no facilities for wheelchairs. In fact, you probably need be pretty able bodied to do this one.
We had a guide who took us slowly from the top to the bottom, stopping to show us the small details we might otherwise have missed, and also to give us a breather! There are plenty of things to see before you reach the upper staircase. But once you are at the top, it provides a spectacular view (though early morning mist can limit this), and there are some extensive ruins. You'll be scratching your head trying to figure out how they got all the bricks up there. Get there early to beat the queues (the stairs are very narrow), or get there later for a clear view. 
Take your pick. Definitely one of the highlights of my trip to Sri Lanka. There's nowhere else like it.
Tips - wear sensible shoes, carry water, and although a hat is useful, it can get pretty windy up the top, so hang on to it.

Title: Telling it how it is
Text:
My Husband and I were here 4 weeks ago and decided to go early in the morning at 7am as the heat and humidity was just horrid anyway and thought it would be less then, but it really wasn't. Anyway we went shortly after opening time which is at 7am. Now, we are both nearly 60 years old and totally unfit fatties and both of us have bad hearts, bad knees and ankles, plus me with an already sprained ankle from a collapsing bridge a week earlier, but hey, I wasn't going to come all this way from Australia and not climb this Sigiriya Rock right?. Anyway we climbed to the very top in 50 minutes from the very start to the very top, including a few stops in between to catch our breath and trying to stop out hearts from exploding, but just quietly were were so very proud of ourselves, so kudos to us. Now just a word of warning, for those of you who have really bad knees or ankles this climb is not for you, and if you have even the slightest fear of heights, this climb is definitely not for you. I'd say go as far as the Lions feet and that's it as it is really frightening after that especially if people are trying to get past you and your clinging to the edge of the rock for grim death while letting them pass. For those of you who are not scared of heights then go on up to the very top, the 360 degree view you will love and you get to see all the ruins also. I must say watch out for the scammers too who will approach you along the way up at different points, they will make conversation with you and try and help you get up rocks etc and they will start to tell you all about the rock and the history and then they will become your guide without you even knowing about it and it will cost you money, but if you want to use them then go ahead, these locals are desperate for money. Also when you get there, there is no signage, well in English anyway, to where you buy the entry tickets from, we found it a bit confusing where to go to get the tickets, and that's a walk in itself too. There are plenty of Tuk Tuks at the bottom when you come back down that will take you back to your Hotels at a reasonable price. Just be aware that where the Tuk Tuks will drop you off at the start where you buy your tickets from is not the same place where you finish up when you come back down from the rock, you seem to get rail roaded out a different exit to an other side of the rock so you end up having to go past all the souvenir stalls. Our rooky mistake was telling our Tuk Tuk driver to pick us up here where he dropped us off, and he failed to tell us this was not the spot you finish up at when you come down from the rock, so once we came down and realised this was not where we started from, we then had to figure out how to get back around to the other side of the rock where the entrance was to meet our tuk tuk driver who was waiting so patiently for us, it was a long walk in the heat.
 All in all, we were both glad we did it and didn't drop dead from heat exposure and blown heart valves. We never want to see another step again as long as we live, our knees and ankles were aching for days afterwards. But done it now and so a big TICK off our bucket list.

Text: This is one of the impressive UNESCO World Heritage Sites we have visited. Steep entrance fee LKR5,460 per person, but it is well worth it! Kashyapa lost the battle and committed suicide, and Moggallana returned to Anuradhapura after winning the battle, and Sigiriya Rock was converted to a monastery. Four parts to appreciate this site: First, the fortress at the foot of the rock with viewing site of Sirigiya Rock from far after passing by the main entrance surrounded by moat. Fourth, where is the last part at top of rock where the ruins of the palace is located. The idea of building a Palace on top of a massive rock is already very incredible! 360 degree panoramic views from the top is amazing with sunset view in the evening. In summary, this heritage consists of intriguing historical background, plus the incredible architecture back then in 5th century. It is one of the highlights of our Sri Lanka trip!

Title: Advice for people with a fear of heights.
Text:
Trip advisor Sigiriya 

I am writing this mainly for people who, like me, have a fear of heights. 

Most reviews focus on the effort of getting up the rock. I am moderately fit and found it hardly taxing at all. My Apple Watch said I had climbed 48 flights of stairs but it did not feel anywhere near that much. 

More of a challenge for me was the height and especially the two separate  flights of iron stairs. 

I had debated whether to do the climb at all and was pretty apprehensive. Having done it, my advice would be to do it if you have a mild fear of heights or a moderate fear that is under control ie not subject to serious panic attacks. It also helps to have a supportive companion. I would suggest not doing it if your fear is more severe. 

Most stairs are stone with balustrades but there are two iron sections:-
One that leads up from the mirror wall via a caged-in iron spiral staircase to the cave paintings. (You go up to the paintings but then have to come down again to continue.) The steps are solid so one cannot see the drop below but of course you can look out as you go round. I managed this by focussing on the central post of the staircase and talking encouragingly to myself! if you are anxious about this you can probably bypass the cave paintings and head straight for the Lions Claw platform, although the paintings are interesting. 

Another section leads up from the Lions Claws level to the top. This has iron sections crossing the rock, again with solid steps, but is more exposed. Going up was easier as one faces the rock. I was more anxious about coming down but my husband went in front of me so I could hold on to his back with one hand and the railing with the other. The walkway gets quite crowded which slows the descent but means you are surrounded by people. This made me feel less exposed. I was nervous but it was very manageable. I have found other places more challenging like going up a tower in San Giminiano and inside the dome of St PaulÂs. 

I would make two other points:-
There are guides along the way who look out for people who look anxious and are quite insistent about holding your hand. Kind but probably better declined. 
The remains at the top and the views are very impressive - well worth the effort - and if you get there with your fear of heights, a real achievement. 

I hope this is helpful - it would have helped me if I had been able to read this before I went.

Title: Very impressive. Must visit
Text:
This ancient attraction is just as impressive and awe-inspiring as websites and other reviewers have said. The site is a massive one and other than the rock fortress (for which there is an entry fee), there are other places which visitors can roam for free. As you get down, you will be approached by numerous guides who will try to dissuade you from buying tickets to the rock fortress by mentioning the arduous 1200 step climb and instead offer you a tuk-tuk ride covering the places which are free. They arent aggressive but can be pushy, so you need to firmly tell them off.
Foreigners need to but tickets from the museum (entry to which is USD 5 if brought separately and complimentary if you purchase the rock fortress tickets). The museum is a good place to start off your visit.
The tickets to the rock fortress are USD 30 for adults and USD 15 for children. SAARC country nationals are entitled to a 50% discount on the adult price but no further discounts for children (so USD 15 for both adults and children). Payment can be made in USD or LKR but change, if any, is returned in LKR.
The climb itself is actually quite difficult, especially if you go in the afternoon. The place is also crowded on weekends because of lots of locals coming for a picnic.
My suggestion would be to go early morning to beat the heat and the crowds. Carry lots of water and snacks as well, as there werent any outlets selling food or water.
The way up is different from the way down, so take pictures as you go up, because you wont get the same view on the way down.
A lot of people have suggested the recommended length as being 3-4 hours but from my experience, it takes a lot longer, especially if you have young children and also explore the whole place. So in my opinion, take your time and enjoy the whole place in all its splendour and beauty. Dont try to rush things through and combine this with another attraction (like Dambulla, Anuradhapura etc) because those places too require more than 3-4 hours and it would be better to comprehensively cover both places rather than do a bit of both.

Title: Best tip: go early!
Text:
We were counting on the climb to the Sigiriya ancient rock fortress to be one of the highlights of our trip to Sri Lanka.  And it certainly was!  The best piece of advice we can give you is to go early.  This will help with the heat and with the crowds.  The rock opens at 6:30 am, which is when we arrived. Be warned that the price is hefty: around $30.  At the gate, a guard will take any label off your water bottle, so you can save time by doing this in advance.  Then, you will proceed on a straight path for about 10 minutes just to reach the beginning of the stairs to climb.  We were pleasantly surprised that the climb, while strenuous and very sweaty, was not as difficult as we expected.  We were not hurrying, and made it to the top in about 20 minutes.  I do feel this is primarily because there was no one else in our way on the stairs.  I can see how this would easily become a bottleneck and slow down your progress.

Once at the top, you will be rewarded with beautiful views of the surrounding area.  The ruins are peaceful to explore when crowds are light.  On our way down at 7:30 am, the crowds were now rolling in, so even 8 am is too late to embark.

Do go early, do take water, and enjoy the experience!

Title: Go early, must visit place.
Text:
Sigiriya is ancient rock citadel located in Sri LankaÂs cultural triangle. The enormous rock towers above the surrounding jungle offering extensive views. I will suggest to stay nearby and start the hike as early as 06:30AM as the temperatures rises to 100 degrees Fahrenheit and humidity around 80%. You have to climb about 1200 steep steps with elevation gain of about 650 feet. My advice is to start early, drink water regularly, wear hat, use sunscreen and go slow. If you are from SAARC countries then carry your passport to get 50% discount on admission ticket. 
Sigiriya is a world heritage site declared by UNESCO in 1982. It is a unique combination of 5th century urban planning, architecture, engineering, hydraulics, garden design, painting and poetry. 
The city is designed in a square module 2750 meter east to west and 925 north to south. 
1. Royal Gardens- This is massive water gardens. 
2. Three water gardens. 
3. Boulder Garden- It begins at slope of hill at base of the rock. 
4. Cistern Rock- Huge stone that has been split. 
5. Audience Hall Rock
6. Preaching Rock
7. Painted maidens- These frescos  are preserved in a cave pocket about 40 feet above walkway. 
8. Mirror Wall- Highly polished surface is original stucco. Most poetic verses had been written in praise of maidens on cliff face. 
9. Lion Terrace. 
10. Palace- It is located on summit but none of superstructure remains.

Text:
An absolute must do for anyone who is able to make the ascent, Sigiriya Rock is stunning! 

Seen from below, the massive granite outcrop looks daunting. ItÂs a  challenge to climb, but mainly because of the heat and crowds. (Go early enough and you can mostly avoid both.)

We made it to the top in 30 minutes, with two young kids, and two adults with bad knees! We arrived around 800 and were glad we had because it was incredibly crowded as we descended. 

The water gardens viewable on the approach are impressive. Incredible feats of ancient ingenuity and engineering prowess. 

The climb is well organized and with the $30 US for adults (kids 6-12 are half price). Most of the way you go up metal stairs the are secured to the rock face. These are narrow, and a bit unnerving when the wind gusts, but we saw people of all ages and fitness levels work their way up.

It is worth the sweat and sore legs when you reach the top!

The palace ruins are incredible, but it is the 360 degree vistas that are the real payoff. We spent close to an hour roaming around and snapping breathtaking pics.

The descent retraces the final section of the climb, at first, before reaching a much easier exit pathway. Again, it took roughly half an hour.

One of the coolest, and most singular, experiences IÂve ever had!

Text:

Title: Must visit museum in Kandy-Revisit the rich tea heritage
Text:
The Ceylon Tea museum was incorporated on 9th January 1998 under Section 21 of the Companies act no 17 of 1982 and declared open to the public on 1st December, 2001. It is housed in the 1925 established Hanthana tea factory, 4kms from Kandy and at a height of 2499 feet. The museum consists of four floors. The ground floor has the Engine room and Rolling room where old machinery connected with the tea industry are displayed. The first floor has Drier room and furnace room and related machinery displayed. The second floor has sifting room and related equipments. The James Taylor museum and the archive room is also located on this floor. The third floor is allocated to Tea sales outlets where one can buy the finest selection of Ceylon Tea.

The entire fourth floor area is a restaurant where visitors are served complimentary tea. They can also take part in Tea tasting session. A panoramic view of the Kandy town surrounded by beautiful Hunnasgiriya Knuckles range and the Matale range of hills can be viewed through a telescope here. This floor also has the original cat walk platform which was used by the superintendent and the tea maker of the tea factory for monthly inspection of the roof and removal of any tea fluff.

The tea industry of Ceylon is in rapid decline because there is a lack of vision for its future.  The British gave this country a wonderful legacy upon which a significant future was squandered away.  The country has lost its European markets and this industry is mired in practices which are known to most people through their own media in the country as totally inappropriate. The sad thing is that most people who can do something about it lack the energy, courage and ability to do anything about it.  Still the Museum as it stands is an effective monument to the creative effort of many good people to provide an opportunity for an outstanding character to take this industry to a better place.

It calls for hard work, courage, fortitude and capability to turn it around. The rewards will be substantial but  the inheritors have taken a long time-about 45 years.

Title: My visit to Colombo National Museum
Text:
A gem of a museum, going by the priceless exhibits in it. 

If anyone wants to know about the amazingly close civlisational, cultural, artistic and spiritual bonds between Sri Lanka and India during the various eras of history, there is no better place to discover it than in this museum. It will surprise and disappoint those who believe Hinduism and Buddhism are dissimilar or mutually antagonistic. The museum has relatively less focus on Sri Lanka's Islamic heritage.

I had gone to see the trilingual (Chinese, Tamil, Persian) stone inscription about the voyage of the great Chinese explorer Zheng He (1371-1433), who visited both Sri Lanka and India. The inscription shows that he offered prayers to Allah, Buddha and Shiva (a Hindu deity) for his own safety and for peace in the world. A good historical example of Sri Lanka-India-China affinity.

My two big complaints about the museum: 1) The Museum Shop is hopelessly small and short of material on sale; and 2) The museum guides should be proficient in English and know more about the history of the museum and its exhibits.

If you are a visitor to Colombo, don't miss it.

Expect nearly a full day here if you are a museum geek like me.

Title: Window Into the Past
Text: This a well laid-out display of important parts of  Srilankan history. The display starts from the Paleolithic era and ends at the recent past (1930-1940). The most impressive part for me as a visitor was from the 12th century until colonisation by Portugal. If I remember correctly, there are some stone works in section 3. This area gives a good overview of how and why stone works were important at that time. They has been used largely to store information, for example land ownership, taxation rights, demarcation points and etc. Also, in day to day live (example toilets, baths) .The details, the precision, the tools available and the material used gives an idea about the knowledge level at that time. The adjacent display was based on craft, jewellery,  weaponry and artefacts. There is a small section dedicated for jewellery worn by kings and queens. It is truly breathtaking. The artists have taken extraordinary care to preserve the original structure of gems embedded, they have handmade minute links connected in multiple dimensions. Some of those jewels are currently in fashion but they are nowhere near what was achieved at that time. You have to see it to understand. This whole room contains the Srilankan craft heritage. Since craft and artistic excellence is a demonstration of how advanced the society is, the ordinary population seems to have lived in a sophisticated healthy society during this time. You will have to allocate three hours to view this complete display.

Title: Just Go - You Really Have To - Show Some Solidarity.
Text:
So, you're on holiday, having an amazing time and there are many reminders of the tragedy that occurred 0n 26th December 2004, but it's fairly easy to skip by and carry on enjoying yourselves; it's hard not to in Sri Lanka.
You really do need the context of what the people who look after you went through and the Museum is an excellent effort to inform and remind us.
Reading the comments from other reviews, yes, there might be underlying issues around the funding and income from the museum, but in the great scheme of things, giving a few Â£ is well worth doing.
Our understanding is that the government provide very little - the community and various foreign aid agencies have done it all themselves, with a huge emphasis on helping children and families in the aftermath. Sri Lanka was a war zone at the time.
The lady and a young guy who were there for us have to bear the reminders of this traumatic time and explain it, repeatedly, to us as we visit - that must be incredibly tough. She said that she lost 2 close relatives and she clearly had been involved in this project since its inception; she could explain everything there, in great detail.
Everyone will take away different but abiding memories. For me, there were 3:
There's a photo of a Western looking lady running towards her husband and kids, who seem to have gone exploring on the beach when the tide initially ran way out. They are now facing a massive wall of water and I would imagine that within seconds these people would have drowned. It could have been almost any of us.
The second was that the railway line runs along the beachside. It was holiday time. An 8 carriage train was packed with well over 1,500 people and it was caught as the wave came 2.5kms inland. They all drowned. It remains the largest loss of life in a rail accident, in the world and it happened right there. How you can you begin to comprehend it?
Lastly, as you walk nearby, there's a superb Buddha memorial. It's about 50-60 feet high ÂÂ the height of the wave as it came over. That puts everything into perspective.
You really should go, just to try and help to show solidarity with the wonderful people you've met on your fantastic holiday.

Title: Moving and Beautiful - not your typical museum.
Text: I went with my husband and three children to this museum and it was a memorable experience.  It is easy when you see the beauty of Sri Lanka to forget the tragedy that it faced not so long ago.  This museum is in the former home of the woman who runs it - the home was nearly destroyed by the tsunami.  There are photos and art work about the day that changed the island forever.   The first building is more factual, explaining about the wave and the other aspects of the tsunami.  The second building has more graphic images.  Our older daughter and my husband went through that part and our younger two children and I hung behind.  It isn't a museum like most you are used to - there is no dramatic lighting, no air conditioning, no gift shop.  It is a dirt floored home full of true artifacts.  You come out feeling a combination of absolute devastation for what the people faced and extreme hope for all the has happened since that.  A truly beautiful and moving experience.

Title: A Must-visit site
Text:
This place is not your typical marble-floored, double-storied museum, instead it's a rather small, open hut, with posters hanging on the mud lined walls. Posters of devastation and desparation. It's hard not o cry when you see some of the pictures of the tsunami that hit Sri Lanka in 2004. There is so much detail and information here. Details of the deatht toll not just in Sri Lanka, but also elsewhere in Asia where the tsunami hit. A detailed map of the regions affected, first-hand accounts of what happened, survival accounts but also of what they saw of the people who weren't so lucky. The before and after pictures of the areas were heart-wrenching. There are also personal items that I believe were recovered from the tsunami aftermath. It's worth a visit to contemplate just how profound and devastating the tsunami was for Sri Lankans. 

There are actually two tsunami museum places a few minutes walk from each other. Both are filled with heart breaking pictures of the tsunami and it's aftermath but one of them also contains some science behind the formation of tsunamis, brief details of how to survive/prepare emergency flood bags and it is run by a lady who was present on that fateful day. You can ask her for her account which somehow makes the whole experience even more real and profound.

There are donation boxes at both sites and as it's maintained by volunteers using the money from donation, there is an expectation that you leave a donation. It can be of any amount and they don't actually watch you while you leave the money in the box so it's not as awkward.

Title: A CULTURAL MEMORIAL
Text:
If the hedonistic delights of the turquoise beaches of southern Sri Lanka can get a bit overwhleming, there is a peaceful getaway in the town of Koggala just off the A2 (Galle Road),beyond Galle and directly opposite the spa hotel intimidatingly called The Fortress.
Titled the Martin Wickramasinghe Museum of Folk Culture,the attraction, to visit which there is a small admission fee, is spread over several acres around his birthplace and has been visualised as a memorial to this doyen of Sri Lankan writers and a man of letters. Such a
initiative was close to his heart and therefore the Trust in his name has built a museum depicting folk arts and crafts and folk technology,and re-creates the work of craftsmen and their role in rural society.
Following entry,one traverses a path through several interesting botanical specimens of trees,
Walking Pine tree,Golden Shower pudding pipe tree,Beauty Leaf Alexandrian laurel and other unique varieties before reaching the small house where Martin Wickramasinghe was born.It was designed as a home typical of the headman,the tacher,and the native physician, the rural village gentry of the early 19th century.A samadhi (grave)where his ashes were interred in 1976  and later his wife's in 2001 are nearby. The samadhi and the house of his birth are symbols that span over seven decades of continuous intellectual exploration and creative writing.
The high-roofed,spacious halls of the Folk Museum house a vast array of artifacts of Sri Lankan folk culture and life.
Traditional vehicles used for travel and transport such as carriages and canoes are displayed in separate sheds.
One can easily spend 2-3 hours in this memorial absorbing the many facets of Sri Lankan culture before being rejuvenated to experience the modern way of life in this beautiful country.

Title: A preview before you embark on the actual site visit
Text:
At first, I thought the museum is free. But no. It is not free. You can enter if you bought the main ticket to the Sigiriya Citadel. For foreigners, the counter to purchase the entrance ticket is also located inside the museum. 

I could have go in for a preview before the actual landing but I came after visiting the actual site. There were photographs taken of the Lion Rock during the colonial days and before the actual restoration works commenced. There is also a video showing a helicopter view of the citadel at the summit of the rock and the other attractions way up the steel ladder. The sound effect of the video was not very good. The volume should be turned on louder.  

The museum also showcased how the restoration and preservation works on the cave frescoes were carried out. It is great laborious preservation work. I was sorry to take a photo of the frescoes earlier at the actual site which could have caused damage to the preserved frescoes. I was lucky to be let off with a reprimand from the staff of the archaeology department. 

The last time I saw such cave frescoes was at the Mogao Caves in Dunhuang, China. The monks who traveled along the old Silk Road and resided in the Mogao Caves left behind such beautiful masterpieces. At that time, I was also advised not to take photos at the frescoes. But when I came here I really forgot about the advice. I should have seen the painstaking effort of the archaeology experts shown in the museum and reminded myself before proceeding to the actual site. 

The frescoes shown at the museum were impressive, colorful and sharper than those actual images at the site. The female figures look voluptuously gorgeous and beautiful. 

Other than those I mentioned, there is nothing much in the museum. I left the museum in less than an hour. It is more a preview before visiting the actual site.

Title: Fairly modern but a little disappointing after visiting Lion Rock
Text:
Sigirya Museum lies just off the main path from the Entrance to the Lion Rock and is probably best visited after climbing the Rock itself, especially if you are visiting early to beat the crowds and the heat.

It's a fairly modern building and sits unobtrusively on the site but the charge of $5 to enter it seems a little much after already paying $30 at the main entrance to visit the Lion Rock.

After passing through a reconstructed angular brick entranceway copying originals found elsewhere on the site there is a fairly obvious route to follow with a series of cased artifacts mainly from Sigirya, along with a fairly nice model of the Lion Rock in it's landscape that helps to put things in perspective.

There is also a full size replica of of the rock overhang and the Apsara Paintings to be found high up on the Lion Rock. Surprisingly, because photography is banned in the museum that means you can take photographs of the original paintings high up on the Lion Rock but you cannot take photographs of the copies down in the museum. Surely this is short sighted especially for visitors who can't make it to the top of the rock due to mobility problems and who would benefit from being able to visit the museum alone. Approaching the exit there is a diorama with an indigenous structure and examples of some traps that seem out of place somehow, almost as though they were put here because no-one quite knew where else to put them because they don't fit in with the rest of the exhibits, though given the museum's size there is plenty of room for more to be added.

If you want a souvenir don't expect to find it or a guide book in the museum itself. There is an official looking store nearby if you turn to the left on leaving with a limited range of reasonably nice but sometimes quite expensive items. There is also a slim but well illustrated guide book in several languages, but if you want a guide book you would do better to keep your eyes open for one elsewhere in Sri Lanka before your visit to Sigirya. Surprisingly one of the best ones I saw was in a shop in the airport.  There is also a smaller independent store nearby on the same block but it too had little to offer and the same guidebook was on sale there as in the larger shop but no cheaper when we visited.

The museum isn't really bad and it's nicely laid out, but I found it  a bit disappointing after the sights and the experience offered by an ascent of the Lion Rock and an exploration of the grounds. Being charged again to go in, instead of being allowed in with the same ticket purchased at the main entrance to the site was also unwelcome. Our visit probably lasted around 20-25 minutes and I in hindsight I don't think we would have been left with regrets had we not gone in. It's ok but nothing special.

Title: Educational and good for rainy days
Text:
Summary:  Your relative happiness with this museum relates to expectations and how much 500LKR means to you. I got what I wanted out of it, but removing a star only because I think that I don't represent everyone.

WHAT THE MUSEUM IS:  The museum is a collection curated by each contributing country around the world that has a long history of Buddhism. The first floor is split with a general overview of Buddha and a number of Central Asia's booths. Upstairs you get SE and East Asia.  The museum gives a brief history of Buddhism for each contributing nation and shows you the sites that are particularly famous in each country's landscape.

WHAT THE MUSEUM IS NOT: Low rating reviews can be divided into 3 groups.  The first, takes issue that the museum is not indepth enough. I would recommend these people just use this museum as an overview and then actual go and visit these countries if you're that passionate.  The second group, feels that there is some misrepresentation that has happened for a given country, for example China. I would remind individuals that Buddhism is not about forcing others to their will. I'm glad they did not use this museum to become political and thus alienate, only to educate. The third group feels that there is some sort of agenda that was espoused.  I did not see it. Mostly, I saw a great exhibit that added places to my travel list. 

THE VIBE:  I thought everyone was pleasant. The museum is requires quiet. Most people adhered to this. Likely for this reason there isn't a lot of talking/guides/etc. Buddhism is about self- contemplation and this museum adheres to that.  Shoes off is very buddhist as is no pictures.  I think those that cringed on all these things, likely have too little experience with this religion.

LANGUAGES:  Most stuff is in English, Tamil, and Sinhalese.  There is SOOO Much reading. There are also videos in the C. Asia exhibits were a nice touch, but other than the one from India, I found them hard to follow. I think perhaps the Buddhist orgs of these two countries might want to work on what they are trying to present and maybe update these videos in the future. 

COST:  Given the nation's average income and that it's only been at peace for 10 years, this is a great museum. Yes, the foreigners pay more, but I didn't find 500LKR outrageous for what it must cost to keep the lights on and staff paid, particularly in low season.  That said, it would be good for the museum to continue to work with other buddhist groups to raise private funding and continue to upgrade the exhibits. 

SUGGESTED UPGRADES:  Since each nation is contributing, possibly Samsung (one of the main sponsors) can provide an app or some device for which all of the different countries can translate a guided tour of the place.  Also, I would love to see them get more artifacts, particularly for C. Asia and China. The rooms were a bit too much text.  China in particularly, could modify the way it presents all the text toward more visual demonstration of the way Buddhism has advanced over time.  I think the best example of a buddhist museum for this place to draw inspiration might be the Angkor Wat Museum in Cambodia. Also, it would be great, if there was an area outside of the museum that could answer questions that individuals had afterwards. I'm not sure how much funding that would cost... maybe they could partner with a university or something. 

FINAL NOTES:  I really enjoyed seeing this overview of Buddhism across countries. I don't think people really appreciate what it might even mean to begin to collect an over 5000 year history of the religion and it's variation across such a ridiculously large land mass. The manner in which some of the leaders were able to blend Buddhism with other religions and cultures is truly remarkable, particularly relative to the other major global sects.  Great start to a museum. Keep going.

Text:

In an effort to avoid the ÂcircusÂ of Yala we chose to come to Bundala instead. We arrived at 6.00 when it opened and were immediately rewarded by seeing a group of elephants emerging from the morning mist! We spent about 3 hours in the park (including having a break on a viewpoint overlooking the amazing coastline) and saw so many different types of birds (indigenous and migratory), crocodiles, mongoose, monitor lizards, monkeys, macaques, and another herd of elephants (there are only 25 in the park so we were very lucky!)  In all that time we only saw 1 other jeep, the rest of the time we were alone in nature. The landscape is spectacular, especially as is the wet season and so very verdant!

The tickets for two cost 6150 rupees. This includes a tracker who joins the jeep at the ticket office. Ours was called Kapila, and his knowledge especially of the different birds was impressive. Avoid the toilets if you can!!

Title: Wonderful natural environment
Text:
We were initially unsure as to whether to do this safari or not, as there had been quite a lot of rain during the day. At around 2pm we decided to go for it, and took the afternoon safari run by our hotel, the Coconut Garden Hotel & Restaurant. The cost of the safari was 11500 LRP, all-inclusive for 2 people. We had the jeep to ourselves.

The drive from our hotel to Bundala National Park was pleasant and we stopped several times to view birds and monkeys. The park itself is quite small in comparison to Yala National Park. The procedure of getting into the park was much smoother than at Yala National Park as there was only one other jeep waiting with us to get into the park.

During our entire two hours of Safari at the park, we saw just one other jeep in the park. As a result we found the animals to be far less acclimatised to safari jeeps and to be more relaxed and wild in their behaviour.

While we were at the park, we saw lots of peacocksÂ one displaying his tail feathers to a group of females; two male elephants - the first 10 to 15 years old, eating vegetation by the side of the lake; the second around 30 to 40 years old having a drink at a waterhole, then covering himself with mud, before heading back into the forest. We also saw several jungle fowl, lots of blue-tailed bee-eaters, many painted storks, Indian darters, many egrets & cormorants, many red-billed lapwings, Ibis, open-billed Ibis, storks, fishing eagles & a large sea eagle in flight and several green parrots. There were also many water buffalo, several medium sized crocodiles basking beside waterholes, and many monkeys, both Macaques and the black-faced variety. Even the monkeys seemed far less stressed at this national park than the ones we have previously encountered throughout Sri Lanka. There were many tiny monkey babies, some only just a couple of days old.

Other animals we saw included several mongoose including a large and rare king mongoose, which we were told, is rarely seen. There were many land monitors, including a large one, sleeping high up on a tree branch. On the way out of the park, we spotted a large hare sitting by a waterhole.

We stopped at a lovely vantage point on a cliff-top to view the rocks below with large waves crashing against them. From there we could see a lovely beach below with fishermen shacks and fishing vessels waiting to go to sea. We also saw a large sea turtle coming up to breathe down below.

One the way back from the national park, we stopped to see the fruit bats rousing from their sleep for their nightly feed. The on these same trees, many of the other birds after a day of foraging, were coming to roost for the night.

Finally, if you wish to see birds and other animals in a truly wild and natural environment, without all of the thousands of jeeps that fight for vantage point in Yala; then this is the national park for you.

Title: Beautiful hike through the misty terrains
Text:
We started our hike through Horton Plains early in the morning to catch a sunrise over the misty hills and terrains. What can I say, it was definitely worth waking up so early. We saw plenty of deers eating fresh grass even before we entered the main gate of the park, and then had an enjoyable walk along the route towards Baker's Falls. 

There are two options: you can start with the Falls and finish by the Little World's End or vice versa. We chose the first option and did not regret it. After we saw the sunrise, the sun quickly disappeared behind the clouds and we did not see it much until we reached the falls and the skies became blue. We took wonderful photos and had our packed breakfast right there on a bench, which was so romantic and enjoyable.

When we continued our route towards the World's End, we realized how right we were in taking that path - we almost always hiked down rather than climbing up and it made our trekking way more comfortable and less tiring. The day before we hiked the Adam's Peak, so we could not feel our legs and feet after that and this path we chose turned out to be helpful :) 

Unfortunately, when we reached the World's End, a big cloud hung on top and covered all the view. We waited for 30 minutes and the situation remained the same. We still were pleased with the hike and the World's End because there was a certain mystery in this endless mist over the edge. You can literally feel you are on the edge of nowhere.

P.S. In my opinion, you won't need a guide to hike Horton Plains. It is super easy and it is impossible to get lost on the way. There is literally only one path and it is a round journey, so whatever way you choose - you will end up in the same place. Only if a lady is solo and scared of being attacked or something??? But generally, for me it seemed peaceful and safe. And if a leopard comes out from a bush, I don't think that having a guide will be helpful right??)))

Also the time you will spend there will be at least 4-5 hrs if you do not want to run along the whole route and wish to take nice pictures and just enjoy the nature around you. So don't listen to people who tell it is like a 3-hour hike. Maybe, if you don't complete the whole circle..)

Title: Unremarkable hike, excessive admission fees... just not worth it
Text:
My lovely wife and I took the morning hike through Horton Plains National Park to World's End. It's a hugely popular hike but in truth is rather unremarkable. 
The trail meanders through rather mundane scenery to the lookout point which offers pretty impressive views. Having said that, I wasn't entirely blown away by them. There are, for example, plenty of vistas in Scotland that are equally if not more impressive.
The high numbers of visitors mean there isn't a great deal of wildlife to be seen. There were sambar deer hanging around near the car park, which I believe there often are, and we were lucky enough to spot a purple-faced leaf monkey while driving back to Nuwara Eliya. But don't expect too much. Leopard sightings around here are almost unheard of.

All in all it was actually a pleasant enough hike. But the trouble is that it costs way too much for what it is. Entry fees for the two of us came to around 8,000 rupees (Â£35, $44, Â40) which is just crazy. You'll also have to pay transport costs on top of that - for example we paid 3,000 rupees (Â£13, $17, Â15) for a tuk tuk from Nuwara Eliya. And it simply isn't worth the money for what it is.

Title: A trek worth making
Text:
This national park is the source for four of Sri Lanka's major rivers, so it's not unusual to experience a bit of rain. Fortunately, the heavy rain dropped the night before our 9.5 km trek through the park, which took in the spectacular World's End. It made some uneven parts of the trail a bit slippery, so solid hiking shoes or, at minimum runners, are essential.

Only a moderate level of fitness is required to navigate the main trail, which takes in World's End and Bakers Falls. However, anyone with some walking or climbing disability should take note that there are those uneven areas to negotiate. 

World's End is so called because of its 900 metre vertical cliff face that drops into the forest of the valley wall. It's hard to capture its scale in photographs. There are two viewing decks at World's End. Beware, particularly for children, that there are few barriers to prevent falls over the cliffs, both on the decks and on the short trail between decks. My impression was that the coiled razor wire would merely lacerate you during the fall rather than prevent it. The higher deck gives a much better view of the main cliff face. The steps down to Bakers Falls are also quite steep.

Hortons Plains features a wide variety of landscape and an explosion of different colours from the many plant species that adorn the plain. The area is also a good place to see Sambar Deer, one of Sri Lanka's larger deer species.

Title: Terrible experience buying tickets
Text:
We had a very unfortunate experience when buying tickets to enter Horton Plains National Park. We visited on the morning of Friday 12th July. Apologies for the long and less than positive review, I am also posting this hoping someone may be able to point me towards a way to lodge a complaint with the Park itself as I havenÂt been able to find this online. 

Ticket prices are not advertised as prices tend to fluctuate so there is no price list at the ticket booth. We asked for Â3 tickets, one person is localÂ, however this was interpreted as 3 tickets plus one local. A foreigner ticket at the time was ~2,650 rupees. With no price list, visitors the transaction is based purely on verbal communication with no calculator or screen to show how prices are calculated (there are three taxes on top of the ticket price). Understandably this is also a quick, rushed process during busy times such as when we visited.

Unfortunately, we were unable to realise we were overcharged until we had driven 10 minutes from the ticket office to the park entrance. At the park entrance we spoke with a number of staff and based on what they advised we decided to enter the park rather than drive back and seek a refund (lucky we did this because as we found out, we would not have been refunded anyway and it would have ruined our visit). 

On our way out we approached the ticket booth and fortunately the same cashier was working (a middle aged man, moustache, larger, has worked at the park for over 15 years). We were very careful to politely inform that we were accidentally overcharged (e.g. we avoided saying Âyou overcharged usÂ, instead saying Âwe were accidentally overchargedÂ) however he immediately went on the defensive, became very rude and irrational and refused to help us. He accused us of being irresponsible and not communicating with him properly. He also said there is no possibility of a refund once a sale has been made and its the customers responsibility to know what they are being charged and that he does not make mistakes so it must be our fault.  

When we tried to explain that we were not trying to pass blame and a simple misunderstanding had occurred, he became argumentative and started insulting our tour guide/driver in Sinhalese and saying he was not looking after us properly. He refused to call the park manager (he said there was no phone reception, although all three of us had reception) and said nobody would help us because it was our fault. There was lots of back and forth about ticket prices not being advertised, no way of knowing what we have been charged for until transaction has been finalised etc. until we finally decided that nothing we did or said would help us obtain a refund. Overall, this left a very sour taste in our mouths and our tour guide/driver felt ashamed that a park ranger would behave in this way. Unfortunately, the cashier did not have an ounce of empathy and his behaviour screamed dishonesty and not a care on the world for doing what is right. Had he at least even tried to help us in the slightest, our experience with him would have been completely difference. 

Lesson: when buying tickets and you have a local guide to accompany you, be very clear to say X foreigner tickets and Y local ticket. Avoid assuming any statements like Â3 people, one is localÂ as this will be interpreted as 3 foreigners, one localÂ.

As for the park itself, it is beautiful and the views are amazing. It was lovely walking through such stunning scenery. However, the price is quite high especially in comparison to similar yet free experiences we have had in Sri Lanka as well as other national parks we have visited around the world.

As walks go it was moderate - some steep slippery sections, and the landscape it crosses was quite interesting - undulating hills, interspersed with grasslands and forests.

I don't know what the park fees were as we did it as part of a package so in some respects it's better not to know and as I think the most expensive fees, it was nice to see the Rangers being very vigilant with hikers as far as long plastics go and to search each bag and advise to bring everything back out. Title: Well worth the early start
Text: We hadn't planned to head up to the Horton Plains before we got to Nuwara Eliya, but decided to on arrival and arranged an early pickup (5am) with our tuktuk driver.  Nuwara Eliya is cold at that time of day,and we were very grateful for our padded jackets - make sure you prep well for a cold morning!  The journey over in the dark was, well, interesting - low-lying mist on the unlit roads, speeding drivers trying to overtake at all opportunities (it is Sri Lanka after all!) and low powered tuktuk lights all made for a memorable trip!  After buying our entry tickets ($45 for two people including all fees and taxes) we headed up to the trail head as the sun was coming up, with a few scattered deer out on the plains - fairly magical!  The hike itself is a circular, so you can head either clockwise or anticlockwise - most guides say to go anticlockwise, as you reach Little World's End before World's End but we opted for the latter and didn't regret it at all - it's slightly easier as you get a flattish finish, and you also avoid most of the crowds - once we'd headed out the only people we saw for the first 4km or so were the quicker hikers heading past us (not sure why, this is the sort of place that deserves you take your time to soak in the atmosphere!)  The early start was a killer at 4.30am, but seemed like a great idea now - the light is beautiful at that time of day and there's still the early morning frost on the ground and low-lying mist in the valleys.  Baker Falls are nice (but no Iguazu!) and the views from World's End and it's little brother are great, but for me the real winner was the hike and the scenery - just magical at that time of day, and we felt at times we were no longer in Sri Lanka but maybe south America!  While we didn't see much wildlife on the outward part of the hike we saw quite a bit when heading back after Little World's End - a couple of giant squirrels and a few purple-faced leaf monkeys enjoying a feed in the early morning sun - plus quite a few birds.  The round trip is around 9km or so, but we took our time enjoying the journey.  Very highly recommended if you're in Nuwara Eliya - indeed, probably the best thing you can do here IMO!

Title: You need to be surefooted
Text: I didn't find this particularly taxing in terms of fitness, but there is a lot of picking your way over rocky and muddy paths, some quite steep. As advised we got there really early - make sure you allow about half an hour to queue for tickets, then drive the couple of miles more to the actual start of the trail (where there is a toilet and small cafe). You need to make sure you don't have any plastic bags, as they will be taken away at the gate, but plastic bottles are OK if the label is removed. It will be cold when you start (15 degrees when we left Nuwara Eliya at 5am, 12 degrees at the gate to Horton Plains at 6am), but once you start walking you will soon warm up, so only one extra layer is fine, and shorts would have been OK. We actually set off walking at 6.45. Shortly after the start you have a choice of which way round you go. We chose anticlockwise, but with hindsight, I think the clockwise route would have got us to World's End quicker. There is a map at the start, but few signs on the way. The terrain was tricky, with rocky paths to start, and a couple of streams to cross. It then got steeper, and much muddier, which slowed us up. Unless you've never seen a waterfall, don't waste time by diverting to Bakers Falls. It's good, but very much the supporting act, and you can always go back after you've been to World's End. We finally got to World's End at about 5 to 9, and were very fortunate indeed - literally within 5 minutes, the view had disappeared, the mist just rolling up the whole valley - quite a sight to see. So disappointing for anyone arriving after that, as there was nothing to see. The rest of the park is pleasant, but not spectacular. Further along the valley there is Mini World's End, but I can't tell you what the view would have been like! Title: A manageable walk!
Text:
As an obese person with a bad right knee and a recovering strained left upper thigh muscle, I was worried that I could not takÃ· on the challenge that was Horton's Plains, especially after reading horrifying reviews about it. Fortunately, all my fears were unfounded!

Walking at a moderate pace, I found the walk entirely manageable though there were some tricky parts such as the rocky sections of the trail. On this note, do make sure to wear good shoes! 

We were also blessed as the weather conditions were in our favour. It did not rain the day before and neither did it on our hiking day. As a result, the paths were not very muddy and therefore easier to traverse. My friend and I, however, could see why the trail might be challenging should the weather be poor. 

A note on safety precautions to take, do not go too close to the edge of the cliff at World's End. According to our guide, a tourist had plunged to her death just a few weeks before our trip in an attempt to take a selfie.

Some tips: 
1. Check the weather forecast
2. It is preferable to have a guide since some paths may not be clear to the inexperienced
3. Bring some food and water
4. Do not bring plastic bags as there are thorough bagchecks before one enters the park
5. It is okay to bring bottled water into the park. However, do remove the plastic seal and label around the bottle before entering the park. 
6. There are rubbish bins in the park. DO NOT LITTER. 
7. Do not make too much noise as that might scare away wildlife. We had an unpleasant encounter with a group of noisy and rude tourists and had to ask them to tone it down. Do respect the environment and be comsiderate to others. That way, the walk will be pleasant for everyone! :)

Overall, I enjoyed the trail as the views were lovely and it was certainly good exercise!

On our way out of the park at dusk, we were still seeing more elephants, walking through the edges of the forest. Absolutely a day to remember.

There are so many jeeps that at times it looks as though the elephants are closed into spaces due to the jeeps all around them.

This isn't all the time which is fortunate and seeing elephants (around 60 on the day), monkeys, plenty of birds and even a crocodile was amazing!

I would definitely recommend Kaudulla National Park and it's worth taking local advice as many people work in tours and can recommend what the animals are doing at that particular time of the year (they are likely to charge you the same jeep hire price regardless of if you go Minneriya or Kaudulla).

Enjoy the amazing animals but let's hope they begin to limit the number of jeeps allowed in at any time, otherwise this incredible national park will look more and more like a cruel zoo.

Title: Minneriya National Park Safari - Elephants are Beautiful but Tourists beware of SCAMS!
Text:
We came to Sigiriya during our roundtrip through Sri Lanka and stayed for two nights at a local homestay. Our plans were to climb Pidurangala Rock for sunrise and for the afternoon of our arrival we had hoped to do a kayaking trip on the nearby river. However, despite mentioned in Lonely Planet's guide, Rasta Rant does not offer those trips anymore.

So, we decided to return to our accommodation and since we are quite new to Sri Lanka and it is our first time here, relied on the help of our hosts to arrange the Safari on short-notice, instead of booking an offer we had found on Air BnB. The trip for two people was quickly scheduled and a driver showed up in his jeep an hour later. After driving for a while, he pulled on to a gas station, where he asked us whether we were going to Minneriya or some other park. We quickly said Minneriya, as this was what we had asked for from our hosts.

Once we got to the park, the driver (whom we had paid beforehand - 13,000 Rupees for 2 people as agreed with our hosts), went to the ticket counter. While he was gone, a man in what appeared to us as a park ranger uniform approached us and told us that today was a great day to see the elephants. When our driver returned, him and the "ranger" quickly exchanged some words, followed by him also getting into our car, shaking our hands and introducing himself.

During the drive he seemed very knowledgable in terms of the different animals and birds, told us he has been working at the park for over 10 years and that he would know all the best spots to see the elephants. Every now and then he hammered against the side of the jeep to make the driver stop and show us something. Everything seemed fine, until at the end of the drive the "ranger" got up to ask us if we were "very happy" and mumbled something about "I really need the tips." That's when we realised that this man is as far away from an official ranger as possible. 

We passed him some money so he would leave us alone and after again exchanging some words with the jeep driver, disappeared into the woods. We already felt quite embarrassed that we had mistaken him for an official ranger, when our driver made us stop at a local vegetable plantation and encouraged us to buy corn. We kindly refused and were relieved when finally returning to our accommodation. Then, when we got out of the car, he claimed that Minneriya was more expensive than the initial quote and demanded an extra 2000 Rupees from us. We were completely confused, but ended up refusing and walking away from his vehicle.

If you're planning on visiting the park - please make sure to compare prices, and don't make our mistake and fall for the false rangers.

BUT: The park itself is beautiful, we had lots of close encounters with elephants and other wildlife, saw different kinds of eagles, water buffalos and jackals - which overall, was worth the hassle - so overall - we absolutely recommend visiting the park.

Title: Very exciting to see such large family groups
Text:
It was great to see such large numbers of elephants in the family groups - matriarch, babies, youngsters, teenagers. Then with the young males who had been kicked out from the herd just feeding a short way from the main herd.  Interesting to watch the antics of some larger males finding their way into the smaller herds to check out the females.   

Yes there are a lot of safari jeeps but it did not seem as chaotic as in the Yala National Park and I think this is due to the fact that this park has a rather large open area of grass around lakes that allow for the army of jeeps to park by the road and allow for viewing by everyone as there were elephants everywhere.  In Yala once an elusive leopard is found, it's a race on for ever driver to get their clients a sighting and the tracks are narrow and not as open as in Minneriya.

I loved watching the babies, and yes the protective mothers keeping their bodies to the jeep side, but both continued grazing whilst we looked on. Watching elephant behaviour was interesting -  a mother comin out from a bamboo thicket as we approached in the jeep.  We stopped. She stopped. She waited - we didn't move.  Then obviously when she thought it was safe, she signalled to the two younger elephants and one by one out of the thicket they came and crossed the track.

I didn't feel the driver of our safari jeep hassled the elephants at all.  All the jeeps seemed to give them the space. If the elephant came behind the jeep, the driver stopped, waited for the elephant to pass or do what it wanted, before the driver proceeded along the track   The park appears to have designated trails that the vehicles can use and the jeeps generally stated on this track or to the side if they needed to pass.

Its main purpose for this park I think is for wild elephant viewing, but we also saw lots of birdlife around the lake.

We did an afternoon safari from 3pm and I found the seats were very nicely padded in our vehicle but seatbelts I think are optional, but then I was standing up a lot when the vehicle was parked or moving slowly along.

It's not for everyone as it's hot, it's bumpy, but I enjoyed it.

Title: Great safari to enjoy wildlife
Text:
While visiting Sirigiya, we decided to visit Minneriya National Park and it was the best decision we could make.
I have seen but reviews of people saying it was crowded. It must have been we went late during the day, but we just came across 2 more jeeps in the whole safari
We arrived just after 3pm. We were travelling with locals who arranged a safari driver that was at the entrance for only Rs3000 (bear in mind that you may be overcharged if you don't have someone to negotiate it). The entrance fee is almost none for locals and quite higher for foreigners, but still quite reasonable. 
We started the safari and were able stand up on the jeep and get amazing views. The first part of the route is a dense forest, but when you reach the opening, the views are stunning. You'll see hundreds of birds, storks, pheasants, beer eaters, herons, pelicans, eagles, etc. There are also spotted deers roaming around. The driver was knowledgeable and would point at different species. We saw elephants far away, then, a lonely one 50 meters away and then we came close to three, i.e. a mum with the two kids. We were totally amazed at seeing wild animals at less than 30 meters away and suddenly the protective and caring mother charged at us. It was terrifying yet astounding. The mum just wanted to ensure that we didn't hurt her kids. 
We drove for over an hour seeing birds, butterflies, tortoises, deers and when we thought viewings were over we saw a young grey leopard. It was just breathtaking, but the young fellow disappeared before we got our cameras out so it only got imprinted in our memories.
Overall, we spent 2 hours enjoying beautiful views and spotting some of Sri Lankan amazing wild life. Highly recommended.
