Title: An absolute highlight, an absolute must-do
Text:
I am not an elephant person.  Never have been.  I would see an elephant or two at the zoo and be ..... meh.  But Minneriya ... ROCKED. MY. WORLD.

It starts with a 30 minute ride in a jeep from the entrance into the heart of the national park.  The roads are good, you can stand up in the back of the jeep and you are racing through the jungle with the wind in your hair; exhilarating!  And we hadn't seen our first elephant yet!

During the next three hours, we encountered lone male elephants (who challenged our small jeep for dominance), a young mum with babies in tow (who was determined to chase us away to protect her babies) and then a herd by the lake.  The herd must have been close to 200 elephants; the sight was mesmerising.  Groups of elephants bathing, males warily standing apart watching the jeeps and each other, baby elephants running excitedly from group to group tooting their little trunks.  It was the most gorgeous experience.

And it is not just elephants, we also saw flocks of birds, a herd of water buffalo and one crocodile sub-bathing.

A brilliant afternoon, we loved this experience so much that we almost considered going back a second time!

Title: Pigeon Island National Park
Text:
Pigeon Island National Park is near the Nilaveli Beach in Sri Lanka. This National Park is amongst the 17 national parks in the country, but amongst the only two marine national parks in the entire region. This area is protected due to the aftermath of the 2004 Tsunami, which caused a lot of damage to the marine and coral life. This national park is also known to have the best coral reefs in the entire country! The rocky island is also home to rock pigeons, based on which the national park gets its name.

Diving and snorkeling are two everyday activities done here, apart from safari and hike.

So many different species of fish, squid, turtles and sharks. We saw 3 (think black tip sharks) at very close quarters on the shore side of the island. On the other side we saw turtles, incl a large hawksbill turtle who we swam with for some time. They have 2 types of turtle in Sri Lanka. 
At the time of our visit there were quite a few jellyfish but then it was just after a storm so itÂs probably not always an issue. They arenÂt poisonous but u may get a mild sting which soon goes. At some times of the year they have the Âred jellyfishÂ which is poisonous so check before u do the trip. The rangers hut on the island has vinegar which will relieve a sting.

Title: So is it a 1 or a 5?
Text:
I was puzzled by the contradicting reviews of Pigeon Island with some rating it 1 and others 5.  So here's the explanation:
1. The bay where everyone heads to is small, massively overcrowded (00's of people) and any coral within 20 metres of the shore has been destroyed.  Anyone who doesn't past here will rate it 1 out of 5
2.  However, once you get past this there is some pretty decent snorkelling. The best coral was to the right as you face the sea so head over there and go out a bit further and there is plenty to see.  I've done plenty of diving and wouldn't be unhappy to see this on a dive.
3.  There is also good fish life here, we saw a Black Tip Reef Shark close up as well as the usual mix of tropical fish.
4. On the side where the boats come in there is a cordoned off area where they are trying to re-grow the coral and you can see an entire bed of new coral.  There is a rope surrounding the area that you can use as a guide - there were very few people here compared to the main bay.  It's good to see what the Sri Lankian authorities are trying to do here.

it is crowded, but if you're an ok swimmer you can swim beyond the hordes and there's a wide range of fish, some of the coral retains its colour and it's really lovely snorkelling, albeit in a small area. (By ok swimmer I mean a very strong 8-year-old or average young teen would be fine.) 
There are lots of jellyfish where the boats land, but a guide with a different group said they were harmless. One brushed against my son's arm with no ill effects, one lady was picking them up to photograph (!) However, the sight of so many of them is off putting.

People do trample the coral, and the stamping about does cloud the water near to shore, but to be fair the coral starts at the beach so it's difficult not to stand on any. There were two roped off protected areas. One tourist, the first thing he did was swim to the rope, and duck under it into the protected area, so obviously the rules didn't apply to him.

The boats pull up on one side of the island, this bit is very crowded and the sea a bit choppy, which could put off under-confident swimmers/ young kids struggling to master their snorkels. Walk over the spit of sand to the other side and there are even more people and more kids, but the water is far calmer and lots of people just stand in the water and don't swim, so once you're past them it's lovely and there are lots of fish - whole shoals swimming by. You can apparently hire a guide for an extra SLR 2,000 (about Â£10) to 'show you the reef sharks, where the turtles are', and I can imagine if he took you to different areas the snorkelling would be amazing. But the standard trip is a good way to spend a couple of hours if you're holidaying in the area - I wouldn't deliberately travel there specifically for this though.

Text:

Title: Beautiful place that's being destroyed, sadly
Text:
Positive points first: we saw some beautiful coral, many colored fish, turtles and reef sharks, very awesome to see! Ideal for snorkeling.

But, the way this island and reef is treated, all the beauty will soon be gone :(

Hundreds of people, 20+ boats. People are walking on the corals constantly. Near the coast the coral is already completely destroyed. But farther out we also saw people constantly hitting the corals and standing on them. 

It's a matter of time before all the corals will die. Then the small fish can't live there anymore. Then medium fish can't feed anymore. Then the turtles and sharks will go away because there will be no food for them. This is basic ecosystem logic. 

If the organizations around pidgeon island don't start to do some serious conservation actions, then they can soon all close their businesses because there will be nothing to see underwater.

Right now pidgeon island is a money machine. It should be about the beautiful underwater world that us humans are allowed to respectfully visit and observe.

Title: These sharks are safe, but still scary!
Text:
This trip is definitely worth it, if you can manage to get out of bed early.

To get there you need to do the following:

1. Get to Nilaveli beach in front of the Anilana hotel.
2. Buy tickets for pigeon island as early as possible (opens at 8AM and costs $10 per person and $8 per group)
3. The people there will show you to your boat which should cost no more than 2000 LKR (can be shared with up to 6 people)
4. Your boat will have snorkeling gear on it (mask, snorkel, flippers) which costs 600 LKR a day per person.
5. Your boat will drop you off in about 15 minutes but will NOT wait for you at the island. It will be busy bringing people to and from the island the whole day.
6. Agree on a time your boat will take you back, and it will be there.

Following these steps we were first to enter the water. There is an area marked by buoys which you are asked to swim outside of to preserve the beautiful reef.

Within the first 50 meters I saw a shark and a turtle having breakfast! It was absolutely stunning, and the reef was very beautiful. I have diving experience in the Caribbean and this place is definitely on par. I saw a bunch of amazing fish here! After about two hours of snorkeling I left the water and went to the other side of the island which is literally 50 meters away. Here you can also swim and snorkel. I spoke to someone who saw a giant eel! The island is very hot and you are quite likely to get a sunburn or overexposed to the sun. There is some shade but take caution. 

This is a must do activity in an otherwise quite simple town (Nilaveli).

Title: Please don't stand on the coral!
Text:
A great (half) day trip by boat from Nilaveli beach, about 10 minutes away.  Don't overpay by going with your hotel, you can do it for a fraction of the price - there's no difference in what you get!  We went with Ashok based at Coral Bay Hotel, our dive centre next door told us about him.

The snorkelling is great at Pigeon Island, plenty of fish especially a myriad of different parrot fish, there are corals too, but sadly much of it is dead and damaged.  We were shocked at the way a lot of visitors were standing all over it - do they not realise the damage they are doing?!  It's good that you can swim and snorkel in any areas but really there should be some control/guidance to help preserve what's left of this precious site.  It was also very busy, perhaps again numbers of visitors should be controlled, You can snorkel on two sides of the island - we saw some impressive reef sharks who swim really close.

Take suitable footwear (we used our wetsuit socks) as the dead coral on the beach is hard/sharp to walk on barefoot when you get off the boat especially with the heat of the sun.

Text:

The park also needs to be stricter with the drivers by reminding them to keep distance and respect the animals.

Additionally, thanks to the Landrover, we were able to access areas of the park that most other trucks could not. There were numerous times where we were the only truck around. We managed to get so incredibly close to the elephants while still respecting the park rules and regulations. I've traveled to a lot of countries and almost never write Trip Advisor reviews but Lahiru is one of the best guides I've had and made my time in the park an incredible memory. If you're on the fence about splurging, trust me it's worth it!

Title: Buddhi is the best!
Text:
We arrived via cruise ship so were later than optimal for viewing the maximum number of birds (usually Buddhi starts at 6 AM and we started around 9:30 AM).  Despite that, Buddhi did a fantastic job for us--due to his keen eyes (and those of his friend, who was poling the pontoon boat through the mangroves), we were able to spot and quickly identify reclusive birds: 50 different species!

It was so quiet and peaceful as we glided through the water, with many stops for sightings.  Too many highlights to mention, but a couple include seeing Sri Lanka's largest kingfisher as well as every variety of egret - all at once!!!! - riding on the backs of swimming water buffaloes!

Buddhi provided excellent high power binoculars, bird books, water and fresh watermelon as a snack midway through the tour.  He is quite musical, too - played a traditional flute-like instrument for us on the way back.  After our tour, we were invited to his home for refreshments:  homemade fresh fruit smoothies (made from fruit from their own trees), thin coconut filled dosas and crisp fried (not sweet) 'cookies' or biscuits.  Yum!

Later, Buddhi sent us a wonderful memory of our trip that he filmed during our time with him.  Tip:  Buddhi arranged our transport from the ship to Kalametiya for us.  We chose an A/C car (which took about 1/2 hour).  This is definitely the right choice. We could have had a tuk-tuk but it would have taken a lot longer and not as comfortable.

To sum it up:  We could not have been happier.  Great alternative to Hambantota choices closer to the ship.

Title: Bird lover's paradise!
Text:
We did the tour with Buddi on 16th Jan and it was one of the highlights of our two week trip. We were staying in Tangalle at the time and had been tipped off by our driver about Kalametiya being much better than Bundala National Park for seeing birds as you can get much closer to the birds. We saw 53 species of birds in total, and as Buddi has an encyclopedic knowledge and great eye for the birds of Sri Lanka, you'll be sure to get to see plenty! It just depends what nature has in store for you that day! 

Buddi has binoculars if you don't have your own and he also carries field guides with pictures for reference. 

You'll get to climb a small rock for scenic views, and you'll actually see some different birds whilst you're on foot. We saw a very low perched shikra on this part! 

The freshly sliced watermelon and bottled water was also a very nice touch, expecially as the morning temperature starts to rise. We also did a quiz back at Buddi's with a glass of fresh wood apple juice, which is well worth trying if you get the chance! 

Overall, a very calm, relaxing morning tour in beautiful scenery, with plenty of birds to see as well as Buffalo and sea/land monitors. If you're really lucky, you'll also get a flute solo from Buddi, a man of many talents!

Title: An out of the world and time place
Text:
Our Sri Lanka tour finished by three days in Ranna and we discovered this bird place into our guide book.
We did visit many birds places and wanted to see this one but we did not expect much.

Thanks to Buddhi who organized a tuktuk pickup from our hotel we arrived on time for an almost three hour tour starting from 3:30 pm. After having a refreshing fruit juice in Buddi home place we started the visit. We boarded on a small boat with our guide Buddi and a boat paddler.

Once on the boat we crossed the laguna and entered into another world. We saw hundred of birds. They were everywhere.
Overall we saw 47 different birds species. as well as buffalos, varans, monkeys. The sunset on the water with birds on the back of water buffalos was outstanding. You could stay a whole day in this paradise where the time seems to have stopped.

The laguna is wide and very quiet. You will listen only the birds music and the sound of the water made by the paddle.
Buddhi is a bird lover and he is a pationate person. He is dedicated to nature and birds. He made this visit the best birds watching we never had. We were amazed by the amount of birds we saw. Most of the time in these kind of visit you see some few birds very far away. Here you are surrounded by birds. They are everywhere just few meters away. You do not need expensive camera with long focal lenses to take nice birds photos.Surprisingly a small fish attacked by an heron jumped on the bench on which I was sitting and it was not a flying fish.

My wife, who is not mad of birds as I am, came with me and was not expecting to discover such an amazing place.
She went in love with the beauty and the peacefulness of the laguna.

The end of the trip was accompanied by the music played by Buddhi on his flute and this added a 48th bird to our visit.
We warmly want to thank Buddhi for permitting us to discover this magical place.

If you are in Tangalle area this is the place you have to visit.

Title: A remarkable orphanage for injured and orphaned elephants.
Text:
The elephant sanctuary in Sri Lanka's pinnawala town is a major sanctuary for orphaned and injured elephants.
The road to the orphanage is perhaps one of the most scenic drive you may come across in Sri Lanka.
The star attraction of the sanctuary was an elephant which has given birth to twins, a rarity.
We were also able to see a few elephants in search of a mate.
Away from the orphanage across the road the elephants were given a cool bath in the river.
There are also a number of souvenir shops near the elephant bathing ghat.
The parking space is spacious and the western style toilets were clean and well maintained.
There is also an ATM near the entrance where the newly arrived foreign tourists can convert their home currency into Sri Lankan rupees.
A fun place for kids to see elephants of all ages at close proximity.
The entry fee is nominal and the place well maintained.
We could not locate a restaurant in the premises.
We could also see a number of birds in the surroundings.
A good place to visit with the kids for a picnic.
Recommended.

Title: Ship's shore ex to the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage
Text:
We ventured to this Orphanage on a ship's shore ex ... it's about a 2 - 2.5 hour drive from the port on a coach.

I think if you can get here with a local guide you would be better off as you can spend as much or as little time as you like at the orphanage, whereas on a ship's tour the time is shorter.

This orphanage is a government run orphanage and at least paying guests are aware of this when they enter and hopefully all money raised goes towards the elephant's upkeep and setting them free back into the jungle.

I found all the public areas where we went and the enclosures we saw were very clean and tidy.

Take Sri Lankan money with you - although you can use CC at the Orphanage shop and other shops in the town, generally speaking they don't take cash unless it's Sri Lankan money.

There is an opportunity to feed the elephants by hand in one areas of the orphanage however Rupees are required - no USD or other currency and definitely no CC there !!  Luckily our guide exchanged some USD for Rupees but the fruit was gone very quickly.

Yes there were a few elephants chained up in another enclosure but of the three enclosures we saw, this was the only one where they were chained.  The reason we were given for this was because they are wild animals... let's face it ... if they are males and are maturing, they could get annoyed about something and cause injuries to other elephants if not their handlers and / or the public if they crashed through the fence.

Indeed at the elephant feeding area I saw one elephant get grumpy with another one for muscling in on the food I was feeding it - the elephant turned around and head butted the second elephant in its side to show it's displeasure at eating its food.

The third area where we saw elephants at this Orphanage, the elephants were roaming free in a large treed area ... I wondered if this was the first stage of getting them used to fending for themselves before setting them free in the jungle.

We had lunch included in our ship's shore excursion at a hotel by the river and luckily for us, they had quite a few elephants bathing there - a lovely thing to see.

IMO, this excursion is not suitable for mobility impaired people because the terrain to get to the elephant enclosures is not paved and the surface is uneven.  There's also a few steps to negotiate within the elephant orphanage area.  Also, the "road" to the hotel where we went for lunch was not paved either.

Sip a cup of coffee or get some juice while watching that at one of the few restaurants there (watch out for those flies!). There are several shops that sell pooper (paper made out of elephant poop) and other trinkets there. I found them exorbitantly priced, so I skipped. But overall a very pleasant place to go outside of colombo.

Title: Visit the site for yourself & make up your own mind!
Text:
I visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage on 15 February 2020 from Australia. 

This was my first holiday to Sri Lanka even though my parents are Sri Lankan. 

I had heard many stories from my relatives about the elephants at Pinnawala and had always wanted to visit. 

In saying that, making the decision to go was a tough one as I am aware that currently Pinnawala is classed as Âslightly controversialÂ & I am an extreme animal lover!

Nevertheless after reading many reviews (some from people whom havenÂt even visited the site!?), I decided that I needed to see it for myself & make up my own mind. 

My honest opinion was that I was pleasantly surprised and I believe that they are genuinely trying to improve the operations of the park. 

Out of the 90 odd elephants I saw there, the majority were free roaming and appeared to enjoy their free time and bathing in the river. 
The only elephants I saw had chains were some of the males which is more for everyoneÂs protection so as not to cause a stampede. There were also 2 that were in pens apparently under veterinary care. 

The only ÂtouristÂ interaction that I saw was the fruit feeding which I avidly took part in - i bought like 4 baskets of fruit to give to 2 beautiful elephants. 

(**And for those people complaining about having to pay for the fruit baskets- get over it! 
It only costs like $2 aud for a basket of fruit! You pay way more than that for animal encounters in western countries and thatÂs not included in your ticket price either!)

No tourists (that I saw) were allowed to bathe with the elephants etc at the park and I didnÂt really see any ÂexploitationÂ as such. Ie, I did not see any elephant rides being provided.

It was just a joy to see them down at the river with many elephants enjoying the water or their mud bath. 

At the end of the day people will need to make up their own minds as to what theyÂre comfortable with. 

I personally am happy I went there and I donÂt believe it is as bad as some people are making it out to be.

Title: More animal torture and rip-off than anything else
Text:
I was more than shocked. On the one hand we only wanted to watch the animals bathing and we were told that we need a ticket for 3000 LKR each (there is a ticket office for tourists and locals. I doubt that they are the same prices) which is not correct. You can just walk down to the river between 10am and 12pm or 2pm and 4 pm and watch the elephants bathing. You need the ticket to see the "orphanage", which was one of the saddest things I have ever seen. The animals have far too little space and no things to play with. 
When we asked why two elephants were chained and kept circling their heads, we were told "their will first has to be broken". 
There was also an enclosure with 3 baby elephants inside, which were made to pose for photos. There were men standing in front of it offering to take photos of us and the elephants. However, this is not a nice gesture (even if the locals are otherwise very nice and helpful), but afterwards the hand is held out again for money. 

 Also the small elephants which are "rescued" are not let back into freedom. Once an elephant is in Pinnawala, it never leaves again. Title: Not the bad place some people write about.
Text:
I visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage just over a week ago and I must say that I was on high alert after a few derogatory articles I had seen written about the facility and its treatment of the elephants. Happily, I found nothing worthy of a complaint.

The elephants parade down to the river and anyone who knows animals can see that they are intelligent beings who are used to the routine and are not at all stressed by the watching crowds - in fact, some clearly loved it and were happy to participate and be patted or fed a morsel along the way.  Once in the river they splash, roll around in the water and clearly enjoy themselves.

Yes, some did have a loose chain around their necks, but this didn't bother them. When you consider the size of an elephant and the general havoc they could cause to a community when aggressive, it's not difficult to understand that there are times when they must be prudently restrained or separated. 
As for returning them all to the wild; these elephants no longer have a place in the wild as they have formed new family bonds within their new herd. Many have already been rescued from the wild where they were close to death and others are on medication or special food.

So if you want to truly help elephants and not just have a pompous rant about turning them loose, visit Pinnawala, spend a few dollars towards their support and watch them happily splash about in safety.

Title: Sceptical but pleasantly surprised.
Text:
Reviews of Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage praise and condemn so our only choice was to see it for ourselves. The stamp of the countryÂs Department of Wildlife Conservation on the park was the deciding factor.

Over a twenty year period, Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage hand raised abandoned babies, treated the injured and integrated displaced elephants into a growing herd.

Currently, 88 elephants are part of the Pinnawala family on their 30-acre property, making it one of Sri LankaÂs largest tourist attractions.

At Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage you will see chains. This is precautionary for large males while bathing, wandering the park Â river path, and when a femaleÂs seductive pheromones spike.

A full grown male can stand more than 2.5 metres weighing  5.5 tonnes. A force to be reckoned with when they want to get down to business.

You will also see mahouts rounding the elephants to keep them in one spot. This is also precautionary to keep them from getting too close to punters.

A disappointing observation was people paying some entrepreneurial mahouts to bathe the elephants. The elephant is chained and made to lie on its side during the encounter. This is not approved and is something the orphanage is trying to eliminate.

Elephants eat an average of 250kg of food per day, multiply that by 88 of them and you have an expensive grocery bill. Modern veterinary equipment and traditional indigenous medicine come at a price and the gallons of milk required to raise a baby elephant is also exorbitant.

Sponsorship programs, donations and your ticket price all contribute to the cost of feeding and caring for these adorable creatures.

Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage is not perfect, but the care for these elephants is obvious.

This is a heavily tourist-trafficked attraction. Vendors take advantage of the captive audience and sell everything from elephant poo paper products (quite an interesting process) to every form of elephant printed clothing you can imagine.

Away from this retail madness, however, is picturesque countryside, a meandering river and comfortable accommodation.

Title: 2 Weeks Volunteering
Text:
Spent 2 weeks volunteering here as a family so gained some insight into the orphanage.
The orphanage would love to see all elephants in the wild, unfortunately this is impossible with pressures on land use by a growing population.  They cant introduce elephants to an existing wild herd as they would not be accepted.  All elephants in the orphanage have been raised in captivity so would seek out people if released and this would in turn create conflict risking the elephants life.
The mahouts do shout and use ashoks with elephants to ensure public safety.  To see behind the public face and watch them tenderly go over the elephants skin for 2 hours looking for problems shows their true feelings towards the animals.  They shout at the cleaners if the elephant houses are not sufficiently cleaned.
The prices are fair for tourists and cheaper for locals to encourage locals to visit, learn and take an interest in their own wildlife.  This is a government run organisation so the prices are set in Colombo, not by the orphanage.  The extra fee for feeding or bathing 
elephants is likewise set by the politicians.
The Elephant in the Room - chains.  These are necessary to manage the herd in a small area to keep public, staff and elephants safe.  Injured, sick and pregnant elephants are kept separate, but still taken for free time at the river away from the main herd. There are 19 elephants housed here which have been seized from illegal owners and are awaiting court cases so can't be put with the herd.  
In all we really enjoyed our 2 weeks here giving us an insight not gained during a short visit.  Volunteering is hard work and not for everybody.  We learnt about the politics behind a lot of decisions and saw the love held for these wonderful creatures by all the staff at the orphanage.

Title: Horrible place. Pinnawala is a glorified zoo - or worse
Text:
I had read up about Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage before I visited Sri Lanka and from what I'd read, I was honestly considering skipping the visit due to claims of animal abuse and unnecessary confinement. But as it turned out, I was part of a group and because the group wanted to go, I had little option but to tag along.

What I saw there truly horrified me.

1. Elephant calves were confined in a circular pen and their legs tied with metal chains that left little room for manoeuvre or free movement.

2. There was a tusker displaying a classic case of depressive symptoms - head swaying incessantly and bobbing up and down. Like the calves, he was also tied with a short metal chain in a small shed. 

3. A herd of elephants we saw there was so scared of the keeper that as soon as he entered the enclosure with his bull-hook, the terrified elephants literally fled away from him. The keeper was careful not to display any aggressive behaviour in front of the tourists but it was obvious from how scared the elephants were, that terrible things go on behind the scenes. 

4. While there, we saw a keeper repeatedly strike a pregnant elephant with a huge pole that had a metal spike at its end. He poked and struck her hard despite the presence of tourists there. I cannot imagine what must be going on once tourist hours are over.

We then headed off to the river adjacent to the orphanage where they take the elephants for a bath - hoping that at least there, the elephants must be free. But they were not. Even here, the elephants were tied with short chains while tourists threw fruit at them.

I would've compared Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage to a zoo but most zoos treat their animals better than this 'orphanage' does.

Pinnawala is not a place I would ever visit again. My money isn't going into a place that has made a business out of abusing animals that should've been returned to the wild. Plus, they breed elephants in confinement at Pinnawala. Real orphanages don't typically do that.

Instead, I would strongly recommend visiting the Elephant Transit Home near Udawalawe National Park. I haven't been there but from what I've heard, they are much more responsible in caring for orphaned elephants. Plus they return the elephants to the wild once they are old enough - unlike Pinnawala.

Title: Captive & captivating elephants!...
Text:
There are clearly divided opinions about places such as these. The elephants here are either orphan elephants, those born in captivity or ex-working elephants in retirement. They are cared for at the orphanage their whole lives and are not planned for release back into the wild,  as they probably would not survive  by themselves, having become accustomed to human handling. We saw them taken to the river for their daily bathing,  and clearly they enjoyed the experience, playing and splashing around with each other (and even trying to mate!) in the water for several hours.. 
Some in our group objected to the chains the elephants wear and the actions of the mahouts prodding them to move. We learned later (contrary to appearances) the elephants are not chained up back in the orphanage - they only have the chains on for use in an emergency and for public protection if they get spooked. 
But as one commentator has already said, if you want to see elephants in a free and natural environment, visit one of the many national parks -  not the orphanage, or a sanctuary.

Title: A great way to support this herd
Text:
There are a lot of misleading reviews about Pinnawala. I've been twice - earlier this month and 21 years ago - and I've enjoyed the experience both times. The price of 2500 rupees (about Â£11 per person) is quite high but much lower than I've seen online where it's often stated at $20 per person.

There's not too much to do. Our driver went in with us which we thought a bit odd until we realised he knew exactly where to go and when to make sure we got the best experience. We went first to the elephant 'paddocks' where the ladies were hanging around eating and waiting for bath time. In a separate area, the boys were getting ready to go the river.

Nothing can really prepare you for seeing a massive herd of elephants on the move. The boys went first, strolling through the orphanage, out to the road and down to the river. Some are chained - for their safety and everybody else's. I don't think it's a bad thing. Once the boys were on their way, the lady elephants followed.

We watched the bath time for nearly 2 hours. Our driver urged us to a brilliant watching space in a cafe which we really appreciated. In two hours you have plenty of time to watch and observe the different personalities amongst the elephants. There are the cheeky younger boys, the stubborn old ladies, the frisky and the laid-back all hanging out together.

People have commented on the use of 'spikes' or 'guides'. We was the metal guides being used by the mahoots but always very gently and never with any violence. The love of the handlers for their pachyderm pals was clear to all.

One old lady - quite possibly the grande dame of the herd - spent an hour standing knee deep trying to avoid a wash. Her mahoot gently urged her into deeper water, taking his time and using his 'guide' to help scrape old mud off her head and back. Eventually she gave in and rolled over in the water to let him clean her properly.

Some are chained in the water but didn't seem distressed about it. A couple of young females made a jovial bid for freedom on the far banks and were laughingly chased down and returned to the herd.

If you're looking for lots of action, this may disappoint. If you have the patience to watch and wait, you'll probably love it as much as I did.

One comment. I think the management should consider rebranding this as an Elephant Home rather than an Elephant Orphanage since it seems to create elevated expectations of lots of babies and at present there really aren't many at all. The purpose of the home is to give safe haven to elephants, not to go looking for unwanted babies. Back in the days of the Civil War, a lot of babies were orphaned by their parents being killed (accidentally or intentionally) so there were more little ones to see. These days they do have a few babies but I suspect that's more an outcome of boy and girl elephants getting friendly rather than any kind of captive breeding programme.

Title: Not perfect, but not awful either
Text:
First things first, I saw no evidence of any physical abuse of the elephants during my visit to Pinnewala Orphanage. The elephants look well fed, clean and have no scars from chains or sticks as far as I could see. The keepers used goads to guide the elephants and to prevent the bulls trying to mix with the main herd of females/younger elephants, but I did not see a single one being hit. The chains used on some of the bulls look unpleasant, but they seem to be loosely fitted and not particularly irritating to the animals. Keeping such large and potentially aggressive animals under control is essential when they are in such close proximity to one another (bulls generally wouldnÂt mix with the herd in the wild) and to humans. The animals are corralled to be fed and kept in a certain (quite large) area of the river to be washed, but otherwise roam around a large natural reserve. 

Some of the ÂextrasÂ put on for tourists (photos with the elephants, feeding/washing them etc) arenÂt acceptable. The elephants are wild animals, not playthings or props, and they should be treated as such. A couple of keepers rode some of the bulls back from the river, which again I donÂt agree with. Additionally, perhaps more effort could be made to return some of the animals back to the wild, however I donÂt know anything about the practicalities  and of course this runs the risk of them being killed by farmers (the main threat to wild elephants in Sri Lanka).

All in all, as far as I could tell the Pinnewala Orphanage is not abusive to the animals in its care and is no worse than Western zoos. Keeping animals in captivity is never ideal, but the fraught relationship between farmers and wildlife in Sri Lanka make it impossible for all elephants to live in the wild. Perhaps in the future with better education, people all over the world will be better able to co-exist with animals and places like Pinnewala will be unnecessary. However, for now this place is the best of a bad situation.

Title: I was sceptical too - but then we visited it :)
Text: I read a whole bunch of these reviews before we travelled to Sri Lanka. I really wanted to see the elephants and it was our honeymoon after all. We visited Thailand last year and refused any elephant visits as they are so mistreated over there and we are very against elephant riding. Our experience of Pinnawala was delightfully reassuring and I felt relieved. The elephants are treated very well and no one was riding them or beating them with sticks - as some of these reviews suggest. They were free to walk around and were fed very generously. You can tell that all staff members look after them very well. Yes - there some that have some chains around them. This is unfortunate but we asked why this was and didn't just assume. Title: Please don't participate in the abuse of elephants!!!
Text:
Maybe the intentions of this 'orphanage' were once good, they are definitely not now. 

This is a commercialized elephant breeding factory. Most of the elephants are bred in the park, for the sole purpose of entertainment for tourists. 

Caretakers are encouraging everyone to take photos and touch the elephants in exchange for tips. 

You can pay extra to feed a baby elephant, who is chained by itself in a cage surrounded by tourists. When we were there, the baby was freaking out, trying to get out of the chains and hurting herself. They get fed whenever a tourist pays, not only during feeding times.

Many elephants are chained up all day in the same spot. They get to go to the river 2 times a day (you have seen the famous photos). Even there many are chained up under water and caretakers push them underwater with a stick so they look like they are splashing around. 

Many of them are showing signs of distress, rocking back and forth for hours at the time while being chained up. This does not happen in the wild. These compulsive movements cause life-threatening damage to the feet and joints of the elephant. They are in severe distress and don't let them tell you otherwise. 

People saying that there is no other way to treat them and the elephants would not survive in the wild are wrong. There are way more humane ways to treat elephants in an orphanage and this is not one of them. Please don't participate.

Title: Up Close But Not Personal
Text:
This is a place that has many controversial reviews and so we pondered to whether we wanted to go or not. It was a tossup and I am glad we did go but it did leave some questions unanswered. 
We missed the elephants walking from the park over the road and down to the river. So we purchased our tickets from the ticket office and then headed over. You have to give your ticket to the ticket man at the start of the road so unpaid people cannot get down there to watch the elephants. We got down there and it was quite a sight. All these elephants standing in the water. The group of elephants was split and I did notice the ones that were chained in place. I also noted a small group that kept trying to get out of the water. The mahout would let them go for a while and then he would yell and wave his hook and the elephants obviously fearful of him would get back in the water. I got talking to another visitor who said she had been a number of times and that the river was really low and when it is low they seem to be lethargic. It was the first time she had seen them so disinterested. 
The mahout to me seemed to be a bully. Later on when they were prepping them to leave, this particular guy caught my eye and smiled. I gestured to him that I was not happy with his behavior and proceeded to photograph him. I believe there is a difference to being in control fairly and being a bully. Out of all of them he definitely was a bully. The elephants were swapped  around a bit and it was fascinating to be so close and to watch them for a reasonably long period. It was extremely hot that day so we sat up in the restaurants balcony and had a beer etc. to get some respite. They then moved the elephantÂs to the water cannon by the exit to the river which they seemed to enjoy and then the main girl elephant, she led them back up the road. They knocked over a hat stand in a store which was funny and they seemed keen to get back. 
We followed them closely and when we got back they had taken them over the back of the park and they were being fed. We stood for perhaps half an hour and no one told us what was happening- we just stood and hoped there was something more. Eventually they told us we could go over which we did. 
Yes they were all chained by a foot and they all had piles of food. We stood for a period watching how they ate soft wood, palm leaves and observed what they seemed to prefer to eat, and how they manipulated the food to eat. 
We then went back to another area where they had younger elephants still on milk. We got talking to the assistant curator and it wasnÂt until he answered my questions about containment, feeding, punishment, medical care, that it made any sense. He said there was a lot of misunderstanding and therefore there are negative reviews. I asked why they seemed to be not enjoying themselves in the water and he said, they are just so keen to get back to eat.
The main reason for containment is to stop fighting. In the wild the elephants form packs where there is a boss and they will fight if they encroach on other elephantÂs territory. They are working on a big open area for them but at the moment containment is the best for them. So this parks environment is not normal, but it is the best they can do and they do their best to stop the animals hurting each other. He said that the elephants do not have to work for their food there and life is quite easy and the care is excellent with medical care etc. and it is a good alternative for the orphans. I suggested they educate the visitors more. There was very little education of the visitors and when you donÂt know why things are being done, you come up with your own theory. The experience is not interactive enough. 
I also complained about the bully mahout and he knew who I was talking about and he has been pulled up before about this. I appreciate what this place is doing but think it is a shame that there are even orphans that need care. If they were just left to their own devices, and humans didnÂt interfere, there would be few orphaned anyway. 
I think they actually do really care for them and give them great care, but they need to connect with the visitors more and explain what and why and how they do what they do.

Title: Front Row Seats to 40+ Elephants Bathing and Crossing a River is Priceless
Text:

Once the elephants are guided away from the river, take an hour or so shopping the row of shops leading to the river. Make sure you begin to make your way back toward the river just before 1000am. You will be able to see 40+ elephants guide toward the river. You can stand within 2 feet or so of the procession. Once safe, make your way back to the rocks by the water. Unfortunately I don't have anything positive to say about the actual orphanage. I imagine and believe that they are doing good work, but I can't personally vouch for it. We went before the 40+ elephants were guided back to the orphanage, and I can say that within 10 min, the overwhelming impression my family got was: depression. I would recommend a visit, even for those who do not like to see animals in captivity, they are well kept and far better off here than in the places they were rescued from.

Title: Unforgettable Experience
Text:
We visited Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage on our way to Kandy from Colombo. 
Initially I did not have high hopes of seeing anything extraordinary. 

After entering we had to walk for some distance in the hot sun seeing only one or two elephants chained inside their enclosure. 

But at the end of our walk, we were treated to a fascinating sight of more than 50 elephants roaming about in an open area enclosed by rocks and railings to prevent them from coming out. 

Then we watched some elephants being fed and some people were allowed to feed milk to baby elephants in bottles. 
After coming out, we were told that the elephants would come out, cross the road, walk into the street and take a bath in the river. 

We waited outside for some time and then the gates opened and more than 30 elephants came out, crossed the road and walked into the street within 5 feet of where we were standing. 

It is both awesome and scary to have 25 elephants walking right next to you, trumpeting and swaying and one elephant swerved dangerously close to where I was standing. 

After they crossed us, we followed them to the river by paying the charges and were again treated to a rare sight of so many elephants bathing together in the river. 

All in all, it was a wonderful and unforgettable experience and I am very happy that I paid a visit to this place. 
I have no hesitation in recommending this attraction to all of you who are visiting Sri Lanka.

Across the place there are lots of signs with information about elephants and their care and feeding. 
In a world where human beings are taking space from the wildness to build towns and roads, Pinnawale has a caring aim. Title: Feels dodgy
Text:
When this was advertised as a conservation effort I was excited. I have had some great experiences with turtles in the wild. They are amazing, intelligent, beautiful animals. I paid the 500 rupee entrance fee and was immediately disappointed after walking in. They had large turtles alone in very small tanks (about the size of a single bed), these poor creatures were lifted out of the tank and passed around for each tour group that went through (about 5-10 mins apart).  A couple were obviously injured and I do believe that they wouldn't have survived in the wild, but I'm not convinced that their current circumstances are necessarily preferable. One (which didn't have any obvious injury) was showing signs of distress and biting the edge of the concrete tank. There were chunks missing from a few places of the tank, so she'd obviously been at it for a while despite the fact that we were told she was only there temporarily.

The baby turtles were listless, but I don't think I saw any dead ones. They have a hatchery at the back of the compound which is ostensibly the main part of the conservation effort. They pay locals to bring them eggs from the beach so that they can incubate and hatch away from predators (dogs and birds). I'm sure it has nothing to do with the 1000 rupees they can charge tourists to release a baby into the wild. 

The guide was knowledgeable and friendly enough. When asked whether the centre was involved in any conservation research or formal programs the answer was no.

Overall I was extremely disappointed and feel very guilty for giving my money to this business. I thought long and hard about writing this review because it may be that there is a genuine desire to perform some conservation efforts, however the more i think about it the more sinister it seems.

If you are genuinely interested in turtles, I'd advise you to take your chances and go on one of the may dive/snorkelling tours that are available in southern Sri Lanka. If you just want to see a turtle and have no concern for it's welfare, then this will fulfil your needs

Title: Great rainforest hike with experienced guide
Text:
We (family of 4 from South Africa) visited Sinharaja on 28 February 2022, and stayed overnight at the Kurulu Ella Eco resort, right on top of the mountain. 
Had a pleasant stay at the resort that had a waterfall right in its own back yard, and then arranged with Danushka to be our guide in the rainforest trek the next morning. He came with a safari jeep and driver, picked us up at 8am and we entered the reserve by about 9.30.

The road up was quite windy but extremely scenic. Entry into the Reserve was a breeze. Inside we were given our leech socks that covered till the knee area, and shoes were sprayed. The hike was amazing, we covered two of the three waterfalls, and were given a good explanation of the plants and animals we encountered. The dipping of our feet at the waterfalls was a tingling sensation as the many small fish nibbled on the skin. The rocks were very slippery and even though we had good hiking shoes, they did not grip on the wet rocks, so we had to be very careful. After 4 hours we were back at the jeep and exited. Had a memorable day there.

Leeches still cling onto your knee high socks and shoes, and we got used to removing them with our hands as we saw our guide do this. If you did get stung, they suck your blood, you feel some pain but it is not fatal, so not to worry about these parasites too much.

Best to do in morning, as it rains almost every afternoon.

You cannot hike on your own and must engage a registered guide.

Estimates of cost for 4 persons inclusive of entrance fee, guide, safari jeep, leach socks and spray was 12800 rupees for 4 pax which I thought was reasonable, other guides charge more.

Happy to recommend Danushka. He can be contacted at +94 77 100 5329 (Whats app), or +94 77 525 4486 (tel)

Title: Best birdwatching site in Sri Lanka
Text:
This large rain forest is simply wonderful and I was so pleased that I had decided to stay for 3 days . It fully justifies the appellation of a World Heritage Site .
  On my first afternoon we birdied around the village . Our first bird was Serendip Scops Owl quickly followed by another I endemic Sri Lankan Rufous Babbler . Other sightings included : Hanging Parrot , Small Barbet , Pale-billed Flowerpecker and Indian Pygmy Woodpecker . 
 Early next morning we entered the forest, glad to be on foot  after a steep bone shaking jeep ride . Our first new mammal was the curious Purple-faced Leaf Monkey followed by another selection of great birds , including : Spot-winged Ground Thrush , LeggeÂs Flowerpecker , a pair of Frogmouths , Ashy-headed Laughing Thrush , Malabar Trogon , Velvet-fronted Nuthatch  and Black-rumped Blue Monarch . However the best two birds took a long time to find . Firstly we followed a small track into the forest and made our way slowly and quietly through the undergrowth and crossing streams until we gained clear views of the elusive endemic the Sri Lankan Scaly Thrush . Secondly following advice from a local guide we retraced our steps and left the main forest following the call of our target bird high in the canopy . After much neck breaking scanning of the tree tops we finally had sight of the Red-faced Malkoha . 
  After lunch we changed out plans to return to the Heritage Centre in search of the Sri Lankan Blue Magpie as our early morning visit was disrupted by a large group of school children . However there were still dozens of excited children around , then after an hour the heavens opened . Finally we did see a very bedraggled Blue a Magpie and LayardÂs Squirrel .
  Early next morning we drove up to MartinÂs Rest , one or the first specialised birding accommodation in the forest . Where we had breakfast on the balcony overlooking the forest . Just before breakfast we saw our final endemic bird , White-faced Starling . Thank to a Upali my guide I had now seen all the 34 endemic birds of Sri Lanka . After more birding we returned to the Heritage Centre and were rewarded with excellent close up views of the spectacular Sri Lankan Blue Magpie , plus Oriental Honey Buzzard and a beautiful Forget-me-not butterfly . 
  Late afternoon after lunch we took a steep trek up a winding track in search of roosting owls . However after a strenuous climb we were unsuccessful but we did see a Brown-throated Needletail flying over .
  On our final morning we entered the forest for the last time and although we saw few new birds I did get clearer views and photographs of birds seen earlier , such as : Dark-fronted Babbler , Ashy-headed Laughing Thrush , Sri Lankan Crested Drongo , Spot -winged Ground Thrush , and one until now elusive bird Slaty-legged Crake . After a refreshing drink of tea with a local family we finally walked out of the forest .
   3 days which I will never forget .

Title: A must see when in Sri Lanka
Text:
Fabulous forest reserve for bird lovers and nature lovers in general. This forest has been rescued from and attempted mass logging in late 1970's, when a dedicated group of scientist  mounted a scientifically informed campaign.  Since then it has been designated as a Man And Biosphere reserve as well as a world nature heritage site. 

Today it is the largest intact tract of lowland rainforest in Sri Lanka, which is home to numerous endemic tree, bird and other species. It is considered to be a significant hot spot of global biodiversity and a keystone in evolution.

The majestic towering trees, many clear and pure brooks, hundreds of bird species, and the winding paths within this forest are simply impressive.  Guided hikes are included in the modest entrance fee. These guides are employees of the forest dept, and appear to be very well informed. 

This forest reserve is easily accessible by main roads (last few km on a 4-wheel drive vehicle or on foot). Several options to stay at the boundary of the forest or one option within the border (Martin's Lodge).

Title: Great walking but watch for the leeches
Text: There seems to be a general myth that detergent and soapy water will get rid of leeches and this old timer is here to tell you that it DOES NOT. Out of consideration for the guide, I kept my eyes on the treetops until we reached a tiny store where someone had a "beedie". Then another helpful individual informed us that leeches often hbernate in large balls high in the trees and drop onto warm blooded creatures passing by underneath. I have since asked several other experienced walkers in Sri Lanka to be told that this is true. Don't be put off; just be prepared. Another tip, if you are taken to the Buddhist retreat be prepared for the Austrian monk to insult you if you are (a) Christian (b) Australian or (c) polite. He does, however have a recipe for a kind of herbal infusion which is effective against high blood sugar. So taken with caution, this can be an interesting experience - as you watch those leeches gallop towards your shoe fastenings just light up a cigarette - and maybe wear a hat!!

Title: Biodiversity hotspot
Text:
This is a wonderful place to experience nature. It is home to a myriad of wonderful birds, plants and animals - but be prepared that you will see just a small amount of what is here. Our guide was very knowledgeable, finding Sri Lanka Frogmouth for us when the rain had begun and all the birds had taken cover, but the visit is a walk out to the research centre then back along the same route - limiting the amount of ground that you cover, unless you take the more challenging path up to the cave..
In November it is usual for the rain to come from late morning for a few hours, and expect it to be heavy, so my advice would be to go first thing in the morning, before the rain so that there are more birds, animals and insects in view.

The best place to see birds is in the clearings - there aren't so many of these so take your time when you find one and wait a while at these places hoping for a flock to pass through. It is advisable to take an umbrella. There are also leeches. To limit how much these little nasties get on to you tuck top/shirt into trousers, trouser bottoms into socks, then use leech socks if available - although I and my husband were using waterproof sealskinz socks and these were actually more effect than the leech socks that our guide used. Title: Fantastic birdwatching
Text:
This is my second trip to Sinharaja, the first as a keen birdwatcher was 19 years' ago.

There are a number of entry points to the park but we went to the one which requires a jeep (or long walk) up to Martin's Lodge, birdwatching the trails from there.

Sinharaja is now recognised as a Unesco World Heritage site and an Endemic Bird Area by Birdlife International. The flocking behaviour of birds in Sinharaja is the most intensively studied in the world.

Indeed find a flock and you may well see a decent number of Sri Lanka's 33 (currently, will increase soon) birds, including Ceylon Crested Drongo, White-backed Starling, Sri Lankan Scimitar-babbler and Ceylon Rufous Babbler. Sinharaja also has a very good site for Ceylon Scaly Thrush which was split into a separate species after my previous visit. 

There are also a number of very good guides and rangers who can spot roosting nightbirds including Ceylon Frogmouth and most crucially Serendip Scops-owl, the latter only described to science as recently as 2003 (I think).

Sinharaja has ensured excellent birdwatching on both our two visits and we can't rate it highly enough. However, leeches are abundant so do take leech socks.

Title: South entrance not so much of a wilderness....
Text:
We travelled to Sinharaja from Tangalle today...  About 2.5 hours so a reasonable trek to the southern entrance outside Deniyaya. The road ends and you are in a very small village where tuk Tuks are there to take you up the bumpy trail to the Forest office where you buy your tickets (560 lkr each).  Tuk tuk was 250 lkr each way.  we were told in the village that the guides all had to be hired in village, our driver seemed sceptical but nonetheless we went ahead with a "guide".   On reflection I don't believe he was a true "guide" as on the trail we noted other guys with official polo shirts, rucksacks, and binoculars...  Our guide was in tracksuit bottoms with a bottle of 7-up.  My fears were confirmed when his initial quote for the 3 hour walk was 4600 lkr, rather more than the 2000 lkr I was told  to expect.  Some haggling later we were at 2500 for 3 hour trek and set to go.   It started off promisingly ...  Tiny luminous green snake, massive millipede, rhino fly all spotted in a few minutes, then a couple of lizards...   But then things literally dried up and we diverted off to the track to the conservation centre for 10 minutes sit down, Nothing there apart from some faded pictures...  Then after a total of a 1 hour slow walking on a very, very well trodden path (avoiding locals on motorbikes as mentioned in other posts regarding this southern entrance) we arrived at a picturesque, but hardly awe inspiring waterfall, where we sat for another 10mins before a brisk walk back down the same path and back to base.. Avoiding those motorbikes again.  Luckily we saw a serpent eagle high up in a tree on the way back or else it would have been a zero spot rapid trek back - total time start to finish 2 hours 10 and we only made it to first waterfall.  Should have asked for trip to 2nd waterfall instead of stating a time.  Although, apparently, you do have to wade to get to the second.
So in summary I would have to agree with earlier posts about this southern entrance and say that it is spoiled by the motorbikes which must scare off the timid wildlife and please make sure you get a proper "guide" with binoculars and who has time and inclination to be able to look for and find whatever wildlife does stay close to the main route. To be fair and for reference we hit the trail at 9am and that may well have been too late to see the bulk of the wildlife...  So my advice would be go to the north entrance, go early, get an official guide with binoculars and spend more than 3 hours :-)

Title: Sinharaja Northern Entrance (Kudawa Road)
Text:
Note that there are 2 entrances to the forest area, North and South.
For birdwatching the Northern part seems where most people head, but it's probably more difficult getting there than the Southern entrance. 
This post is about the Northern side only.
Choices of accommodation is limited and expensive in comparison to the rest of Sri Lanka. You really need 2 days minimum or 1 overnight stay close by to make it worthwhile, a day-trip is not realistic in my opinion.
Taking a guide is compulsory Rs1000 + Rs 650 pp entrance fee. 
The road up to the Ticket Office and parking area is tarmac & accessible to any vehicle. At the Ticket Office you pay your fees, sign the foreign visitors book and get your guide. The guides are all very experienced and know their stuff so don't worry. 
You then have to walk to the actual park entrance about 2 km uphill along the Park Road (pedestrian only) that goes through forest. (Some people get ferried uphill by arranged jeep, but this is back on a completely different track - Martin's Rd - and it's not very pleasant + expensive.) See the map on my photo uploads - the one in Google maps is completely incorrect.
Once you reach the Entrance Office, they will sign you in and let you through.
The main trail is very broad and fairly flat with resting shelters and toilets along the way. You are not "trekking" through the jungle. It's more like an easy stroll really.
In March the forest was very dry with not a single leech in sight either.
The main trail from the Entrance Office leads to a Rangers Station a few kilometres further on but there are other smaller side trails too. I was very content walking the main trail at a slow pace to spot as many things as we could, finding a feeding flock of birds is brilliant and you can easily spend an hour rooted in one spot trying to pick out different species. I found the fact that none of the guides use binoculars amazing! 

Note for birders - If you have spare time walk the access road between the Ticket Office and Kudawa Bridge below. Some good birding to be had here as well as in the actual Ticket Office grounds.

Title: Very pleasant rainforest experience with guide Chaminda
Text:
It is very difficult to find prior information on internet regarding reliable and knowledgeable forest guides and prices of a trip into Sinharaja rainforest from the south (Mederipitiya) entrance. Eventually we were advised by our taxi driver (Niron, owner of Unawatuna Tours) to hire a guide called Chaminda. Price was 5000 rp per person for our family of four, inclusive the park entrance fee of 1250 rp per person, for a full day trip (07:00 - 14:00, from our accomodation at 1 km from the park entrance). We agreed to meet Chaminda in the afternoon to discuss things further.

Our accomodation (Sinharaja Forest Sanctuary - certainly advisable for a pleasant stay!) also advsed Chaminda without being informed by us about our previous arrangements; they were very enthousiastic about his qualities. In the reviews in this Tripadvisor topic, ChamindaÂs name appeared once, also with good judgement. A couple that had made a trip with him on our arrival day was also quite pleased with him, only a bit set back because of the price (16000 rp for the two of them including entrance fee). After meeting him, we were convinced of his quality. The price seems fair enough in comparison with tourguide costs in other Sri Lanka parks. Obviously, cost per person decreases somewhat for a group of four compared to only two persons - the guide has to spend his full day in both cases, isnÂt it.

The next morning Chaminda picked us up at our hotel; he had already stored the packed breakfasts and lunches in his backpack and off we went. He immediately showed to have a keen eye for all kinds of creatures, large and small, and knew their names well (as a biologist, I was very keen on that aspect of his guidance).

The first 4 km led along a track that was also used by local villagers, as this is their only way to go there. A new road is slowly being realized through difficult terrain south of the river bordering Sinharaja on the south, and hooefully will be completed in 2 years from now. The motorbikes were certainly there but kept a reasonable pace (the track hardly allows for speeding...). We then reached the park centre where we ate our breakfast and we were registered by a park ranger; entrance fees were paid. From there we went to first waterfall, and continued in easterly direction along a steep climb to a second fall. There we had lunch and had our feet being cared for by small fish (Garra or similar species: a free jungle spa experience). We returned to the park via another trail and continued along the main path back home. Total distance was 17 km (from 7 am till 2 pm).

Leeches were hardly a problem, but we were lucky with hardly any rain so this may be the explanation. Wildlife was abundant: snakes, macaques (and purple-faced langurs heard, not seen). Grey hornbills, hand-sized spiders, large millipeds and various beautiful lizards. A beautiful experience of a primary and seemingly untouched piece of rainforest!

Chaminda can be reached via his local phonenumber 041 5633209.

Title: Amazing hike with knowledgeable naturalist
Text:
Sinharaja was a highlight of our trip to Sri Lanka.  We spent about 4.5 hours there and could not get there earlier than 10:30am (the full drive from Colombo took about  3.5 hours plus a half-hour stop) so we were only able to do the "short" loop of about 6km.  We took a tuk-tuk from the main road, arranged by our guide/driver, to a small cafe from whence we hiked to the ticket office and then into the rain forest. This is Sri Lanka's last remaining virgin forest and is a UNESCO world heritage site. Because we arrived in the middle of the day we did not get to see the full range of bird or animal life  because their natural activity is limited in the middle of the day; nonethless we heard their calls, which our naturalist often identified for us (hornbill, monkeys, etc.). 

One of the reasons we loved this hike was because of our naturalist (you cannot hike unaccompanied in the forest both because the government naturally wants to protect the fragile ecosystem but also likely because there are some poisonous snakes around), Sanjaya. He lives in the local village of about fifty families and has extensive knowledge of both the plants and animals at Sinharaja. He was eager to show us (at our request) many of the snakes--including a green pit viper and a bronze back--and reptiles including a couple of hump-nosed lizards and kangaroo lizards. We also saw large milipedes, a giant squirrel at close range, some large fish and a few other things. It was instantly obvious that Sanjaya knows every leaf, twig, nook and cranny of this forest and likewise knew exactly where to look for each kind of creature we wanted to see.  He also pointed out giant vines, wild cinnamon and some other unusual plants, some used for Ayurvedic medicine. Sanjaya was very conscientious and careful, always keeping an eye on our nine-year-old daughter, holding her hand at more difficult points in the hike, carrying her bag when she got too tired, warning us when we should keep our distance from a snake/riverbank/motorbike, etc.  

The hike was virtually flat and the only challenge was sometimes navigating major tree roots or uneven terrain. Some other reviews mentioned perilous leeches. We saw two miniscule ones, the size of inchworms, between four of us, but that was it the whole time. It was a dry day when we were there so it may have affected things. 

The short hike does involve crossing a river in order to get to a beautiful waterfall and swimming hole. I did not originally want to do this and ended up not swimming but it was fun to watch the others, who had a great time.

Title: PITADENIYA ENTRANCE-a waste of Time, Money, Sleep and Perspiration
Text:
We have noted the negative comments regarding this entrance and they seem well founded as we just had the most negative Rainforest Experience in 3 decades.
A two and a half hour trip from Mirissa most in darkness to get there at dawn. At the village it was 2280 rupees for us as a couple plus 2000 for the Guide (variously Freddie or Prandi who allegedly had worked there for 5 years and was abysmal-and I am being kind), and then 800rupees for the tuk-tuk to carry you from the village to the restaurant at the edge of the Rainforest itself. In fairness it was a diabolical track but are you going to refuse have travelled for probably hours and hours to get there. You are pressed to order a meal and the indifferent breakfast for 2 was more expensive than we would pay in Spain at our coastal resort for a full English breakfast.
On to the rainforest experience and what an experience it was as we constantly had to quit the path in order to avoid being flattened by motorcycles and scooters. You see the track runs between 2 villages and is used for foot and cycle traffic. Then again there were the pedestrians although for the most part they were all smiles and 'good-mornings'  to which we replied in good part.
So what did we see-Birds-ZERO, mammals-Zero, 6 Spiders, a small snake that crawled through the leaf litter-a whole 3cm long, a 5cm green tree snake, a chameleon and a kangaroo jumping lizard. And that was it. We have seen more wildlife in our hotel garden in Weligama including a 2m Monitor, a Mongoose, and Indian Cobra (which was duly collected by the snake man), and umpteen lizards.
We arrived at the bridge some 3km on thinking we would get to the waterfall! Wrong again, you have to parallel the course of the river and then wade across. I ask you-shouldn't we have been warned. No the guide just wanted to shoot through because of course as soon as he had got rid of us he was then free to inveigle another punter to part with his/her hard earned money.
At the bridge I spent some time talking to a local villager who said that the whole thing was nothing but a scam. The local fauna is just not in evidence due to the nature of the current disturbance and that anyone wanting to see the real Sinharaja and its wildlife should enter from the north where the fauna is much more acclimated to human intrusion. I know this seems somewhat contradictory but perhaps he meant that there were no noisy 2 wheelers shrieking by every 5 minutes or so.
The pace set by the Guide was anything but conducive to studying nature and you had to keep your head down to avoid slipping and tripping. No Leeches.
In conclusion, and as a world traveller of 40 years plus a thoroughly negative experience although possibly less so to the uninitiated and ON A GOOD DAY. Whatever you do avoid this entrance and state this to your Tour Company.

Title: Wonderful place.
Text:
Sinharaja is a lovely place and we saw some exciting and uncommon birds. Sinharaja is for those who are serious about bird-watching are prepared to do a fair bit of walking and are equipped with good binoculars and leech socks. 

Our naturalist guide was very knowledgeable and was able to spot and identify birds quickly. 

I would recommend an early arrival around 7am because it seems they run out of guides and Jeeps. 

Having obtained our tickets and found the naturalist guide, we had to wait 20 minutes or so for a Jeep (even at 7am). This took us up the hill on an extremely rough road (15 minutes) and left us with the naturalist guide to walk through the reserve. It would be possible to walk up the hill but it would take a long time to get to the heart of the reserve.

After some 2 - 3 hours, the naturalist guide suggested we go to the Âvillage areaÂ in a Jeep where he reckoned we could see a number of birds not previously seen. So we waited 20 minutes or so for another Jeep and started back down the hill. Halfway down, we met the original Jeep coming up and changed vehicle. At the bottom we met our chauffeur/guide who had taken us to the reserve and he explained that if we took the Jeep to the ÂvillageÂ, which it appeared was outside the park area, it would cost extra (some 3500 rupees). He explained that what we had paid for was one Jeep trip up the hill and down again. We declined the Jeep but the chauffeur/guide took us in the car as far as he could and we agreed to walk the rest with the naturalist guide. We never really reconciled whether the naturalist guide was simply trying to get us the best bird-watching experience and see the most interesting birds, or whether he was trying to rip us off by luring us into extra charges.

I donÂt know what our agent in Sri Lanka expected and had paid for the package that we had but, from the contract we were sent, I had expected that the Jeep and naturalist guide would be at our disposal for the day.

However, we saw lots of exciting and uncommon birds, had a lovely day in the rain forest and came away happy and content. What more could we ask?

Title: A really good contrast to other places
Text:
We spent a couple of nights a Sinharaja Forest Reserve in the middle of a dry spell, so I don't know what it is like when it rains.

I really enjoyed our stay here, it's a tourist location but not touristy. The relatively small number of guests gives it a country house hotel feel as we had conversations with a number of other residents.

The accommodation is in T shaped metal buildings, they are large enough for two with good showers, bed and settee. They also have a number of UK sockets, we also had an extension lead. Interestingly we were able to sleep with the windows open as there does not seem to be any flying biting creatures at all. 

Breakfast and dinner were both good, although there is only a choice of two main courses for the 5 course dinner. Our travel agent said they do not serve alcohol which is not true.

The WIFI is a little erratic but it did not prevent me from doing everything I wanted to do online.

The high spots are the very relaxed walks with the personable and knowledgeable guides. We did 3 in one day the 6.30 am bird watching 3.3 miles along a road, the rainforest walk around 3 hours over reasonably easy ground and the waterfall walk somewhat steeper. On the latter walk one can paddle in the water and let the fish clear any dead skin of your feet. The walks are free and there is nothing to stop you going on the same one twice. There was an evening walk on offer as well. 

As others have said leech socks are provided I wore them on the second walk but not on the last one when I had shorts and crocs on.

The journey to the hotel is 'interesting' as it's pretty steep and narrow, our driver had no problems but others did especially if it was the first time they had done it.

Text:

BTW If you do get a leech, the current science recommendation is to just pry it loose with your fingernail.

Title: Beautiful Walk
Text:
We (my wife and I) booked this through the hotel we were staying at, the Cinnamon Citadel, Kandy. We only had a few hours to spare before moving south down the country and were glad we took this opportunity.

We were picked up in a car at the hotel, and driven there in what only took about 15 minutes. It was early morning, roughly 7am, and the park was empty. Other than our guide we did not see anyone else. This made it all the more peaceful. If you're an early riser, i'd recommend going early. It lent itself to some wonderful scenes of mist clearing and the sun starting to break through the trees. Good photo opportunities.

As others have said, there are plenty of monkeys going about their daily business. Additional wildlife we encountered included a deer, a few species of butterfly and a kingfisfer.

One of the unexpected points of note, was the enourmous Puss-well (Giant Liana) tree. It's about 200 years old and spreads over an area of nearly 2 hectares. That information is thanks to a photo I took of the sign rather than my memory, but the way which the trees branches twisted and grew were certainly memorable and something i'd never seen before.

There were longer routes to take, so you could spend more than the couple of hours we did, depending upon how much you enjoy such walks. The scenary within the forest was very good throughout and you also get to see some good views over Kandy at one point. Wildlife was intermittant, which was fine for us. The sections we did were fairly flat. There was one steep section to see a cave, which was optional rather than on the main route.

If you book via that hotel, we found the guide Nithan to be very knowledgable. He is someone who is massively passionate about wildlife, and we got on to talking about his current research papers on plastics and how Sri Lanka might implement policies to address the amount currently impacting the wildlife in Kandy and beyond.

Overall we throughlly enjoyed this and would happily recommend to enyone who likes fairly easy walks in a beautiful surrounding with a spot of wildlife.

Text:
We visited the Royal Forest Patk, Udawattakele, yesterday morning and spend a couple of hours wandering around the interesting trails. There is also a temple on the map however the route down to this was closed of, we did however find some of the caves which were interesting to see.

In terms of nature & an enjoyable walk I would give the forest four stars, but because some of the points of interest in the park seemed difficult to find/we weren't permitted to see, (perhaps could do with a few more signposts,) I gave it three. Definitely would still recommend as an enjoyable way to spend a couple of hours.

Title: A very pleasant forest walk
Text:
A lovely, pleasant, forest walks, easy level paths - I managed fine with my ordinary sandals. Not many flowering plants at the time when I visited (late March) but the trees, the climbers and the general greenery are beautiful. Especially lovely on a sunny day when the trees provide shade.

Saw groups of monkeys in a couple of places - they seemed quite bold and let me come up very close. Heard plenty of birds but couldn't see them high up in the trees - not being a bird person I couldn't tell what they were, but for a bird expert armed with binoculars this forest must be very exciting!

Signage is variable and the map (which is provided on a leaflet you get when you pay for your entrance) is a little confusing - the man who took my fee explained which is the best way to go for the amount of time I wanted to spend there - I wouldn't have known without his advice.

Plenty of stone benches scattered around the path.. Beware of the small blood-sucking leeches though - I've been warned about them but this was my first experience of these creatures in 2.5 months, only noticed some hours later when changing my clothes that about 4 of the blood-suckers were having a party on my left leg!

Title: Lovely peaceful rainforest in the middle of Kandy town
Text:
Altho they charge foreigners - even residents-  Rs 600 considerably more than locals (Rs28!) , if you feel like a long forest walk away from the madding crowds it is well worth going for 2-3 hour ramble. Fabulous indigenous rainforest vegetation including the world's biggest liana (Pus) and giant bamboos. It is very little visited even at a weekend. There is a cycle track for mountain bikers but we didn't see any bikers. Note last entry at 4.30pm.
From here you can walk down to the Garrison cemetery (alot of steps down & up!) which is interesting for its recording of the British colonial history in this area. And also visit the Trinity College chapel which is said to be one of the most beautiful Anglican chapels in the country. We didn't manage to get past the gate (have to wear long trousers, not shorts) but some friends managed to charm the guard later in the day and raved about it. 
All off the beaten path, and a welcome change from the crowds at the Temple of the Tooth and Botanical Gardens.

Title: Enjoyable early morning walk
Text:
