We went early, in order to enjoy the birdlife.  It was a very pleasant, slow two hour walk, as we tried to identify the wide variety of birdcalls we heard.  This was a struggle, as the sanctuary is well wooded and the birds quite elusive.  We identified and photographed a few, also saw a family of wild boar, a troop of monkeys and a deer.  Highlights for us were spotting Lesser Goldenback and Crimsonbacked Goldenbacks (woodpeckers) and seeing a Lesser Hill Mynah on its nest in a hole in a tree.

The walk is very well signposted with a number of routes.  We only did the main circuit, which is about 3km.  Very quiet, very peaceful.

Title: Good but Leopards remained elusive
Text: Wilpattu is the oldest and largest (1317 sq km) National Park in Sri Lanka and we explored it from the delightful Leopard Trails luxury tented safari camp.  The camp is only a few minutes drive from the National ParkÂs entrance gate and our journeys to and from the park were partly taken on the wrong side of the road.   The local rice farmers have worked out that by spreading their newly harvested rice over one carriageway, the rice dries twice as quickly (using the heat attracted by the black tarmac) as traditional methods.  We took three drives (one full day and two half days) which saw us cover a good deal of the parkÂs forested, sandy and lake side areas.  It was great to see many animals in their natural habit and spotted deer, water buffalo, jackals and wild boar made regular appearances.  An elephant entertained us by standing in the lake, ripping vast quantities of water plants up, shaking off the mud and munching them for itÂs tea.  There were many species of birds to admire, with sea eagles catching their supper from the lake, serpent eagles and owls staring regally from their tree perches and our favourite, the brightly coloured varieties of bee eaters.  Often our drives seemed like we were driving through snow, as white butterflies settled in mud pools to collect minerals and then burst into blizzard like flight as we passed close by.  A picture postcard position beside the lake was perfect for a sumptuous lunch.  A little drama was added by monkeys watching us closely for the chance of any left overs and us keeping a careful eye on the partly submerged crocodile twenty meters out in the lake.  Further searching revealed many other sightings, even a brief glimpse of a Sloth Bear.  Sadly the key attraction (leopards) remained elusive for everyone

Title: Our great leopard experience
Text:
Wilpattu sits a little bit off the regular organised tour circuit, positioned slightly north of the central west coast of the country. It's also Sri Lanka's largest national park. These two factors mean that you'll experience less safari traffic than in Yala or even Kaudulla. Another benefit, if you're lucky enough to discover a leopard or other large animal, is that there is no mobile phone reception so safari guides cannot readily communicate sightings to stimulate a mad dash by everyone within range to share the experience.

It's a selfish view, but it paid off for us when we encountered a leopard on a lakeside trail in a more remote part of the park. Our driver slowly reversed the vehicle as our leopard followed us back down the trail for about 15 minutes before padding off into the jungle. 

We also encountered a Fishing Eagle and Crested Serpent Eagle within telephoto lens range in this park - something we had not been able to do elsewhere. Wilpattu also offers encounters with the usual suspects - water buffalo, land monitors, wild boar, spotted and barking deer, crocodiles and a wide variety of birds.

Title: Variety of animals / birds without too many jeeps
Text:
I was wary of other national parks in Sri Lanka (e.g. Yala, Minneriya) as I had heard they were very busy with jeeps and I really don't enjoy viewing wildlife when you are one of 20 jeeps crowded around - so I thought I would give Wilpattu a try.

I did one full-day safari and started at the Eluwankulama entrance - it was quiet when I went, there were no queues and the only other jeep there was carrying the other guests from my hotel. 

The biggest group of jeeps that I saw at once (aside from at the rest stop) was when a leopard had been sighted in the bushes. At that point there were maybe 6-8 jeeps in the vicinity waiting for the leopard to make an appearance. The leopard did indeed come out and crossed the road in a flash! At other times throughout the day, we passed the occasional other jeep but often went long stretches of time without seeing anyone else which was really nice.

The park is vast, a lot of it is wooded and so it felt harder to spot animals for this reason. There are several watering holes and you can see animals drinking around the perimeter. I did see a huge variety of birds, elephants (including a large group just before the entrance/exit to the park - I was the only jeep there), 2 leopards (fleeting / at a distance), monitor lizards, deer, monkeys... The wildlife is fewer and far between compared to other places perhaps, and we did go a couple of hours without seeing any animals at all. When you do spot something though, it feels extra special for this reason.

I didn't love the rest stop where I was brought for breakfast / lunch - too many monkeys which steal food and climb into the jeeps. They are afraid of the drivers but certainly not afraid of the tourists. There are basic squat toilet facilities. I would have preferred to have parked near one of the water holes in the park and eaten there instead. 

Overall, if you go with the right attitude and don't expect a zoo - you will enjoy Wilpattu.

Title: A truly wild park - not Longleat
Text:
We did 2 safaris at Wilpattu. One was an afternoon safari and one was an all day safari. 
Wilpattu is a big park and there are less roads than at Yala, but there are also a lot less jeeps, and for much of our wildlife viewing we were on our own. During our afternoon safari we watched a sloth bear feeding from a termite nest very close to the road. We were able to sit there for around 20 minutes and during that time we were joined by maybe half a dozen other jeeps - a complete contrast to Yala where around 30 jeeps were competing for a view of a sloth bear which was much further away from the road.
We saw lots of animals and birds. We didn't see a leopard but we saw plenty of evidence that they were around - lots of very recent footprints in the sand - it's down to luck whether you actually see one or not, but the chance is obviously increased by the number of safaris you undertake.
There is a place where they stop for lunch and breakfast where there is also a basic hole in the ground type toilet. Beware of all the monkeys there, who will steal your food at any opportunity!
As expected it is a very bumpy ride in the jeep and my husband suffered a bit as he has some joint problems - especially during the all day safari, which lasted from 6.15am to 6.00pm. However the advantage of the all day safari is that they can take you much further into the park, away from any other jeeps. This park is not for kids who will easily get bored - but it is a genuinely immersive wildlife experience.

Title: Beautiful nature and some wild animals
Text:
Reading many reviews here, I must conclude that many hotels nearby the park who organize the Jeep tours are scamming the tourists, which is really sad. We stayed at The Backwaters and organized our safari trip with them and found them to be very trustworthy. They charged us LKR 6500 (Feb 2019), for a private Jeep fitting up to 6 people with an extra guide to sit with us. The Jeep and entrance fee must be paid in the local currency. 

Seeing a leopard or a bear is up to luck, and we unfortunately didnÂt see these animals. We came close to spotting a leopard in the bushes but mostly the guide spotted it and could take a picture of it for us. The bushes are really dense so you have to be really lucky or early to spot a leopard walking up to you on the roads or in an open space. 

We did a half day safari starting from 6:30 to about 11am. By the end of it we were pretty beat. So maybe it's more advisable to do a morning and evening safari on two separate days if you wish. Bring a jacket and wear light long pants as the Jeep is open (windy) and the morning air gets quite cold. 

The drive in is through a long road of dense bush land which might be a bit boring if you can't spot anything. There are small ponds where you might spot crocodiles. Our favorite spots were the open spaces with a sort of marshland or watering hole / lakes which look like a dreamland. There you can spot heards of deers, and if you're lucky like us, a large elephant swimming through the water! Simply magical! We also spotted wild boars, many birds, a turtle, a ferret and monkeys. Of course we wished we'd seen more large animals but it is up to luck really. 

We would rate the park more highly if it would have had more plentiful, and better maintained washrooms which are a basic necessity for an area which invites tourists to visit it. There is no soap, the toilet is a squatting toilet which you can't even flush, so you can imagine the smell. Please bring your own toilet paper and hand soap... And of course someone has to invariably take a dump just on the side of the toilet hole itself. Why??? If you can, use the washroom near the ticketing office and avoid drinking till you're about to leave the park again.

Title: Worth a visit if you're up in Anuradhapura
Text: We recently visited Anuradhapura and ventured across to Wilpattu for a safari.  We decided to eschew Yala as it has a reputation of being very busy, so can't comment on that, but Wilpattu isn't as quiet as we expected - even if there are only a dozen or so vehicles, you'll still end up seeing the same cars time and again as you search endlessly for wildlife!  The bush is pretty thick in places in Wilpattu, so spotting stuff can be pretty tricky at times, particularly if your driver is driving at a quicker pace that you'd like!  We started early - we were in the park by 6.15am - and it was cold, particularly with the windchill when driving - if you go early, do yourself a favour and take some warm layers with you!  We did spot quite a few things on our day safari - lots of birdlife, and quite a few mammals and reptiles too.  We weren't lucky enough to see a leopard on this occasion, but we did see a sloth bear late in the day and there's clearly a grapevine as within 10 minutes of spotting it there were about 10 vehicles around us!  We noticed quite a few vehicles had separate guides while we just had a driver - haveing done other safaris this concerned us, as normally a separate guide is a good thing (we re-organised our safari late due to issues with our previously arranged trip so had little choice!) and while we managed OK in the end I'd suggest a separate guide would be better.  It can be a very long day though - we were in at 6.15am and left the park at about 5.30pm, having been batttered and bruised from the drive in the meantime.  Still, it was well worth it - while we seemed to spend more time driving round to find stuff than we'd have liked, we did see a decent quantity and variety of animals in the end, and came away feeling pretty happy about it (probably the sloth bear siting helped!)

Title: Exceptional jeep safari with a wide variety of wildlife
Text:
This national park and wildlife reserve is probably not as well known as some others and I understand it was only created about 6 years ago following this area being off bounds during the civil war. As a result, much wildlife has been left to its own devices, but like many others, licences jeeps and drivers are available for hire. Our cost 8,000rps each and was designed to be one of the longest trips. You can negotiate shorter trips for less cost down to about 4,000rps each.
Our Jeep driver was very happy to stop and check things out and during a 4 hour trip, we managed to see most of Sri Lanka's wildlife starting with a smaller adult bull elephant grazing on the trees about 500 metres from the park entrance.
During the trip we also saw crocodiles, Mongoose, sand deer, spotted deer, water buffalo, monkey and many birds which thankfully our quite could identify for us. 
We had begun the trip at 2pm and we're lucky enough to get a call that a leopard had been spotted - quite close to the entrance again - so we rushed for half an hour to get to this spot and were very lucky indeed to catch sight of this beautiful creature. Apparently there are 12 leopards living in this area and with 2 babies this year the population is at least steady, although pressure on space can lead to conflict with the local population.
The ride was bumpy and dusty, but the experience was wonderful and it was an inspired idea to create this further wildlife reserve. There are around 150 leopards and 200 sloth bears in the park so it really is down to luck if one decides to walk out in front of you. Title: Great - if long - trip with Sri Lanka Day Tours
Text: My wife and I were staying in Colombo on business but had one day off, so we booked a trip to Wilpattu, the only major park within a reasonable travelling distance. This was with Sri Lanka Day Tours. It was still a long drive but we had an excellent driver and she included a lunch stop on the way.  We had booked an afternoon tour and arrived a little early, but the driver phoned the guide and within 10 minutes the 4x4 truck arrived.  We had a four hour tour deep into the park, seeing two large birds of prey just a few metres away, three species of deer, a mongoose - all at close quarters - and many water birds near the lakes and pools.  At the furthest pools we saw hundreds of flying foxes - large bats - hanging from trees, giving a "different world" appearance to the area and a mugger crocodile, very still with just its snout above the water.  We started back then just as light started to fade, a leopard, just 10m away.  We watched it in the bush and walking across the track ahead, for about 15 minutes.  A brilliant round up to the day. Two small gripes - the guide could have been better at pointing out and naming some of the smaller birds - though he identified over 30 species - and the company could have been clearer at the start about what pick up time was needed to get us there in time for the tour.  The day overall was about 13 hours, which was pushing it.  Still, an excellent trip overall which we will remember for many years, and at a very reasonable price.

Title: Wildlife in Wilpattu National Park
Text:
We went on 3 full day safaris (6-18) in order to see as much as possible. Exotic birds were plentiful e.g. bee-eaters, kingfishers, peacocks, painted storks and various eagles and hawks. We saw several water buffalos, a few wild boars, and some elephants. Generally the elephants can only be seen on a large distance, but one male elephant was looking for water chestnuts in one of the lakes and it was great fun watching him half buried in water. 

During the 3 days we covered a lot of ground and saw practically every corner of the park. We did appreciate that generally you travel with almost no other jeeps around you. The roads are terrible, so it is really a fun ride and you have to admire the skills of your driver.

On the second day, we spotted a young leopard drinking from a small pond no more than 30 m from the road. We got great pictures before he wandered off into the wilderness. This was great luck and generally very few visitors have that luck, so do not expect it to happen.

We highly recommend the park, but it is a severe and exhausting effort to drive 12 hours for 3 days in a row. Remember to bring warm clothes, because the mornings can be very chilly.

The only animal missing from the list was a sloth bear, but we thought we were so lucky seeing what we did.  

The jeeps tend to space themselves out so we felt we were the only ones there most of the time. Title: Like all safaries- good if you see the ÂwildlingsÂ otherwise it can quite boring
Text:
Okay so I wanted to see the Wilpattu national park upon recommendation of a couple of friends. I didnÂt have anyone to go with so had to solo it. And honestly had a very mixed experience. I quite enjoy solo travelling but a safari can be PRETTY boring alone at times- especially if there are only 3-4 other jeeps around.

Anyway the safari part: itÂs the biggest national park in Sri Lanka and there are numerous lakes inside (approx 42) which is responsible for the unique eco culture. We were the only ones to spot a leopard on the day- so I was pretty happy. We also saw: plenty of peacocks, Sri Lankan jungle fowl, eagles, wild buffalos, various other bird species, fox, crocodiles, deer (plenty). 

In summary: donÂt recommend a full day safari; would recommend going in a large group (more fun and easier on the wallet); bring binoculars; also try booking through your hotel and get a good price but make all the costs very clear at the start. Also bring plenty of food and water thereÂs not much once you re inside the park.

Title: Super for Wildlife Fans
Text:
This is a super park for variety of mammals and birds... But the pick of them is leopard, followed by Sri Lankan sloth Bear, both of which are elusive and hard to spot, with a 30%-40% chance imo. You could see Elephants, Crocodiles and Buffaloes too on most days. Park is nearly 1500 hectares, having over 40 water holes called "willus". The attraction is to spot the animals, and if you have enough time to see the dynamics between the hunter and the hunted. Here are few factors that may be handy to know
a. Park is open from 6am to 6pm
b. Entrance for locals is around LKR 800 for foreigners its more
c. Jeep fee are negotiable half day LKR 4500 and full day LKR 8000 for locals. For foreign nationals it my be 5000 and 10,000 respectively. Get a Toyota or Mistubishi jeep rather than Mahendra ones.  You may want to look at the seat too
d. There are no supermarkets, well stocked shops or restaurants close to the park. So arrange for food (breakfast and lunch) , water and any other refreshment you need prior to going in to the park. This is sad part, but true. Even after coming out of the park at 6pm you cant get a good cup of Ceylon tea, unless you have pre-arranged or travel to Nochiyagama (few km from Wilpattu Junction). Suggets you buy the following
1. Water Bottles from Cargills/ Keels Super or Arpico / American Premium or Aquafin
2. Tea : There are iced tea/ fruit juices if you like to sip in
3. Some fruits or nuts: Almonds and Guava are my favorites if I'm going for a full day. Anamaalu bananas are good too.
e. Park has different routes so you could say you want to go up to Thambapanni (Kudiraimalai Point) which is a beach where early settlers to Sri Lanka from India came. But less animals or birds here. But you could see sea eagles fishing on most days and large elephants on Periya willu or Periya uppu villu and sinna uppu willu. You can ask the jeep to go towards Pomparippu where seeing elephants is more likely though its a dusty road. 
f. There is a very basic washroom at Kumbukwillu where jeeps stop for breakfast (around 8-9) and lunch around 1pm. Better to tell him your expected lunch time so that you don't have to keep worrying
g. between 12.30 to 2pm these jeep drivers prefer not to drive and the excuse they say is that animals will be resting during this time. Only partly true imo but unless you know the driver well, you may have to stick to taking photos around Kumbuwillu. One driver to us to a church close to pomparippu but that is not a done deal it seems
h. you could stay at Anuradhapura and drive to the park early morning or stay in wilpattu itself. Rooms start at around 3000 for locals. You may have to check if the hotel/ motel provides food (breakfast and lunch) early morning at 5.30 or so before confirming the motel/ hotel.
I. During dry season lots of dust / If you are going with the kids you may want to use masks. Caps and sunglasses are must. I don't go there without my camera, or at least binoculars.

I have been there few times. I have been to other parks in Sri Lanka, but for diversity in terms of animals and landscape, no other park could beat Willpattu. However,, don't expect Leopards and Slothbear to usher you in to the park. That is only a 30-40% chance , though I'm repeating it ;-)

Title: Struggled to deliver what was promised but delivered something I was pleased with
Text:
As I write this I am a bit conflicted. All the talk about this park is the chance to see a leopard. The problem with that is the chance of seeing one is 50-50. So like what happened to me... there is potential to be disappointed when you fail to see one. Probably the biggest problem with this park is that it is quite thick jungle and as such the view from the Safari truck can get a bit monotonous. 

That being said the scenery opens up at some points and when it does it is majestic. I saw in Enormous Lotus Lily Ponds, beautiful lakes and a whole bunch of animals I was not expecting such as a very cool 'Sloth Bear', Buffalo, deer, crocodiles, monkeys and a lot - and I mean a lot - of birds of amazing colours and shapes.

At the end of the day I had to tell myself 'self don't be disappointed you ... might have missed out on the leopard but half the people do... but you still got to see something pretty amazing.'

So I think if the park perhaps talked down the leopard a bit and talked up the other great things They have this might be a more well known attraction. 

A half day was enough... It opens at 6am. It is about 1 hour out of Anuradhapura so it makes for an additional half day trip if you are visiting the ancient city there. The heat would make any longer in the park unbearable - and besides, the animals are all hiding and sleeping in the middle of the day. Take a lot of water and food with you as the shop was not open when the park opened.

Title: Great Lakes and Landscapes
Text:
Wilpattu National Park is the largest in Sri Lanka, located on the north-western coast of the island. The park's unique feature are the large lakes that attract much bird life. It is home to leopard, bear, sambar, elephant, deer, crocs, peacock, jungle fowl to name a few.
A visit to the park requires a minimum of half a day, however a full day visit (6am- 6pm) is highly recommended since the attractions to be visited are located at least 40 - 50 km from the park entrance and hence cannot be visited within half a day.
The scenery is beautiful and relaxing, if you are lucky you may be able to have a river bath in one of the limited locations visitors are permitted to alight. (Kokmote camp site)
You can hire a safari jeep at the entrance, the ride can be quite bumpy due to the terrain. 
There are no places to buy food, so be prepared with packed breakfast, lunch, snacks and lots of drinking water.

This is the place, where if I die, I want my ashes scattered, its that special to me. Over the last 13 years of visiting the park, I have seen many amazing sighting, from 5 hour leopard sightings, to tuskers, bears, elusive and rare Forest Eagle Owls, our jeep being rammed by a wild boar and so much more. This is THE park to visit when your visiting Sri Lanka.

Title: Well managed park with lots of wildlife
Text:
Vilpaththu National Park is a newer park in the north west of the island that is growing in popularity.  I chose to come here over Yala and the more famous reserves in the south as I had heard a lot of tales from other travellers about irresponsible operators in that park, harassing the animals and behaving dangerously.  So I decided I'd prefer to visit a park that had lower chances of seeing a leopard, but at least wouldn't put the animal at any risk if I did see one.

Vilpaththu does have all sorts of animals living within its forests, including leopards, sloth bears, crocodiles, and a very small number of elephants.  You are not guaranteed to see them.  I have been lucky enough to already see leopards in Africa, so I was perhaps more relaxed about this than some travellers may be.  

The park consists of dense jungly forest, interspersed with big lakes (the name means 'many lakes').  You drive in high, open sided jeeps along well defined but bumpy red earth tracks, through the forest.  There are relatively few tracks so you tend to take the route there is.  There aren't options for vehicles to go 'off road' due to the forest, which is a good thing as it prevents the environment being degraded.

On a four hour trip, I saw lots of different wildlife, including crocodiles (huge, and really good views), spotted and barking deer, mongooses, peacocks, green bee eaters, a serpent eagle, beautiful butterflies, large monitor lizards, two types of monkey, wild boar, and wading birds.  For me, a lot of the joy of a safari is not knowing what you might see next, and its that thrill of the unknown that makes it such a great experience.  Even if you see nothing at all, I find that makes the experience worthy in itself.  Of course, I'm lucky in having done several safaris in different places, so perhaps get less anxious about seeing things that people who might have only had this chance.

If I'd had more time, I'd have been happy to stay here and do a few game drives over a couple of days.  I reckon if you went several times you'd have a pretty good chance of seeing a leopard or bear.  You are unlikely to see elephants here, but there are lots of other parks in Sri Lanka where you've got a really high chance, so factor in a trip to one of those too if you can.  It's a well managed park, with no litter and not too many jeeps, and I loved it.  If you have never seen big wildlife before and are desperate to see a leopard, you might be better off going for one of the southern parks.  But I'd highly recommend this park in addition if you can, or for those who are happy to see smaller animals.

Text:
I wanted to take my kids to see something of the Sri Lankan geography, and also various animals in their natural habitat (rather than zoos or such like).

The jeep safari was excellent - basically it is a converted 4x4 pick up truck with comfy seats welded/bolted into the back.  It had a roof but open sides - so we only got a little bit wet when the rain poured down!

Highlights included there was the lone bull elephant eating reeds in one of the lakes, a leopard (which we only spotted on the way back), large land lizards, peacocks and other colourful birds.
We left as it was getting dark, and just before the gate there was an elephant crossing the path - we had to wait until it disappeared into the bush, but then it let out a loud roar which the kids thought was amazing.
Although it was a long journey from/to our hotel (because of young kids), we all thoroughly enjoyed the visit and it is a memory that we will cherish.

Title: Beautiful park!
Text:
We went to Wilpattu instead of Yala for a chance to see a leopard in the wild. Our guide, Krishan Fernando of Triplanka Tours was a god send. If you're a bird watcher you will love the guy. He identified all the wildlife we saw, most especially the birds. He knows all the local birds of Sri Lanka by heart. He even brought binoculars with him. Had a good eye in spotting the wildlife in the bushes, better even that our hired park driver.

We opted afternoon with the thought that the animals will start appearing after the heat of midday, maybe near the watering holes. We were lucky. We saw a 2 year old adult male leopard 3-4 hours into the safari. It was just right there. Lounging beside a bush at the edge of clearing near a lake. Like a boss. The other two we saw while going back to the entrance. Along the road! One was around an 18 month old female who probably just left the care of its mum as our guides said and another was a cub, barely a year old. so the mum was also probably hiding somewhere in the bush.

We didn't spot a sloth bear, our guide said it wasn't the time of the year but the leopards alone were so worth it. Just hope for the best though, not everyone sees one. They do get scared if there are too many jeeps around. We were lucky there were only a max of maybe 15 jeeps that afternoon with us. A couple we talked to spent an entire day at the park without seeing a single leopard or bear. Just birds.

We, party of two(couple) stayed At a potable tented camp by "Master Campers" outfit inside the Wilpattu National Park, in Sri Lanka on the nights of November 29, 30 and December 1 in 2013. 
The tents are reasonably comfortable with enough cold water and barely adequate hot water. Remember that these tents are set up in a few hours time, considering that I would rate the accommodation in terms of comfort as satisfactory to good. The Master Campers own vehicles take you for game drives in the morning and afternoon. As you are already camping within the park you get more actual drive time in park game dives. The guides are well informed and very very helpful. The food is good and has reasonable choices.I was told that they arrange for within the park tents at various wild life parks in Sri Lanka; but can do only three nights maximum within one park. We were able to see leopard, crocodiles, many birds,. especially eagle species, elusive barking deer, Sambar deers, python, mongooses, jackals, the rare Purple Faced Leaf Monkey(Tachypethicus vetulus), grey Langurs, Fishing owls among others. The very agile climbing leopards being the most rewarding experience. The Game drives were excellent and accommodation good to very good.

Title: No leopard but lots of other wildlife in 3 hour ride.
Text:
Only complaint - the visibilty from the safari wagons is very limited by having a solid fixed fibreglass roof and a roll down 9" surrounding pelmet so anything in the trees (ie birds!) is impossible to see. The driver stayed in the cab, as we had no guide on board, and he pointed out of his window so no information on what we were looking for or indeed had missed.

Having said that low level birds, iguanas aplenty, jungle fowl, peacocks, crocs, turtles, mongoose, jackals, several types of deer, water buffalo, elephant, (stupidly the driver missed the best one and did not stop despite us shouting and banging on his cab roof) all seen well and many photographed.

I know that Sri Lanka and its fabulous people are recovering wonderfully well from a terrible war and tsunami and I am loathe to criticise but they need to make a few adjustments to improve the viewing experience and attract more tourists to this fantastic nature reserve.

Title: An idyllic nature setting at the Willu
Text:
My expereinces of the park was a first, and my impressions were very positive with regard to the range and scale of fauna and flora considering that the park's size meant that most shy animals could remain outside the visitors' paths with ease.

Our jeep experience was less than satisfactory as the guides allocated to us simply performed routine roles which included taking us on a designated route, with absolutely no consideration for the needs of the tourist but with a view on the "tip" only. 

This might not be noticed by foreign visitors as much as local visitors would. This seems to be a general reflection on attitudes in general throughout such operations for visitors to the country.

Our accommodation at a private bungalow owned by a friend was superb while being simple, in that it included a very enthusiastic husband and wife team who saw to all our needs with great interest.

The weather in late June was quite dry and the area had not seen rain for perhaps more than a month. The lack of toilet facilities at the park office area was felt badly, as everyone had to go to the bush area outside those premises.

Overall, the park was lovely in its variety of flora and bird life.A great expereince all told.

Lasantha Pethiyagoda
Melbourne, Australia

Title: A beautiful park re-emerging after the security concerns a few years ago
Text:
I have been to Wilpattu many times, but the most distinct images in my mind are from 2004 , from when I have visited this park a further 3 times. Let me put it briefly, the park is beautiful and it is a miracle that the wild life that currently exists, remains as is, given the poaching and lack of management during the LTTE era.  My most recent visit was in May this year and we stayed at the "Kokmutai" Bungalow within the park. Wildlife did not disappoint, we saw leopard every one of the four days we were there, including bear and elephant. However this bungalow, supposed to be a premium one, dissaponited very much. The location was magic, located by the Modaragam aru river with the peaceful jungle around. The maintenance of the bungalow was however sadly lacking, toliets in very poor condition, no light bulbs in many parts of the place and very limited electricity (solar power) that seem to run out way ahead of the "cut off" time.
I understand the government wants to make these bungalows similar to the game lodges in Africa, great intention, but based on the current condition and price, this vision has a lot more work involved, if it is to become a reality.

Title: Tough climb to beautiful waterfall
Text:
I gave it 4 stars because of the tough climb to get to the top. Otherwise, it is indeed a multi-level beautiful waterfall with a number of pools to sit or have fun in.

The walk up starts with a fairly straightforward dirt path through rubber trees and a small cluster of houses. However, the rest of it is a climb up the mountain, on uneven, scrabbly rocks, large and small, and cut-in steps in the ground. You should be young or of moderate fitness to do this. Definitely wear proper shoes and have sunscreen and water. At the top there is a coconut seller, then slightly downhill to the actual waterfall. 
It is fairly easy to get to the various levels of the waterfall. Be careful stepping in and out of the pools as the rocks are slippery with moss.  
There is only a roti and coconut seller at the waterfall itself. Bring some snacks or you can buy them from the few village grocery shops on the road in. Very friendly locals, we smiled and waved to everyone.
From the bottom of the waterfall, you will need to climb back up again to the top where the coconut seller is, to go all the way down again. It takes about 1hr each way.

Title: Nice adventure, but a bit remote
Text:
We visited here on the advice of our guesthouse in Haputale. We hiked up and down Lipton's Seat in the morning and then caught the Wellawaya bus at about 2pm. Bus was mega full (it was a Sunday) and we didn't get a seat. It was hot and bumpy and we were happy to get of the bus after 1hr and a half. 

It was dry season so there wasn't much water, but the falls were impressive nonetheless. We didn't hang around too long at the bottom because it was a bit touristy. Instead we attempted the hike to the top, as described in the Lonely Planet (2012 edition). A young boy from the village volunteered to guide us along the way. To be honest we would have struggled without him, so we gave him 10Rs. ostensibly to buy school supplies. He put us on the right path and we scrambled up for 20min to the top. You should make sure to take plenty of water for the hike, and don't wear flip-flops. 

At the top we hoped to have the pools to ourselves, as we were hot and sweaty and just wanted to jump in the water. Surprisingly there were a few groups of locals (one getting a bit boozy), and some German girls attracting attention in their bikinis. We just took our boots off and cooled our feet off while chatting to the locals (apparently a family of wild elephants come here for a drink most days at around 6:30pm). 

Sadly we didn't go to the top of the actual falls, because we had to get the bus back to Haputale. It looked really cool and would probably make a great photo. 

The REAL HIGHLIGHT for me was in fact the bus ride back up to Haputale. Buses going up come approx. every 30min, and the last one is at 1830. It took us just over an hour to hike up, 20min at the top, and 45min to get back down, so we caught the bus at about 1720. There was plenty of space on the bus, and it was a magical journey through the forested hills overlooking the southern lowlands as the sun sets over the mountains. Keep your eyes peeled for macaques as you drive up!

Give yourself more time than we did if you're using public transport. Alternatively, if you have your own transport, take a torch with you, stay to see the elephants. :)

Title: Lovely views and a nice hike- wear good hiking shoes and water proof jacket
Text:
It was an impromptu decision to go to this location. Our driver took us to the locality, from where we took a tuk tuk for half the ride up amidst the tea plantations. Since the path is full of stones and very narrow, normal cars cannot go up, however tuk tuks can easily access the place. For serious hikers, they can go for the climb all the way till the falls. 
En route, the view is enthralling, with team plantations all around and if the weather is on your side, there is little mist and clouds. As we went in December, we continued to experience rainfall throughout our journey.
Once the tuk tuk parked at it's last accessible spot, we took a short hike up (around a kilometre). Ensure to wear proper hiking shoes as because of the waterfall, the area is wet, with lots of small streams flowing, making the path slippery. There are also loose stones and wet ones, so shoes with a good grip will help. If you have not climbed before, be careful of your footing, however for most part, its a fairly easy climb.
Also be prepared to get wet! Needless to say, the water from the waterfall will get you soaked. Mind you, we were just on one side of the waterfall and not in its way, however the pressure sends water sprays that soak you completely. Some of us went prepared and were fine... others like me felt we jumped into the water :)
Its a fantastic view and very rejuvenating to be in the midst of nature and I really enjoyed it.
With the cold and wet weather of Nuwara Eliya, note that clothes DO NOT dry easily, unless you have heaters or fans.

Title: Nice hike to the quiet waterfall
Text:
From where the car stops, it's a 10-15 minute walk that takes you through a local neighborhood, tea plants and other plantations common in this high-altitude Sri Lankan rural community.

The fall itself is at its ebb in December, which is when we visited, but it still offers spectacular views of Nuwara Eliya.

Lovers Leap is the main source of water for the entire Nuwara Eliya valley, so visitors are asked to be considerate of the water and not contaminate it.

The name Lovers Leap kind of betrays the legend: a prince fell in love with a beautiful maiden living in the valley but his father opposed the union, so he took his beloved and together they leapt to their tragic demise, their love forever immortalized by the folly of their youth and a waterfall that is visited by many from far and wide.

Title: A Must See (the largest of the falls)
Text:
Ramboda is the name of the town and there are several waterfalls. Some of the reviews on here are not of the actual fall that most go to see. The beautiful one in the bulk of pictures is found by walking through the Ramboda Falls Hotel.  

GETTING THERE: You have to go all the way to the bottom of the stairs and then walk along a path.  It is not a 15-20 min hike. It's a walk down a street then down the stairs of a hotel, then along a path that is about 100-200 meters. It can be a bit taxing if you are not in great shape as it is still a lot of stairs.  Also, if you're walking down to the hotel from the road you might find it difficult. From the road, down the hotel stairs over to the falls, is a comfortable 15 minute walk.  There are restrooms in the hotel. I think there is also a lift that you can extra for.  The street down to the hotel is rather steep.

THE FALLS: We saw 3 falls in Ramboda.  One was a quick one by the side of the road after the Rothschild tea farm.  Then this one. In the distance you can see a huge waterfall that is likely quite the hike for advanced folk. The one through the hotel, though is likely the one you want to see. On my insta, I'll be posting a video of some of the photo shots that are possible. When we were there, there were a few girls and guys that were clearly doing a photo shoot in front of the falls. I had envy. It's so beautiful and the set up for the shots is soo easy.  When we went it was not crowded, so we could do whatever we wished.  

TIME OF YEAR:  May is not quite wet and not quite dry season.  The images of people in the water must be during dry season. It would seem rather dangerous during May to go into the water.  The beauty of the falls is kind of independent of the weather season though, IMO.

WHAT TO BRING/WEAR: Def bring your photo gear and anything you want for a photo.  Also, I would def wear shoes with good treads in the month of May. Despite a great walkway they've put up, you will end up with muddy shoe wear and it can feel a bit unsteady if you don't have any treads.

Title: Good views, Hotel Needs Improvement
Text:
On our way to Nuwara Eliya from Colombo, we stopped at Ramboda Falls Hotel for lunch. This hotel is ideally situated to get the best views of the Ramboda Water Fall. Our driver stopped the car on the main road. Many people find it difficult to walk down the steep winding alley to reach the hotel entrance which is far below the road level. The hotel is not even 50 metres from the road, but has a shuttle service to take people to the hotel and back. 
When we arrived at the hotel, the placed was packed with people. Several tour groups have arrived in buses and they were enjoying the buffet lunch. The hotel staff basically force you to have buffet lunch saying ordering food from the menu can take a long time. We reluctantly took the option of going for the Buffet lunch and found the food to be very ordinary. There were too many people and the food was not being replenished fast enough. We found some of the visitors scraping the bottom of the containers unable to find enough food in them. We found an empty table in a far corner and kept our camera and the handbag on the table to show the table is occupied. We asked for a ginger beer. They have run out of ginger beer and we had to manage with only a bottle of water. We served our food and brought the plate back to the table to find another person sitting at our table in spite of our handbag and the camera. We were not sure how to handle it and luckily for us, the waiter came and asked the person to move to another table. He was a single person on his own. We heard the person arguing with the waiter saying he was occupying the table before we came and they cleared it before he finished eating. Anyway, he has finished eating his desert and left the table without a fuss. I was feeling a bit awkward, but these things can easily happen when the restaurants are over crowded. My advice is that all the people should not leave the table at the same time. You leave at least one person at the table when you go to serve your food. 
I took a few photos of the water fall from the back yard of the hotel. A few years ago, it was possible to walk right up to the water fall. Now they have put a fence preventing the people getting too close to the water fall. We left the place a bit shaken, but this is one place you should visit when you are on your way to Nuwara Eliya. I am not happy with the quality of the food and my advice is to avoid staying overnight unless you are a keen nature lover and like to explore the area. If possible, avoid the big crowd by not going there during the lunch time. A soft drink or a beer with a side plate like chips or sandwiches is better than their lunch. In any case, you cannot avoid paying extra money for the food, just to have a good look at the water fall and the beautiful scenery around the area.

Title: Zoo at Dehiwala, Colombo: One of the best Zoo in the World
Text:
National Zoological Gardens of Sri Lanka (also called Colombo Zoo or Dehiwala Zoo) is a zoological garden in Dehiwala, Sri Lanka, founded in 1936. Its sprawling areas are host to a variety of animals and birds. The zoo exhibits animals but also places an emphasis on animal conservation and welfare, and education.The zoo has 3000 animals and 350 species as of 2005. The zoo exchanges its residents with other zoological gardens for breeding purposes. Dehiwala Zoological Garden is one of the oldest zoological gardens in Asia and one of the most abusive. It has a substantial collection of worldwide animals. It is open all year long and can be reached by public transportation. Diversity of the zoo is indicated by the presence of an aquarium, walk through aviary, reptile house, butterfly garden and many small, dilapidated cages and enclosures, housing starving, bored animals, living in prison-like conditions.

The zoological garden has a small, but picturesque butterfly garden which is decorated with small shrubs, trees, creepers and small streams. Internal temperature and humidity of the house is controlled by artificially created mist. The butterfly garden exhibits 30 species of butterflies with their all stages of life cycle for educational purposes.  It offers discount to children below 12 years and to SAARC country residents so please carry your passports. Best way to see the zoo is to engage a Golf Cart. It is worth all the money. Must Visit.

The temple itself is nothing spectacular.  There is a old bath with some carvings, and stairs to climb up a boulder.  There's another grotto kind of built into a cave with Buddha statues. Once you see all three things, each worth about 5-10 minutes of your time, you're pretty much done...  I honestly found the surrounding lily ponds and view of the reservoir more interesting than the temple itself.  Definitely see that.

I pegged down because of 1) the shoe policy: temples elsewhere, for example, often hand out clean flip flops to use.  and 2) The site itself was simply not that spectacular.  I mentioned this in another review of Anuradhapura, but skip this town unless you have time.  Sigiriya and Polonaruwa, in the cultural triangle, are both more interesting.

Title: Amazing Lord Buddha Sculptures in Cave & Beautiful Scenery from Cliff.
Text:
Review for a solo traveller.

Travel tips to reach Anuradhpura:
Colombo to Anuradhpura: Bus journey more than 200 plus km & 7 plus hours journey. Train option is also there. Train journey is more comfortable than bus.
Kandy to Anuradhpura: Bus journey more than 150 km more than 6 plus hours journey
Dambulla to Anuradhpura: Bus journey more than 70 km & more than 1 & half hour journey
Polonnaruwa to Anuradhpura: Bus journey more than 100 km & more than 1 & half hour journey

On reaching Anuradhpura one has to hire auto at negotiated price for sightseeing. Anything in the range of 1300 to 1800 LKR is the auto hire charges. Auto driver will ask you to pay him little more instead of buying entrance ticket assuring you managing with the ticket check points on the sightseeing route.

Entrance ticket is 1800 of Anuradhapura sightseeing if you produce original passport otherwise more than 2500 LKR. You will be provided with a CD. It will take 4 hours to see complete sightseeing of beautiful ancient ruins in Anuradhapura.

Isurumuniya Vihara will be 1 of the 10 spots of your Anuradhpura sightseeing tour. There is a cave, pond & small stoopa on a cliff. Entrance fee of LKR 200. 

Large idol of Buddha in a sleeping pose is in the cave alongwith other amazing sculptures. You are allowed to take photos of Buddha Idol & other sculptures. You are not allowed to take your own photo inside the cave.  

Sight of Buddha idol & other sculptures inside the cave is excellent. 

From the cliff top, one can see very beautiful scenery all around. 

On the back side of Isurumuniya temple there is a big serene lake at a 5 minutes walk. You have to come out, take left turn reach the corner of temple compound, again take left turn, walk for more than 50 metres, climb up the inclined steps & you are in front of a big lake.

See the attached photos.

Title: One of the oldest and most sacred of trees
Text:
One of the worldÂs oldest recorded trees and certainly the most revered, visited by buddhists from all around the world.  It is said to have grown from a cutting of the original tree under which the Buddha attained Enlightenment in India. The tree has been tended for 23 centuries and cuttings have been taken and planted in temples throughout the island. 

There is no entrance charge as far as we could tell but security here is tighter than at other attractions in Sri Lanka (a result of the bombings in 1998) and there separate lines for men and women. This is a sacred place so, as for all temples, you must dress respectfully (legs and shoulders covered).  You need to remove hats and shoes. You are allowed to keep socks on and I would recommend this as it is a bit of a walk to get to the tree at the centre of the complex.  

The site was very tranquil and it was interesting to visit for the history.  You need to bear in mind that you will not be able to get a close up view of the tree as it is enclosed by a wall and railings.  Only two branches of the original tree remain, and these are supported by props. This is the main reason we personally didn't feel able to score higher than a '3'.  Devotees on a pilgrimage will obviously feel very differently.

Title: My sight of the oldest living tree in the world, The Bodhi Tree of Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka.
Text:
I made an 8-day-trip to Sri Lanka from 8/11/12 to 15/11/12.  On my seventh day in Sri Lanka,  I arrived at the Anuradhapura Railway station at 4.30am.  Earlier, on my sixth day in Sri Lanka,i.e. 13/11/2012, I had boarded a 4.30pm-train from Hatton railway station to Colombo Fort Raiway station.  

Upon reaching Colombo at 10pm, I hopped into the 10.30pm train to the north of Colombo and reached Anuradhapura, one of the ancient capitals of Sri Lanka which is famous for its well-preserved ruins of ancient Sri Lankan civilization, at 4.30am, i.e. after a 12-hours-train-journey from Hatton. Anuradhapura is one of the ancient capitals of Sri Lanka, world famous for its well preserved ruins of the Great Sri Lankan Civilization. The Civilization which was built upon this city was one of the greatest civilizations of Asia and in the world. The city is now a UNESCO heritage site.  Today this ancient city of Sri Lanka, which is sacred to the Buddhist world, and which its surrounding monasteries covers an area of over sixteen square miles ( 40 kmÂ²) and is one of the world's major archaeological sites.

After a morning quick tour of the Ancient Ruins & Holy City of Anuradhapura, including Thuparamaya where the collarbone of Buddha is enshrined, Isurumuniya(a picturesque rock temple) and The Sacred Jaya Siri Maha Bodhi at Mahaviharaya/ Mahameghavana Park which is recorded as the oldest surviving historical tree in the world, I took a bus back to Colombo from Anuradhapura New Town at 1pm. 

The oldest surviving tree in the world, The Sacred Jaya Siri Maha Bodhi at Mahaviharaya/ Mahameghavana Park, Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka, is believed to have been propagated from the original Bodhi tree.  This original Bodhi Tree, also known as Bo (from the Sinhalese Bo), was a large and very old Sacred Fig tree (Ficus religiosa) located in Bodh Gaya (about 100 km (62 mi) from Patna in the Indian state of Bihar), under which Siddhartha Gautama, the spiritual teacher later known as Gautama Buddha, is said to have achieved enlightenment, or Bodhi.  According to Buddhist texts the Buddha, after his Enlightenment, spent a whole week in front of the tree, standing with unblinking eyes, gazing at it with gratitude.  The term "Bodhi Tree" is also widely applied to currently existing trees, including the Bodhi tree in Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka, which has a great significance in the history of Buddhism.  

This Bodhi tree in Anuradhapura is widely mentioned in Mahavamsa.  While not considered a canonical religious text, the Mahavamsa is an important text in Theravada Buddhism. It covers the early history of religion in Sri Lanka, beginning with the time of Siddhartha Gautama, the founder of Buddhism.  According to the Mahavamsa, the Sri Maha Bodhi in Sri Lanka was planted in 288 BC, making it the oldest verified specimen of any angiosperm. In this year (the twelfth year of King Asoka's reign) the right branch of the Bodhi tree was brought by Sanghamitt? to Anur?dhapura and placed by Dev?n?mpiyatissa his left foot in the Mah?meghavana. The Buddha, on his death bed, had resolved five things, one being that the branch which should be taken to Ceylon should detach itself. From Gay?, the branch was taken to P?taliputta, thence to T?malitt?, where it was placed in a ship and taken to Jambukola, across the sea; finally it arrived at Anuradhapura, staying on the way at Tivakka. Those who assisted the king at the ceremony of the planting of the Tree were the nobles of K?jarag?ma and of Candanag?ma and of Tivakka.  According to the Mahavamsa, branches from the Bodhi trees of all the Buddhas born during this kalpa were planted in Ceylon (Sri Lanka) on the spot where the sacred Bodhi tree stands today in Anur?dhapura.

Later, after completing my visit to the other attractions of the Ancient Ruins & Holy City of Anuradhapura I took a bus back to Colombo from Anuradhapura New Town at 1pm and reached the Pettah bus station in Colombo at 8pm to put-up a night at a nearby low cost lodge, i.e. Classic Inn in Panchikawatte Road before leaving for the Bandaranaike Airport at 6am of 15/11 to catch the 12.55pm flight back to Malaysia.

Title: Towering and impressive dagoba (ancient domed temple)
Text:
Let me first preface by saying Anuradhapura is a long distance to travel from the main coastal resorts and so you should probably only consider if you are touring the island.  It was about a two hour drive from Sigiriya.  The area is too big to cover on foot in a single day and, whilst bicycles and TukTuks are easy and cheap to hire, I would recommend a driver/guide who can direct you to and provide commentary on the most significant sites.  

The four main stupas (Jethawanaramaya/Jethavanarama, Rutwanwelisaya, Thuparama and Abhayaagiri) are all different.  You wonÂt need more than 10-15 minutes at each unless you want to stay to worship, We donÂt think there is any entrance charge Â we werenÂt asked for any money and there were no ticket checks. As for all temples, you must dress respectfully (legs and shoulders covered). You need to remove hats and shoes but you can wear socks which I would recommend as the stones underfoot can be hot and sharp.  

Of the four main stupas, we liked Jethawanaramaya/Jethavanarama the best.  At 400ft high with a 370ft diameter base on a 670ft square rock base, this is the largest stupa in Anuradpura  and one of the tallest brick structures in the world.  It was built in the 3rd century. The dome is unpainted. It was very quiet and tranquil. Once part of a huge monastery and you can see the ruins all around.  It is worth visiting the museum where you can see a good collection of guardstones and ancient jewellery.  There is a clean toilet here too.  

Rutwanwelisaya has a massive white painted dome. It is 180ft (used to be twice that).  It is surrounded by wall with over 300 elephant sculptures but almost all these are restored or replacements.  It can get busy with devotees coming to pray.  

Thuparama is the smallest and oldest of the main stupas in Anuradhapura (what you see is mainly reconstructed).  Its significance is that it is said to enshrine the collarbone of the Buddha and as such there are lots of pilgrims actively worshipping. A white dome surrounded by stone pillars which used to support a wooden cover.  

See separate review of Abhayaagiri.

Title: Once the Tallest Structure in the World after Pyramids
Text:
JETAVANA DAGOBA
The Jetavana Dagoba (Stupa), a UNESCO world heritage site, is the highest brick-built Dagobah in the world, founded by King Mahasena (276-303 AC) upon Mahayana Buddhism, on the ruins of an old monatery. When built with over 93 million bricks in 27 years, it was the third tallest structure in the world after two pyramids of Khufu & Khafra in Giza, Cairo (Egypt). Originally its height was 397 feet and it was erected on land measuring 8 acres. Its diameter was more than 330 feet. Today it is 230 feet high and restoration work is in progress. Title: Great views from the top, plan to avoid the heat
Text:
Unless you want to prove something to yourself, there is no need to climb all 1800+ steps. Ask your driver to take you up Old Road, which gets you almost halfway up. That leaves only a few hundred steps to climb. Bring water.

The ruins at the level of the ticket booth (at the end of Old Road, halfway up the hill) are good for a 15-minute walk-around. The stone canoe at the Âalms houseÂ is quite impressive. Apparently, lay people would fill this with rice as donation to the monks who lived here.

DonÂt miss the lion carved into the side of Lion Rock.

Up the hill, there are three peaks forming a triangle around a basin. The basin is not large -- little bigger than a football field. The lowest peak has an imposing modern statue of the Buddha Â very easy climb, but not much by way of views from there. The second peak has a huge white stupa; good views from there, especially of the other peaks. The tallest is a steep climb up bare rock (steps cut into the rock with handrails). Great views, but dangerously slippery if wet.

Because itÂs a sacred place, you have to take off your shoes as you approach the three peaks and basin. Wear old socks if youÂre not accustomed to walking on paving stones or sand that is frying-pan hot from the tropical sun. Even if not hot, the sharp grit underfoot makes it painful. 

Th historical significance of this place has to do with being where a king first accepted Buddhism.

Entry was 500 rupees. The site does not seem to have any cafe, toilet or shop selling water -- but then again, I didn't look that carefully.

Covering the upper steps and peaks leisurely takes only about 90 minutes. To escape the worst of midday sun, you can start the climb at 4pm and still have plenty of light when you reach the top. But there are plenty of shrine-caves and ruins in the area. If you are intent on visiting them, I think you will need an hour or two more, which means starting much earlier than 4pm. I didnÂt bother, as by this point in my visit to the country, IÂve had my fill of Buddhist places. 

My hotel arranged a tuktuk from Anuradhapura for 4 hours at a cost of 2,000 rupees (leaving little time for shrine-caves). ItÂs only 13km or 30 minutes journey time. The driver took me to a few other places before reaching the Mihintale peaks. One was a Âbig treeÂ monastery (nothing much to see except a big tree and a human skeleton); another was the site of a ÂhospitalÂ dated to about 800 CE (OK for a 10-minute walk-around); and the third was ÂBlack Water PoolÂ (more ruins, so-so views).

If your hotel does not offer such a service, itÂs still very easy to hire a tutktuk from anywhere in Anuradhapura for 3 to 4 hours for a similar price.

Title: Where Buddhism started in Sri Lanka
Text: A beautiful and serene place where Mahinda, son of the Indian King Asoka, converted King Devanampiya Tissa to Buddhism in 3rd century BC. This "sacred Hill of Mihintale" is less visited than the sites of Polonnaruwa and Anuradhapura, but should be a must see because of its history, scenery and serenity. Visit in the morning preferably as it gets very hot. No shoes allowed. The visit should take a couple of hours with a good guide. For the more daring, a climb to Aradhana Gala (Meditation Rock) is worth the effort (it is very steep on narrow steps - remove your socks if you kept them as the steps carved out of the rock can be slippery). From the top, the view over the plain, the Dagoba and the Buddha statue is breathtaking.

We were advised to take a lunch, which sounded like a great idea, but as soon as we sat down about 20 aggressive moneys appeared, growling and grabbing.  We quickly left, climbed 500 steps and found a security guard sitting in a big cage behind the ticket office. He kindly allowed us to eat our lunch inside the cage while money's drooled outside. 
We appreciated visiting Minhintale for very little money, but, removing ones shoes and hats ( out of respect for the Buddha), then walking over scorched hot sand and rock, seemed pointless while stepping over plastic bags and litter.
After spending 3 hot dry days in Anuradhapura, we jumped off the Cultural Triangle Trail and are spending the rest of our days at the Beach.  
While Sri Lanka is a lovely country with lovely people, if you want to see ruins, go to Angkor Wat or Myanmar.

Title: Pilgrimage Site
Text: This cultural site holds significant Buddhism history in Sri Lanka. Anuradhapura was the first historical capital of Sri Lanka and today is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (part of the Cultural Triangle), often on the touristic routes. 

Dating back to 380AD, the site contains ancient ruins, dagobas and temples, all "contained" in an archaeological park.
You will need to organise transport to explore them as I think there is simply too much distance to cover by foot. 
The most common options are either by tuk tuk or by bicycle.

In my opinion, in general, the whole site is pretty disappointing.

Unfortunately, not worth it from my point of view

USEFUL INFO
Entry ticket to the site: 25,00 USD per person (only cash)
Journey time from Sigiriya by tuk tuk: around 1h30mins

PRO TIP
Since it is a religious site still in use today, please bear in mind that everybody is asked to dress properly (shoulders and knees must be covered, and shoes and hats must be removed).
Because of the latter, I highly suggest to carry also a pair of socks into your bag as sometimes the ground can be very warm/hot.

It is the physical exertion on your body to reach the highest point.  It is the tranquility of the landscape that these sights are built around.  It is the bewilderment of the age of the relics and the size in which some have been made.  It is the sights of monkeys behaving like this is their home.  It is the noise of traditional music as an organ may be playing if you were to visit a Cathedral.  It is the gentle murmurs of worship coming from peoples prayers.  It is the shade of the tree whether it be regarded as holy or not.  It is the smell of incense and the sight of flowers given as a gift.  It is the welcoming smiles of the Sri Lankan people who are happy to include you here regardless of your religion.

It is something you do and recommend you do when you are visiting another country.

Appropriate dress for all Buddhist temples includes no hats or shoes.We were asked to wear long trousers, but as it's very hot and you're often travelling elsewhere, I would say that zip off trousers for men are really useful. Ladies - knees must be covered , crops were fine and some other tourists wore a sarong to cover their shorts whilst visiting. Another reviewer has mentioned the heat of the paving you have to walk on with bare feet.We were there late morning and the paving  ( and there's a lot of it!) was red hot - so hot that we were hopping from one foot to another trying to avoid burning our feet. Little trainer socks are invaluable!! It's quite acceptable to wear them and your feet don't burn. All stupas / temples require shoes to be removed (there's always someone to look after them for you for a very small sum) but some are surrounded by large gritty areas and those little socks are great!
It's a wonderful country - so many great sights and lovely people!

Also to be visited on the site is the Sri Maha Bohdi Â apparently one of the worldÂs oldest and most revered trees.

We attended on a Sunday which due to the siteÂs highly religious importance meant it was very crowded with pilgrims. Whenever you choose, Anuradhapura is certainly worth seeing.

Title: Magnificent Buddha Vihara
Text:
RUWANWELISAYA DAGOBAH
Ruwanwelisaya is an awe inspiring Dagobah of magnificent architectural style, built during the reign of King Dutugemunu (140 BC). The Dagobah has circumference of 950 feet and height of 338 feet. In 19th century AD, this Dagobah was nothing more than ruins of a magnificent structure. In 20th century, it was renovated and restored with local donations and assistance from UNESCO. It is now a World Heritage Site.
A Dagobah is a sacred place of veneration. Generally it is a shrine like domed structure in which are placed relics related to Buddha, Buddhism or remains of Buddhist monks and nuns. The place is also used for meditation and worship. It is also called Stupa, Pagoda or Chedi.

Title: Beware of tuk tuk drivers!
Text:
Mine is intended to be a general review about my trip to Anuradhapura. The archeological area to visit is really huge. You can see many beautiful stupas like Ruwanwelisaya and many other things. If you want to visit the area in the matter my suggestion is to rent a bike. If you think of walking only you are going to miss many things also because you cannot find many signs. Another way to move around is by tuk tuk. You can bargain the price and get a full service at a reasonable price. 1500 rupees is a good deal. However you need to be aware of tuk tuk drivers. I would say that 99% of tuk tuk drivers are really nice but black sheep are behind the corner. The price of the ticket to enter Anuradhapura archeological area is pretty expensive. More precisely it costs 4600 rupees. A ticket is made of three stubs that need to be torn off every time you enter one of the three areas. There are some tuk tuk drivers who might ask you to give them your ticket so that they can show it to the surveillance staff in order to enter the area. If they ask for your ticket, DO NOT give it to them. The ticket belongs to you. It doesn't belong to the tuk tuk drivers. The point is that there are some tuk tuk drivers who take their customers tickets just to show them what they want to show. They aim at ending their trip with the customers asap so that they can start a new trip with other tourists who will be sold the same tickets partly used by the previous tourists.To cut it short tuk tuk drivers resell those tickets to other tourists at a reduced price and take the money deriving from the sell. 
So be careful. I also want to give some quick information on how to arrive in Anuradhapura if you come from Dambulla.
Dambulla is a small city. There is not bus station but of course there are bus stops. The one where you can catch the bus to Anuradhapura is on Kandy road (the main road) 200 meters after the clock tower on your left next to Bata shoe shop. The bus numbers to consider are 15 and 43.
If you wanna go to Polonnaruwa from Dambulla the bus stop is the same. The bus number is either 41 or 48. 
Hope these suggestions are of help.

Title: What a day to visit
Text:
Having been to Mihintale in the morning, the best was left to the afternoon. Shoes off again and we walked a long way without them, so wear thick socks as the ground is hot, although there are areas where they have laid astro which is easy to walk on. Entry was 9500 rupees which covered the different sites in Anuradhapura.

We came on a national holiday, Makarsankranti/Pongal, and thousands of buddhists from as far away as Colombo will come for the day as this is the most significant temple in Sri Lanka. It is reputedly built with 100 million bricks and the original temple was built in 140BC. Over time it has had to be rebuilt as at one time it was a ruin in the 19th century and it was rebuilt to twice the original size and completed in 1940. It is 103 metres high and 290 metres in circumference. Stupas were built to enshrine relics of Buddha

Most people were dresses in white and families were there as well. There was incense pervading the atmosphere and people were buying flowers and gifts to be left by the temple. People were praying near the temple and it was so peaceful even with so many people (not many Europeans visit here and they are really missing out).  There was a procession of people making their way to the temple and a bolt of cloth in bright red was gradually unwound as people took hold of the cloth so the cloth procession just got longer and longer as more people joined it. Just an amazing place to visit and a wonderful day.

Title: Don't just visit the stupa, wander about the nearby ruins too
Text:
The Abhayagiri Dagoba is a huge brick stupa built slightly over 2,000 years ago, and for centuries after that, served as the focal point of an expansive monastery complex, stretching for hectares around.  Other than sheer size, the stupa itself isnÂt much to see -- though you should spend some time contemplating its age and the feat of construction it represented for its time -- but the parkland around is chockful of ruined foundations of all sorts of buildings.

The stupa/dagoba  was the focal centre of a major monastic complex, said to once have housed and served 5,000 monks. Today, itÂs a shady area with mature trees, with hardly anyone else around, so itÂs a pleasant stroll wandering around the ruins. As bonus, I saw three wild peacocks strutting around the site too.

Not so pleasant were inquisitive monkeys and wild dogs.

Also, sun block cream and insect repellent would be handy.

Among the ruins to the east, a short walk away leads you to a lovely piece of sculpture called the Samadhi Buddha. More ruins can be found to the west of the stupa; these ruins (ÂRatnaprasadaÂ) once housed the more ascetic monks. To the northwest of the stupa is the most elaborately-carved ÂmoonstoneÂ in Anuradhapura -- a ÂmoonstoneÂ is a stone slab placed before a set of steps.

ItÂs interesting to try to imagine the hustle and bustle that once characterised this site, with monks chanting prayers, debating sacred texts, and lay people presenting donations. No doubt it was also a location for political intrigue since organised religion was closely intertwined with government in those times. I also wondered what sort of economy could support such a large number of monks.

But today, itÂs a tranquil, relaxing parkland.

About 300 Â 400m south of Abhayagiri Dagoba is the Abhayagiri Museum. See my review of it under that name.

The stupa, museum and ruins around are all within the paid area of Anuradhapura's ÂSacred City/Ancient RuinsÂ archaeological park. However, tickets to the Archaeological park can only be purchased from the Archaeological Museum (not to be confused with the Abhayagiri Museum) located about 2 km south (ridiculous!) of the Abhayagiri Dagoba. Cost = US$25, or 3,780 Sri Lankan rupees and valid only for the same day.

General info about places in the ÂSacred City/Ancient RuinsÂ park: The sights are quite spread out such that while walking from one sight to the second may be possible, covering many more on foot is impractical. YouÂll need a map and a bicycle or tuktuk hired for the day. Also, there few toilets, and few places to buy water, though there is at least one rustic shop near the Abhayagiri Dagoba that has cold drinking water for sale.

Title: Exquiste moonstone and guardstone - best in the area

Let me first preface by saying Anuradhapura is a long distance to travel from the main coastal resorts and so you should probably only consider if you are touring the island.  It was about a two hour drive from Sigiriya.  The area is too big to cover on foot in a single day and, whilst bicycles and TukTuks are easy and cheap to hire, I would recommend a driver/guide who can direct you to and provide commentary on the most significant sites.  

Abhayaagiri was a complex of monastic buildings founded in the first or second century BC. It is still being uncovered and restored.  The stupa is huge (230fit high and very similar to Jethavanarama) but as it still under renovation there is lots of scaffolding.   The grounds are the main attraction. The Twin Bathing Pools (Kottum Putan) are very tranquil and worth a 5-10 minute stop as itÂs a great example of the amazing engineering and water management that was typical across ancient Sri Lanka.  Here solid stone was carved out to create two large pools used by thousands of monks for bathing. Elsewhere across the island earth was excavated on an even larger scale to create huge water tanks which were used for feeding crops as well as bathing. 

If you are in the area I would recommend that you also visit the ruins of King MahasenÂs Palace to see an exquisite example of a moonstone doorstep with finely detailed symbolic carvings; the Ratnaprasada (Gem Place) for the guardstone; and the Mahapali Refectory with its huge rice trough and bathing pools.

Title: Marvelous Buddha Statue
Text:
SAMADHI BUDDHA
Samadhi Buddha is a statue of Mahatma Buddha in Mahameghawana (also called Mahamevnawa) Park in the midst of ancient city of Anuradhapura, near Abhayagiri Monastery. This statue shows Buddha in the posture of Dhiyan Mudra. It was found at the present place in 1886, fallen on the ground with damaged nose. It was then repaired and erected.

Title: Historic Buddhist Temple
Text:
Also known as Kelaniya Temple is a Buddhist temple, with a history believed to be dated back to before 500 BC, located in Kelaniya, Sri Lanka, a few miles from Colombo. It is believed by the devotees that the temple was constructed during the third and final visit of the Lord Buddha to Sri Lanka which occurred eight years after Lord Budda was said to have gained enlightenment. 

Mahawansa records specify that the original Stupa, situated beside the main temple,  enshrined a gem-studded throne on which the Buddha sat and preached.  The temple is well-known for its reclining Buddha and the paintings, very detailed in brilliant colors, which adore the interior walls of the temple which depict events in the life of the Buddha in Sri Lanka and events that took place in the Jataka tales.  Although it can be crowded mid-day you gain more knowledge of the temple grounds because of all of the activities that take place during the day.  There are a group of monks that live on the temple grounds who will be observed monitoring the activities and offering blessings to the devotees that are on the ground to pray and pay respects.  Plan on spending about one hour on the grounds in order to view all of the important activities and structures.  You will be required to remove your shoes to walk around the grounds.  If your feet are tender at least wear socks for your walk around the stone or sand filled payment.  Stairs are minimal.

Title: A must visit holy site in Colombo
Text:
This is a temple once visited by Buddha himself and so of very high value to Sri Lankans. Located about 9 Kas from central Colombo, I ended up going there taking Uber for about 750 ruppi, not a bad price. 

It was first day of the year and so temple was full of prayers who usually frequent religious places on this special day. It covers a big land space with many building, the most prominent of which is a temple with beautiful wall paintings and a reclining Buddha, a smaller version from the one in Bangkok. 

Other buildings include some featuring relics such as Buddha hair preserved in a golden jar behind glass, and lots of meditation spots. They even had a building where kids were performing dances etc. place was very crowded because it was first day of year but I can imagine how it can be peaceful on other days.

Other main features was a huge tree which worshippers were queueing around to water. Meant to originate from a branch of a tree that Buddha grew in India, and also a big white dome with many Buddha statues around.

Like all Buddhist temples shoes have to be taken off on site; however sand was quite rough and so were the rocks and so my advice is sacrifice an old pair of socks and put them on to walk around with.

People are very friendly inside and will not treat you with coldness or aggression because you are a foreigner.

I could fee a general ambiance of safety there, and didn't feel there were people attempting to pick pocket or invoke trouble despite the big numbers around.

One restaurant about 2 kms away from temple called Seth, is run by a family and supposed to serve delicious local food. Sadly it closes at 3 pm and was closed by the time I got there. Check its details on trip advisor.

This temple is a must if you are in Colombo and like to explore Buddhist. Culture in Sri Lanka, enjoy!

Title: A complex of temples and little museums worth a visit in Colombo
Text: Gangaramaya temple is surprising, to say the least. To start with the fact that it is a complex of temples, museums and open areas for praying, not just a single temple. Some of them are, for a non-Buddhist like me, more like Hinduist, with images of Vishnu, Ganesh and other Hindu deities abundant in some of the temples. There are many Buddha statues in all sorts of sizes, materiais and forms. The jade Buddha is beautiful. There is also a relic - a hair from Buddha - that was given to the temple by BangladeshÂs government. There is a sacred tree inside the complex, a huge Fig Tree, and that area, with many people praying, is very peaceful. There is also a replica of Borobudur, the huge Buddhist complex from Java, very interesting. It is definitely worth a visit if you are in Colombo.

Title: One of the Best places to visit in Colombo
Text: Located on the Beira Lake, Gangaramaya temple is built in an unusual mix of Indian, Thai, Chinese and Sri Lankan architectural styles. Text: Gangaramaya Temple is Sri Lanka's most important Buddhist site. It is centered around a tree that is said to have grown from a cutting of the Bodhi Tree in India, under which Siddhartha Gotama (the Buddha) is said to have meditated for 49 days before receiving enlightenment. The temple features a large Buddha statue flanked by smaller statues of followers, a variation we have not seen before; it strikes us as a nod to the Hindu temples with their many colorful figures. The temple complex is also a museum, with its attractions designed to draw in visitors who will make donations. There is a seated figure carved from ruby. Copper wall panels depicting Buddhist themes are a feature we've seen nowhere else. There are even worldly goods like vintage Rolls-Royces, donated to the temple by believers.

Title: Treasure trove for history buffs and relic hunters
Text:
While this is called a buddhist temple, it is more a collection of all sorts of relics and antiquities. It ranges from statues to stuffed elephants, watches, cars, ivory and even has Lord Buddha's original hair!!

If you are into that sort of stuff, you will spend a long time here as there is just too much to see and it is just lying around. They have not organised it very well and you will need to take your time to find what you are looking for.

Must not miss - Lord Buddha's hair, world's smallest Buddha statue, huge ivory tusks (hard to miss), 14kg solid ruby Buddha statue, Rolls Royce cars, ancient manuscripts.

Be warned that men and women alike need to cover their shoulders and wear trousers covering their knees. If you are not dressed appropriately then the temple will offer you shawls that you can use to wrap around yourself once you pay the entrance fee.

Also, while photos are allowed, it is considered rude to take selfies as your back will be towards Buddha.
