We joined the queues during morning prayer. There are two queues to get in: one for the men and one for the women. Like most things in life, the men's line moved faster. This is mainly due to two things: 1) most women carry bags that need searching (most men don't) 2) the women perhaps face a little more scrutiny over what they can wear and must cover-up. Shoulders and legs need to be covered, so make sure you have a light scarf and sarong. Men too should carry a sarong to put on although some western males it seemed were managing to get through in shorts.

Once inside make sure you follow the tourist crowds to the right and enter the temple through the tourist entry. Here you leave your shoes, you will be expected to tip after collection. 

Inside, at prayer, this place is busy. At times you are moved along with the crowd. The locals are of course queuing to leave gifts and to pray so don't feel too bad if you 'skip' queues and glide past those locals waiting on the stairs.

The relic itself can't be seen. Instead, you can peer into the golden shrine where it is stored, but at this point in the temple, the crowds are at their busiest so you main only manage a cursory glance.

The best part about the temple is exploring the grounds and additional rooms and buildings. The carvings and sculptures of Budha are beautiful, and in most spaces, you can take photos. Just be mindful of people worshipping and not to take pictures with your back to any Budha statue.

The grounds of the temple are beautiful, and there is an elephant on the site too, which is used in ceremonies. Although, it is clearly an old elephant and seeing it so heavily chained doesn't make for the best view.

At night time, around the temple and Lake, there is a cacophony of noise as bats and birds come to roost in their hundreds. It is the most spectacular site in Kandy and a must-see.

The museum of World Buddhism, which is on the site is also worth a visit, and with a tourist ticket to the temple, you have access.

Location_Name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
Title: Interesting Cultural Site
Text: This is another UNESCO World Heritage Site with interesting history and background. The site is located in city centre of Kandy right in front of Kandy Lake. Tooth Relic is believed to be sacred for Buddhism and the royal family was responsible for the safekeeping of the tooth relic. It is believed to be brought from Anuradhapura to Kandy Kingdom. Two storeys building was constructed for safekeeping the tooth relic. But the building was destroyed several times. Each time it was restored whenever it was destroyed. There will be ceremony everyday for the blessings by the devotees. We visited around late afternoon and waited for the ceremony around 6pm plus. Interesting cultural sights, but be prepared for uncontrollable crowds and haphazard situation during the ceremony. The tooth relic is said to be kept within a gold plated ornament, hence it cannot be seen by anyone even during the ceremony. The international Buddhism Museum within the compound is worth to check out too for the interesting architecture and interior design. Overall, it is still worth the entrance fee of LKR1,500 per person and appropriate attire is required and tight security check at the entrance.

Location_Name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
Title: Not really worth it
Text:
We are a couple in early 30s with 9 and 10yr old daughters.
Firstly we hadn't dressed appropriately so had to rent sarongs to cover up. The guy was nice enough but still 400rs down.
It's a bit of a faff to get in, we went through one lot if security then you get your bag checked again before you go in. We had a tip off from the sarong guy that they take away your cigarettes and lighters so I hid them well in the bag.
You have to put your shoes in a shoe storage area. Other reviews are correct about them asking for a donation, I was aware of this and just played deaf when they asked me, I had to assist my child... Oh and don't think you can put your shoes in your bag - that's not allowed! 
The ticket machines don't give change so you do have to have the right amount on you. There was an attendant who said we didn't have to pay for the children which was good and we didn't have the right change but he helped a guy behind us which then gave us the right change. So that was kind.

First off you walk on boiling hot pavement in bear feet. Then I guess the rest is interesting if you like architecture and religious history. As atheists we were a little bemused by all of it. There's nothing to tell you where the tooth is. We assumed we were in the right place by the people praying on the floor... But there's no signs etc and we didn't have a guide.
There's a museum which was a little interesting.
The saddest part is the taxidermied elephant. Poor thing was captured and kept for a good 50years before he died. He's now stuffed in a glass cabinet. There's a photo timeline of his life since capture but it doesn't have any translation so we don't really know the story...

If you like this sort if thing and are in Kandy then maybe pay it a visit... But I definitely wouldn't drive to Kandy for a day trip just for that. In my husbands words "I wouldn't go again even if it was outside my front door".

Location_Name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
Title: Crowded but worth it
Text:
Get your information and timing right if you wish to visit this ancient and holy place. The door to the main relic is opened at specific timings, so check before you plan your trip. While the doors to the main shrine are closed, the crowds start building up, so if crowds scare you this place is an absolute no. Although the crowds are quite well behaved. 
Be sure to cover your shoulders and legs else shell out money to locals for giving you wraps etc. 
You need to buy tickets at the entrance from kiosks which need exact change. You will need to remove and deposit shoes at the counters outside. Once inside it gives you the feel of an ancient place but well preserved and maintained. Lots of devotees with offerings throng the temple every day. 
Do not miss the oil lamps lighted outside by numerous devotees. You are allowed to take pictures but take care not to have your back towards the main shrine - else you will be asked to delete them by the vigilant guards.

Location_Name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
Title: Temple of Lord Buddha 's sacred tooth relic at Kandy, Sri Lanka
Text:
Considered as a sacred temple complex containing the sacred tooth relic of Lord Buddha, Shri Dalada Maligawa also known as Palace of sacred tooth.

This temple is a must visit for every Buddhist.

The tooth relic was originally housed in a rock carved temple in Anuradha pura before it was moved to the present palace / temple at Kandy about five hundred years ago.

This centuries old temple is serene and the worshippers pray in silence.

The temple was originally built as a royal residential palace by the royal family of Sri Lanka long time ago.

The remarkable features of this temple is the renowned recital of Kandy drums is a joy to hear.

The musical performance is unique for Sri Lanka.The musical instruments are two drums and a pipe instrument. The performance lasting about half an hour is precisely choreographed.

The puja timings are fixed  lasting about half an hour three times in a day - morning, noon and evening.

The temple premises are very well secured and spotless maintenance is visible everywhere.

You need to be properly dressed to enter the temple. Ensure that your shoulder and knees are covered.

The temple management treats every body equal. No preference seems to be given for any one. There is no shouting at or pushing of the pilgrims in the sanctum sanctorium. Everything is done in dignified silence.

The temple is a must visit while you are in Kandy, Sri Lanka.

Highly recommended.

We visited this temple as part of a G Adventures tour in the evening when the doors of the area where the casket that houses the tooth relic is open,  This allows the locals as well as the tourists to see this casket.  

Due to problems with possible terrorists, there are high security measures taken before you can enter the temple.  You must also be appropriately dressed with women wearing clothes that cover their shoulders and knees and men should wear full length pants.  Most of the locals wear complete white outfits to show their respect when visiting the temple.

It is a very busy in this temple and you cannot wear your shoes in it.  I had a guide help me through the temple, which I would not have been able to do if he had not helped me up and down the numerous stairs you need to use to see the entire temple.  

The museum that is attached to the temple was also interesting to see as it held many sacred texts about Buddha's life.

Title: Stunning UNESCO Religious Centre
Text:
It was early evening when we arrived at the temple of five caves of varying size and interior dated 1st BC.

There are more than 80 caves in the area with the 5 caves most worth viewing. The first king turned the caves into a temple complex and many kings added to it later until the 11th century. It is still a functioning temple complex till this day.

The spectacular murals on the ceilings were of sheer magnificence. They depicted BuddhaÂs life and sermons. 

The guide pointed out the large statue of the reclining Buddha on his deathbed judging by the way the feet was displayed. Stupas, a hundred small Buddha statues, some gods and goddesses and kings statues were on display. 

One of the five caves was under repair, and we managed to take a quick look of it. The second cave was the largest and most impressive.

They say you must never turn your back to the Buddha when taking a photo. I felt intense spiritual power in these ancient caves and decided against taking any pictures out of respect.

There was a small basin with water dripping down from the ceiling that the guide said would never dry up and have healing powers.

Once out of the temple caves we realised how the temple was cut out of a massive overhanging rock. We went under a huge Bodhi tree and made a wish. It was just too bad we could not find time to see the ancient Bodhi tree at Anuradhapura. 

A very moving spiritual experience indeed.

Title: Well worth the climb; a must-do visit
Text:
The climb up the steps to the temple offers some wonderful views including a panorama of Lion Rock and Pidurangala Rock.  It is steep in places, so take some water with you; there's nowhere to buy any at the top!

You need to leave your shoes (100 Rps per person) and entry to the temple complex is 1500 Rps each. Remember to dress appropriately for visiting a temple.

There are 5 caves; the newest being the furthest away.  Perhaps worth starting here and working back as the older caves have the better workmanship.  The statues and wall paintings are very impressive. You can get up close; which is maybe not such a good thing given the age of some of the caves.

There is little (or no) information whilst walking around.  If you are touring Sri Lanka with a guide, then not a problem as the guide will relay the important information.  Otherwise read up beforehand as part of what makes it really impressive is the knowledge that some parts are over 2000 years old!

The whole visit only takes an hour or so.  For us it was a really convenient stopping off point on the drive between Kandy and Habarana (where we based ourselves to see Lion Rock, Minneriya and Polonnaruwa)

Title: A small but unique cave temple complex
Text:
Having been to a large number of buddist temple sites in SE Asia - including other cave temples - I found Dambulla interesting and beautiful but not entirely unique. If you have not been to many other places that are similar it is definitely a must visit. Otherwise, I'd recommend it if you have time and interest in this type of attraction but I would not rearrange my schedule to fit it in.

The caves themselves are not very large and are quite warm inside. The walls and ceilings are painted and beautiful to look at - more so then the Buddhas in my opinion. The lighting is ROUGH for photography unless you have specialized equipment. The caves are dark with spotlights in various areas. This makes the location less of an Instagram-worthy location if that's your thing but most people should enjoy the sights just fine. 

I'd recommend going first thing in the morning to avoid crowds and to avoid the heat. The caves were already hot at 8 am so I can't imagine what it gets like later in the day. Also be prepared to climb stairs to get there. About 365 of them. Its steep and while I thought it was worth the cardio workout - someone who is out of shape or who has impaired mobility may not be able to make it.

Tips:

- don't forget to wear long pants and tops with shoulders covered. Men included. or bring a sarong to wrap around if you have shorts on. 

- This is a Buddhist temple so you need to leave your shoes near the entrance (there is a safe location to do so) and walk around barefoot. You will be walking on stone/concrete. 

- With the climb up and plenty of time spent in each cave we did the whole thing in 1.5 hours. 

- There is plenty of parking and clean bathrooms at the bottom of the stairs for public use.

Title: Very beautiful and definitely worth a visit!

Once you climb the steps and reach the top, the view is absolutely beautiful! There is a place to store your footwear near the cave complex just besides the entrance.

The caves themselves are very beautiful and I would recommend that you take your best night/low light photography equipment you have. The paintings on the top of the caves are very colorful and detailed and you would definitely want to take a few shots of these pictures. The statues of the Buddha's in various poses are a real sight to see. The cave complex itself is very well maintained and shouldn't take you more than 50-60 minutes to complete.

TIP: if you plan to visit the Temple complex during the evening I would highly recommend a torch light and some mosquito repellent. It can get very dark once the sun sets and there were many mosquitos on the way down mainly because of the surrounding forests.

This place is definitely worth a visit with family and friends.

Title: Dambulla Cave Temple: Ancient Art and Stunning Views
Text:
The Dambulla Cave Temple, also known as the Golden Temple of Dambulla, is a must-visit attraction when traveling to Sri Lanka. Located just 10 minutes away from Dambulla village, the temple can be easily reached by bus or tuk-tuk. The Dambulla Temple is divided into two parts: the temple cave and the golden Buddha. It's important to note that if you want to see the golden Buddha, you should not go back to the main entrance. Instead, continue on to the lower level of the temple, where the golden Buddha is located.

Inside the temple cave, visitors will be amazed by the intricate and well-preserved ancient cave paintings and statues of the Buddha. The peaceful atmosphere of the temple is truly awe-inspiring, and visitors can take their time to explore the cave and take in the stunning surroundings.

Overall, the Dambulla Cave Temple is an unforgettable experience that shouldn't be missed when visiting Sri Lanka. The climb to the temple may be a bit challenging, but the reward of exploring this sacred and historical site, along with the breathtaking views of the mountains, is worth the effort.

The 5 temples are cut into the side of the rock - put there by different kings across time, to show their devotion to Buddhism. Do beware of the "guides" that will talk you through the first cave and then offer to take you around the others in return for payment - you can just say no and they will leave you alone.

Title: A MUST TO VISIT IF YOU IN DAMBULLA
Text:
Dambulla cave temple also known as the Golden Temple of Dambulla is a World Heritage Site in Sri Lanka. The largest and best-preserved cave temple complex major attractions are spread over five caves, which contain statues and paintings. These paintings and statues are related to Gautama Buddha and his life. There are a total of 153 Buddha statues, three statues of Sri Lankan kings and four statues of gods and goddesses. The latter include Vishnu and the Ganesha. The murals cover an area of 2,100 square metres. Depictions on the walls of the caves include the temptation by the demon Mara, and Buddha's first sermon.

And in 1956, in an underwater exploration , the old temple ruins were found, Besides a lot of inscriptions about the temple etc were also discovered . All the bits and pieces dicovered were put together and now a grand temple is there once again for us to worship.
A great work of reconstruction of the temple as well as the history.
The temple is sung about gloriously by the great poet saints. Sambandhar and Arunagirinathar. 
the Pandya Chola and Chera kings of south India  were said to have patronized and visited the temple.The Vilva tree is the Sacred tree of this temple.
In 2013, when the civil works were undertaken for the temple, a beautiful Nandhi idol was discovered and it was found to belong to 11th Centurt AD.
People believe that there many be many more to be excavated.
The temple is also a seat of Sakthi Peetam, where the feet of the Amman were supposed to have been assocoated.

Title: Most Tranquil Poetic Place
Text:
I spent a few hours up at Koneswaram Temple which is only a five minute bicycle ride from me. It stood here since 400 BC, one of the sacred sites for Hindus, and is mentioned in Mahabharata. I wasnÂt looking for the temple, just felt like climbing up above the ocean, but there it was.

You will be given a piece of fabric to wrap around your deliciously brown knees if you happen to wear shorts. It is free, give it back on return. You will need to take off your shoes and leave them in the box rack. Walk barefoot on the baking hot slab stones and sand of the main approach. It will make you hop and run into the shade of temple real fast.

I loved being up there. It sits atop the Swami rock over the Ocean into the vertigenous cliffs, the crows fly between the columns, there is an air of gentle decay, abandonment and a spirit of generations who lived, believed, perished; nothing, but a fairytale left. The breeze from the ocean sings in the ears, and a giant statue of Golden Shiva gazes past you into the distance of the harbour. So peaceful, no crowds, no tourists. I shudder to think about this becoming like the Pyramids. When I saw those at 25, I wanted to cry.. from a shrill sense of impossibility to be one to one with eternityÂ bloody crowds, and sure I was one of them too.

A Temple worker perceptively told me ÂYou love it here, donÂt you.. come any timeÂ. Title: Visiting the Siva Ishwarams (Pancha Ishwarams) in Sri Lanka.
Text:
Visiting the Siva Ishwarams (Pancha Ishwarams) in Sri Lanka.

The reunion with relatives in Jaffna took us to four of the Siva Temples in Sri Lanka during the first seven days of our Sri Lanka Odyssey.

Our first stop, on March 3rd, was at the Munneswaram temple situated in a village in the Puttalam District. Hindus believe that it is one of the the five temples they need to visit in their life time. The others being Naguleswaram temple which we visited in Keerimalai in the Kankesanthurai district on March 4th and Thiruketheeshwaram in Mannar District and the Koneswaram temple in Trincomalee (Thirukonamalai) -- both the next day.

All these, including Rameswaram in India form the five ancient temples (Ishwarams) dedicated to Shiva.

According to Hindus, the Munneswaram temple near Puttalam is the temple where King Rama prayed to Shiva after killing Ravana to seek forgiveness over the death of many in the war.

Hindus believe that the Naguleswaram temple's adjacent water tank, the Keerimalai Springs, has curative properties. The temple was largely destroyed by Jesuit missionaries following the Portuguese conquest of the Jaffna kingdom, restored by Arumuga Navallar in 1894.

The Thiruketheeshwaram temple had existed for more than 2,400 years. During our visit to this temple, we witnessed a temple devotee from Vavunia singing Thevarams. His aim was to complete the 800 thurmurai thevarams in one month.

The Trincomelee Koneswaram temple was built by the Cholas/Pandian kings. The temple is situated atop Konesar Malai, at a commanding position overlooking the Indian Ocean. It is also known as the "Mount Kailash of the South".

The temple, mentioned in Mahabaratha and Ramayana, was visited by Arunagirinathar and is the easternmost shrine of the five ancient Ishwarams of Shiva on the island.

Title: Fantastic visit to our first Hindu Temple. Nallur Kandaswamy temple
Text:
We were not sure of procedure or how to approach our visit to this temple.  However, we did our research and donned a sarong to cover our lower half.  The Hindu Temple Nallur Kandaswamy temple is situated in the not so tourist area of Jaffna. Visitors before entering the Temple complex must remove their shoes; men need to remove their shirts as well.  

The Temple is about 1.5km northeast of the centre. It is exceptionally beautifully colourful, as one would expect from a Hindu Temple dedicated to sacred deity is Lord Murugan (or Skanda).  

One thing that struck me was the friendliness of the devotees and visitors entering the Temple complex.  Even though we could not speak Tamil or Sinhalese the people actually pushed us into places where we could view the ceremony of the "Puja" and then took us by hand to the following 3 or 4 places so as we could be and feel integrated into the ceremonial process. 

In western religions it's normally first come first served and you're pushed out of the way by the surge of petitions and penitents trying to gain a favour or miracle from the devotion.  But here the people were so keen for us to see the adoration of their gods and the ceremony unfold that we were at times led by the hand to "the next installment" - for want of a better phrase.  

Then once the ceremony had finished we wandered around the Temple complex and some visitors - from the southern part of India,  took us to one side and helped us understand what we had just witnessed  

Several friendly priests, some of whom speak English, can answer questions about the temple and its traditions. Do go to this and any Temple that you find near you on your visits and be inspired and blessed as we were that day at The Nallur Kandaswamy Temple.

Striking are the two newer gopurams on the north and south completed recently.  to enter the temple you must go barefooted and males must be bare waist up. No photography.
